Code
# ── Visual Intuition: How KNN Classifies a New Point ─────────────────────────
# We'll plot a tiny 2D toy dataset and manually show how KNN works for K=3

# Training data: two classes (red = 0, blue = 1)
red_pts  <- rbind(c(1, 2), c(2, 1), c(1.5, 3), c(2.5, 2), c(3, 1))
blue_pts <- rbind(c(6, 7), c(7, 6), c(5, 6.5), c(6.5, 5), c(7.5, 7))

# The mystery point we want to classify
query <- c(4, 5)

all_pts    <- rbind(red_pts, blue_pts)
all_labels <- c(rep(0, 5), rep(1, 5))
dists      <- sqrt(rowSums(sweep(all_pts, 2, query, "-")^2))
ord        <- order(dists)
k_nearest_idx <- ord[1:3]   # K=3

plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, 9), ylim = c(0, 9), xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = "Feature 2", main = "")

points(red_pts,  col = "tomato",    pch = 16, cex = 2)
points(blue_pts, col = "steelblue", pch = 16, cex = 2)
points(query[1], query[2], col = "gold", pch = 8, cex = 3, lwd = 2)

# Draw lines to K=3 nearest neighbours
for (i in k_nearest_idx) {
  col <- if (all_labels[i] == 0) "tomato" else "steelblue"
  lines(c(query[1], all_pts[i, 1]), c(query[2], all_pts[i, 2]), lty = 2, col = col, lwd = 1.8)
}

# Draw the circle that just reaches the 3rd neighbour
r <- dists[k_nearest_idx[3]]
symbols(query[1], query[2], circles = r, add = TRUE, inches = FALSE, fg = "purple", lty = 3, lwd = 2)

# Verdict
votes  <- table(all_labels[k_nearest_idx])
winner <- names(votes)[which.max(votes)]
title(main = sprintf("KNN Intuition (K=3)\nVotes -> Class 0: %d, Class 1: %d  ->  Predicted Class: %s",
                      sum(all_labels[k_nearest_idx] == 0), sum(all_labels[k_nearest_idx] == 1), winner))
legend("topleft", legend = c("Class 0 (Red)", "Class 1 (Blue)", "Query point (?)"),
       col = c("tomato", "steelblue", "gold"), pch = c(16, 16, 8), bty = "n")

cat("Step-by-step:\n")
for (rank in seq_along(k_nearest_idx)) {
  i <- k_nearest_idx[rank]
  cat(sprintf("  Neighbour #%d: point=(%.1f, %.1f), label=%d, distance=%.3f\n",
              rank, all_pts[i, 1], all_pts[i, 2], all_labels[i], dists[i]))
}
cat(sprintf("\nMajority vote: %s  ->  Predicted class = %s\n",
            paste(sprintf("%s: %d", names(votes), votes), collapse = ", "), winner))

title: Chapter 04: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
text:
5. KNN From-Scratch
Building KNN from scratch helps you understand exactly what happens under the hood. Every line below is annotated so a complete beginner can follow along.

The Algorithm in Plain English
For each new test point:
    1. Calculate the distance to EVERY training point
    2. Sort those distances from smallest to largest
    3. Keep only the first K entries (K nearest neighbours)
    4. For classification: take a majority vote of their labels
       For regression:     take the average of their values


Code
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#  KNN CLASSIFIER — from scratch, line-by-line explanation
# ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

KNNClassifierScratch <- setRefClass(
  "KNNClassifierScratch",
  fields = list(k = "numeric", metric = "character", X_train = "ANY", y_train = "ANY"),
  methods = list(
    initialize = function(k = 3, metric = "euclidean", ...) {
      # Store hyperparameters — these are set BEFORE training
      k <<- k; metric <<- metric
      X_train <<- NULL; y_train <<- NULL   # placeholders — filled during fit()
      callSuper(...)
    },

    fit = function(X, y) {
      # 'Training' step — KNN is a LAZY learner, so fit() just stores data.
      X_train <<- X   # memorise features
      y_train <<- y   # memorise labels
      invisible(.self)   # allow chaining: clf$fit(X, y)$predict(X_test)
    },

    compute_distance = function(a, b) {
      # Compute the distance between two points a and b.
      if (metric == "euclidean") {
        sqrt(sum((a - b)^2))       # sqrt(sum (ai - bi)^2)
      } else if (metric == "manhattan") {
        sum(abs(a - b))            # sum |ai - bi|
      } else {
        stop(sprintf("Unknown metric '%s'. Use 'euclidean' or 'manhattan'.", metric))
      }
    },

    predict_single = function(x) {
      # Predict the class label for ONE query point x. This is the core KNN logic.
      # STEP 1: distance from x to every training point
      dists <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(X_train)), function(i) compute_distance(x, X_train[i, ]), numeric(1))
      # STEP 2: sort by distance (closest first) & STEP 3: keep only the K nearest
      k_nearest <- order(dists)[seq_len(k)]
      # STEP 4: labels of those K neighbours
      k_labels <- y_train[k_nearest]
      # STEP 5: majority vote — the most common label wins
      tbl <- table(k_labels)
      as.numeric(names(tbl)[which.max(tbl)])
    },

    predict = function(X) {
      # Predict labels for a matrix of query points.
      vapply(seq_len(nrow(X)), function(i) predict_single(X[i, ]), numeric(1))
    },

    accuracy = function(X, y_true) {
      # Convenience: predict and compute accuracy in one call.
      y_pred <- predict(X)
      mean(y_pred == y_true)
    }
  )
)

cat("KNNClassifierScratch defined!\n")




Code
# ── Test the from-scratch classifier on an Iris-like toy dataset ─────────────
# Features: [petal length, petal width]
# Labels:    0 = setosa, 1 = versicolor, 2 = virginica

X_train_toy <- rbind(
  c(1.4, 0.2), c(1.3, 0.2), c(1.5, 0.1),   # setosa (short, narrow petals)
  c(4.7, 1.4), c(4.5, 1.5), c(4.9, 1.5),   # versicolor (medium petals)
  c(6.3, 1.8), c(5.8, 1.8), c(7.1, 2.1)    # virginica (long, wide petals)
)
y_train_toy <- c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2)

X_test_toy <- rbind(c(1.6, 0.3), c(4.8, 1.6), c(6.5, 2.0))
y_test_toy <- c(0, 1, 2)

cat(strrep("=", 55), "\n")
cat(sprintf("%4s  %20s  %9s\n", "K", "Predictions", "Accuracy"))
cat(strrep("=", 55), "\n")

for (k in c(1, 3, 5)) {
  clf <- KNNClassifierScratch$new(k = k, metric = "euclidean")
  clf$fit(X_train_toy, y_train_toy)
  preds <- clf$predict(X_test_toy)
  acc   <- clf$accuracy(X_test_toy, y_test_toy)
  cat(sprintf("K=%2d  Predictions: %14s  Accuracy: %.2f\n", k, paste(preds, collapse = ","), acc))
}

cat(strrep("=", 55), "\n")
cat(sprintf("\nTrue labels: %s\n", paste(y_test_toy, collapse = ", ")))
cat("\nAll K values get this small toy dataset correct!\n")




Code
# ── KNN REGRESSOR — from scratch ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# For REGRESSION (predicting a continuous number) the only difference
# from the classifier is STEP 5:
#   - Classifier -> majority VOTE  (pick the most common label)
#   - Regressor  -> AVERAGE        (take the mean of K neighbours' values)

KNNRegressorScratch <- setRefClass(
  "KNNRegressorScratch",
  fields = list(k = "numeric", X_train = "ANY", y_train = "ANY"),
  methods = list(
    initialize = function(k = 3, ...) {
      k <<- k; X_train <<- NULL; y_train <<- NULL
      callSuper(...)
    },
    fit = function(X, y) { X_train <<- X; y_train <<- y; invisible(.self) },
    predict_single = function(x) {
      # Compute distance to every training point, nearest first, average their K targets
      dists <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(X_train)), function(i) sqrt(sum((x - X_train[i, ])^2)), numeric(1))
      k_nearest <- order(dists)[seq_len(k)]
      mean(y_train[k_nearest])   # return their AVERAGE (not a vote!)
    },
    predict = function(X) vapply(seq_len(nrow(X)), function(i) predict_single(X[i, ]), numeric(1))
  )
)

# Demo: predict house price from size (in hundreds of sq ft)
X_houses <- matrix(c(10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40), ncol = 1)
y_prices <- c(150, 200, 250, 310, 350, 410, 480)   # price in $1000s

reg <- KNNRegressorScratch$new(k = 3)
reg$fit(X_houses, y_prices)

queries <- matrix(c(12, 22, 38), ncol = 1)
predictions <- reg$predict(queries)

cat("KNN Regression — House Price Prediction\n")
cat(strrep("-", 45), "\n")
cat(sprintf("%18s  %21s\n", "Size (x100 sqft)", "Predicted Price ($k)"))
cat(strrep("-", 45), "\n")
for (i in seq_along(predictions)) {
  cat(sprintf("%18d  $%19.1f\n", queries[i, 1], predictions[i]))
}

title: Chapter 04: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
text:
6. KNN on the Iris Dataset

The Iris Dataset
A classic ML benchmark: 150 iris flowers from 3 species.



Feature
Description




sepal length
Length of the sepal (cm)


sepal width
Width of the sepal (cm)


petal length
Length of the petal (cm)


petal width
Width of the petal (cm)


target
0=setosa, 1=versicolor, 2=virginica



We will load the dataset using our from-scratch load_iris() loader, explore it visually, then train and evaluate our from-scratch KNeighborsClassifier — covering the full classification pipeline: split → scale → fit → predict → evaluate.


Code
# ── Load and explore the Iris dataset ────────────────────────────────────────

iris_data <- load_iris()

df <- as.data.frame(iris_data$data)
colnames(df) <- iris_data$feature_names
df$species <- iris_data$target_names[iris_data$target + 1]
df$target  <- iris_data$target

cat("Shape:", dim(df), "\n")
cat("\nFirst 5 rows:\n")
print(head(df, 5))

cat("\nClass distribution:\n")
print(table(df$species))

cat("\nBasic statistics:\n")
print(round(sapply(df[iris_data$feature_names], summary), 2))




Code
# ── Pairplot: visualise all feature combinations ─────────────────────────────
# A pairplot shows:
#   - Diagonal:      distribution of each feature per class
#   - Off-diagonal:  scatter plot of two features, coloured by class
# This reveals which features separate the classes best.

GGally::ggpairs(
  iris, columns = 1:4, mapping = ggplot2::aes(color = Species),
  diag = list(continuous = "densityDiag")
) + ggplot2::theme_bw() +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Iris Dataset — Pairplot of All Feature Combinations")

cat("\nKey observations:\n")
cat("- Setosa is clearly separated from the other two species\n")
cat("- Petal length & petal width are the most discriminating features\n")
cat("- Versicolor & virginica overlap slightly — harder to separate\n")




Code
# ── Train and evaluate a KNN classifier on Iris ──────────────────────────────

# --- Step 1: Select features and target ---
X_ir <- iris_data$data     # all 4 features, shape (150, 4)
y_ir <- iris_data$target   # class labels: 0, 1, or 2

# --- Step 2: Split into train (80%) and test (20%) ---
split_ir <- train_test_split(X_ir, y_ir, test_size = 0.2, random_state = SEED, stratify = y_ir)
X_train <- split_ir$X_train; X_test <- split_ir$X_test
y_train <- split_ir$y_train; y_test <- split_ir$y_test

cat(sprintf("Training set size : %d samples\n", nrow(X_train)))
cat(sprintf("Test set size     : %d samples\n", nrow(X_test)))

# --- Step 3: SCALE the features ---
# KNN is distance-based -> features must be on the same scale!
scaler <- StandardScaler$new()
X_train_sc <- scaler$fit_transform(X_train)   # learn mean/std from train, then scale
X_test_sc  <- scaler$transform(X_test)        # use SAME mean/std (never fit on test!)

# --- Step 4: Train the KNN model ---
knn <- KNeighborsClassifier$new(n_neighbors = 5, metric = "euclidean", weights = "uniform")
knn$fit(X_train_sc, y_train)

# --- Step 5: Predict on the test set ---
y_pred <- knn$predict(X_test_sc)

# --- Step 6: Evaluate ---
acc <- accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
cat(sprintf("\nTest Accuracy (K=5): %.4f  (%.1f%%)\n", acc, acc * 100))
cat("\nDetailed Classification Report:\n")
classification_report(y_test, y_pred, target_names = iris_data$target_names)




Code
# ── Confusion Matrix ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Rows: TRUE labels. Columns: PREDICTED labels. Diagonal: correct predictions.

cm <- confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)
rownames(cm) <- iris_data$target_names
colnames(cm) <- iris_data$target_names

op <- par(mar = c(5, 8, 4, 2))
image(seq_len(ncol(cm)), seq_len(nrow(cm)), t(cm[nrow(cm):1, ]),
      col = colorRampPalette(c("white", "steelblue"))(50),
      axes = FALSE, xlab = "Predicted Label", ylab = "")
axis(1, at = seq_len(ncol(cm)), labels = colnames(cm))
axis(2, at = seq_len(nrow(cm)), labels = rev(rownames(cm)), las = 1)
mtext("True Label", side = 2, line = 6)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(cm))) {
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(cm))) {
    text(j, nrow(cm) - i + 1, cm[i, j], col = if (cm[i, j] > max(cm) / 2) "white" else "black")
  }
}
title(main = sprintf("Confusion Matrix — KNN (K=5) on Iris Test Set\nAccuracy = %.1f%%", acc * 100))
par(op)

cat("How to read:\n")
cat("  Each cell [row i, col j] = number of times class i was predicted as class j\n")
cat("  Large numbers on the diagonal = good model\n")

title: Chapter 04: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
section: 7. Decision Boundaries - Seeing What KNN Learns
text:
7. Decision Boundaries - Seeing What KNN Learns
A decision boundary is the line (or surface) that separates different classes. For KNN, this boundary is determined by where the majority class changes.
We’ll use only 2 features (petal length & petal width) so we can draw it in 2D. We colour every point in the 2D space with its predicted class — this creates the “background”. Then we overlay the actual training and test points on top.


Code
# ── Decision Boundary Plot (2 features only) ─────────────────────────────────

feature_idx <- c(3, 4)   # petal length, petal width
X_2d <- iris_data$data[, feature_idx]
y_2d <- iris_data$target

split_2d <- train_test_split(X_2d, y_2d, test_size = 0.2, random_state = SEED, stratify = y_2d)
X_tr <- split_2d$X_train; X_te <- split_2d$X_test
y_tr <- split_2d$y_train; y_te <- split_2d$y_test

sc2 <- StandardScaler$new()
X_tr_sc <- sc2$fit_transform(X_tr)
X_te_sc <- sc2$transform(X_te)

knn_2d <- KNeighborsClassifier$new(n_neighbors = 5, metric = "euclidean")
knn_2d$fit(X_tr_sc, y_tr)

colors_bg  <- c("#FADBD8", "#D6EAF8", "#D5F5E3")   # light pastel backgrounds
colors_pts <- c("#E74C3C", "#2980B9", "#27AE60")   # solid colours for dots

grid_info <- decision_boundary_grid(knn_2d, X_tr_sc, grid_resolution = 100)

plot(NULL, xlim = range(grid_info$gx), ylim = range(grid_info$gy),
     xlab = "Petal Length (scaled)", ylab = "Petal Width (scaled)", main = "")
image(grid_info$gx, grid_info$gy, grid_info$Z, col = colors_bg, add = TRUE)

for (cls in 0:2) {
  mask_tr <- y_tr == cls; mask_te <- y_te == cls
  points(X_tr_sc[mask_tr, 1], X_tr_sc[mask_tr, 2], col = colors_pts[cls + 1], pch = 16, cex = 1.1)
  points(X_te_sc[mask_te, 1], X_te_sc[mask_te, 2], col = colors_pts[cls + 1], pch = 17, cex = 1.5)
}

acc_2d <- knn_2d$score(X_te_sc, y_te)
title(main = sprintf("KNN (K=5) Decision Boundary — Petal Features Only\nTest Accuracy = %.1f%%", acc_2d * 100))
legend("topleft", legend = c(paste(iris_data$target_names, "(train)"), paste(iris_data$target_names, "(test)")),
       col = rep(colors_pts, 2), pch = c(16, 16, 16, 17, 17, 17), cex = 0.7, bty = "n", ncol = 2)

cat("\nKey insight:\n")
cat("The coloured regions show where KNN would classify ANY new point.\n")
cat("Notice the jagged, non-linear boundary — this is characteristic of KNN.\n")

title: Chapter 04: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
text:
8. How K Affects the Model
K is the most important hyperparameter in KNN. It controls the bias-variance tradeoff:










K value
Boundary
Bias
Variance
Risk




Small K (e.g. K=1)
Very jagged, irregular
Low
High
Overfitting


Medium K
Smoother
Medium
Medium
Best sweet spot


Large K (e.g. K=n)
Very smooth, almost flat
High
Low
Underfitting




K=1: Model perfectly memorises training data — predicts training labels with 100% accuracy, but fails on new data. K=n (n = number of training samples): Predicts the same class for everything — the majority class.

Let’s visualise this with 4 different K values side by side.


Code
# ── Side-by-side decision boundaries for K=1, 5, 15, 50 ──────────────────────

moons <- make_moons(n_samples = 300, noise = 0.25, random_state = SEED)
X_moons <- moons$X; y_moons <- moons$y

split_m <- train_test_split(X_moons, y_moons, test_size = 0.2, random_state = SEED)
X_m_tr <- split_m$X_train; X_m_te <- split_m$X_test
y_m_tr <- split_m$y_train; y_m_te <- split_m$y_test

k_values <- c(1, 5, 15, 50)
par(mfrow = c(1, 4))

for (k in k_values) {
  clf <- KNeighborsClassifier$new(n_neighbors = k)
  clf$fit(X_m_tr, y_m_tr)
  train_acc <- clf$score(X_m_tr, y_m_tr)
  test_acc  <- clf$score(X_m_te, y_m_te)

  grid_info <- decision_boundary_grid(clf, X_m_tr, grid_resolution = 100)
  plot(NULL, xlim = range(grid_info$gx), ylim = range(grid_info$gy),
       xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = if (k == 1) "Feature 2" else "", main = "")
  image(grid_info$gx, grid_info$gy, grid_info$Z,
        col = colorRampPalette(c("#D73027", "#FFFFBF", "#4575B4"))(50), add = TRUE)
  points(X_m_tr[, 1], X_m_tr[, 2], col = ifelse(y_m_tr == 0, "#D73027", "#4575B4"), pch = 16, cex = 0.7)

  label <- if (k == 1) "Overfit (High Variance)" else if (k == 50) "Underfit (High Bias)" else "Good Fit"
  title(main = sprintf("K = %d\nTrain: %.0f%% | Test: %.0f%%\n%s", k, train_acc * 100, test_acc * 100, label))
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

cat("Observations:\n")
cat("  K=1  -> jagged boundary, overfit (train=100%, test drops)\n")
cat("  K=5  -> smoother, good generalisation\n")
cat("  K=15 -> even smoother, still good\n")
cat("  K=50 -> very smooth/flat, losing the shape of the true boundary\n")

title: Chapter 04: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
section: 9. Choosing the Best K with Cross-Validation
text:
9. Choosing the Best K with Cross-Validation

What Is Cross-Validation?
Instead of evaluating on a single train/test split (which can be lucky or unlucky), k-fold cross-validation splits the training data into k equally-sized folds. For each fold: - Use that fold as a mini-test set - Train on the remaining folds - Record accuracy
Finally, average the k accuracy scores. This gives a much more reliable estimate of model performance.

⚠️ Note: The “k” in k-fold cross-validation is different from the “K” in KNN!



Code
# ── Find the best K using 5-fold cross-validation ────────────────────────────

X_full <- iris_data$data
y_full <- iris_data$target

scaler_full <- StandardScaler$new()
X_full_sc <- scaler_full$fit_transform(X_full)

k_range  <- 1:30   # test K from 1 to 30
cv_means <- numeric(length(k_range))
cv_stds  <- numeric(length(k_range))

set.seed(SEED)
for (i in seq_along(k_range)) {
  k <- k_range[i]
  # cross_val_score runs 5-fold CV and returns 5 accuracy scores
  scores <- cross_val_score(function() KNeighborsClassifier$new(n_neighbors = k),
                             X_full_sc, y_full, cv = 5, scoring = "accuracy")
  cv_means[i] <- mean(scores)
  cv_stds[i]  <- popsd(scores)
}

best_i <- which.max(cv_means)
best_k <- k_range[best_i]
cat(sprintf("Best K = %d  |  CV Accuracy = %.4f +/- %.4f\n", best_k, max(cv_means), cv_stds[best_i]))




Code
# ── Plot CV accuracy vs K ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

k_arr <- k_range; cv_means_arr <- cv_means; cv_stds_arr <- cv_stds

plot(k_arr, cv_means_arr, type = "n", xaxt = "n", ylim = c(0.9, 1.01),
     xlab = "K (Number of Neighbours)", ylab = "5-Fold CV Accuracy",
     main = "Cross-Validation Accuracy vs K — Iris Dataset")
axis(1, at = k_arr)

# Annotate overfit / underfit regions
rect(1, 0.9, 5, 1.01, col = adjustcolor("red", alpha.f = 0.05), border = NA)
rect(20, 0.9, 30, 1.01, col = adjustcolor("purple", alpha.f = 0.05), border = NA)

# Shaded region = +/-1 standard deviation
polygon(c(k_arr, rev(k_arr)), c(cv_means_arr - cv_stds_arr, rev(cv_means_arr + cv_stds_arr)),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", alpha.f = 0.2), border = NA)

# Mean accuracy line
lines(k_arr, cv_means_arr, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2.5)
points(k_arr, cv_means_arr, col = "steelblue", pch = 16, cex = 0.8)

# Mark the best K
abline(v = best_k, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 1.8)
points(best_k, max(cv_means_arr), col = "red", pch = 16, cex = 1.5)
text(best_k + 1.5, max(cv_means_arr) - 0.005, sprintf("Best K=%d\nAcc=%.4f", best_k, max(cv_means_arr)),
     col = "red", cex = 0.8)

text(2, min(cv_means_arr) + 0.001, "High\nVariance", col = "red", cex = 0.8)
text(25, min(cv_means_arr) + 0.001, "High\nBias", col = "purple", cex = 0.8)

legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Mean CV Accuracy", "+/-1 Std Dev", sprintf("Best K = %d", best_k)),
       col = c("steelblue", adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.4), "red"),
       lwd = c(2.5, 8, 1.8), lty = c(1, 1, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.7)

cat("\nHow to interpret:\n")
cat("  - Left side  (small K) -> accuracy is lower and noisier (overfitting training data)\n")
cat("  - Middle     (optimal K) -> best generalisation\n")
cat("  - Right side (large K) -> accuracy drops off (too much smoothing)\n")

title: Chapter 04: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
text:
10. KNN for Regression
KNN isn’t just for classification. For regression (predicting a continuous number), it works exactly the same way but returns the average of the K neighbours’ values.
Example use cases: - Predicting house prices from nearby comparable sales - Predicting a patient’s blood pressure based on similar patients - Forecasting stock price from historically similar patterns

Comparison of K values for Regression



Small K
Large K




Follows the data closely (wiggly line)
Very smooth line


Can overfit noise
May miss real patterns


Low bias, high variance
High bias, low variance





Code
# ── KNN Regression on synthetic data ─────────────────────────────────────────

set.seed(SEED)
X_reg <- matrix(seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200), ncol = 1)   # 200 evenly spaced x values
y_reg <- sin(X_reg[, 1]) + rnorm(200, 0, 0.2)                 # sine + noise

split_reg <- train_test_split(X_reg, y_reg, test_size = 0.25, random_state = SEED)
X_r_tr <- split_reg$X_train; X_r_te <- split_reg$X_test
y_r_tr <- split_reg$y_train; y_r_te <- split_reg$y_test

k_values_reg <- c(1, 3, 10, 30)
X_plot <- matrix(seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 500), ncol = 1)
y_true_plot <- sin(X_plot[, 1])

par(mfrow = c(1, 4))
for (k in k_values_reg) {
  reg <- KNeighborsRegressor$new(n_neighbors = k)
  reg$fit(X_r_tr, y_r_tr)
  y_pred_plot <- reg$predict(X_plot)
  y_pred_test <- reg$predict(X_r_te)

  rmse_k <- sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_r_te, y_pred_test))
  r2_k   <- r2_score(y_r_te, y_pred_test)

  plot(X_plot[, 1], y_true_plot, type = "l", lty = 2, col = "gray40",
       xlab = "x", ylab = if (k == 1) "y" else "", ylim = range(c(y_true_plot, y_r_tr)))
  lines(X_plot[, 1], y_pred_plot, col = "tomato", lwd = 2)
  points(X_r_tr[, 1], y_r_tr, col = "steelblue", pch = 16, cex = 0.5)

  label <- if (k == 1) "Overfit" else if (k == 30) "Underfit" else "Good"
  title(main = sprintf("K = %d  [%s]\nRMSE=%.3f  R2=%.3f", k, label, rmse_k, r2_k))
  if (k == 1) legend("topright", legend = c("True sin(x)", "KNN", "Train pts"),
                      col = c("gray40", "tomato", "steelblue"), lty = c(2, 1, NA), pch = c(NA, NA, 16),
                      cex = 0.6, bty = "n")
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

cat("Metrics explained:\n")
cat("  RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error): average prediction error in y units — lower is better\n")
cat("  R2   (Coefficient of determination): 1.0 = perfect, 0.0 = as good as just predicting mean\n")




Code
# ── KNN Regression on the Diabetes dataset (loaded from scratch) ─────────────
# load_diabetes() is defined in the setup cell

diab <- load_diabetes()
X_d <- diab$data
y_d <- diab$target   # disease progression score after 1 year

split_d <- train_test_split(X_d, y_d, test_size = 0.2, random_state = SEED)
X_d_tr <- split_d$X_train; X_d_te <- split_d$X_test
y_d_tr <- split_d$y_train; y_d_te <- split_d$y_test

sc_d <- StandardScaler$new()
X_d_tr_sc <- sc_d$fit_transform(X_d_tr)
X_d_te_sc <- sc_d$transform(X_d_te)

# Try different K values
results_diab <- data.frame(K = 1:30, RMSE = NA_real_, R2 = NA_real_)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(results_diab))) {
  k <- results_diab$K[i]
  reg <- KNeighborsRegressor$new(n_neighbors = k)
  reg$fit(X_d_tr_sc, y_d_tr)
  y_pred <- reg$predict(X_d_te_sc)
  results_diab$RMSE[i] <- sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_d_te, y_pred))
  results_diab$R2[i]   <- r2_score(y_d_te, y_pred)
}

best_k_reg <- results_diab$K[which.min(results_diab$RMSE)]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot(results_diab$K, results_diab$RMSE, type = "o", col = "tomato", pch = 16,
     xlab = "K", ylab = "RMSE (lower = better)", main = "RMSE vs K — Diabetes Dataset")
abline(v = best_k_reg, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
legend("topright", legend = sprintf("Best K=%d", best_k_reg), col = "red", lty = 2, bty = "n")

plot(results_diab$K, results_diab$R2, type = "o", col = "steelblue", pch = 16,
     xlab = "K", ylab = "R2 (higher = better)", main = "R2 vs K — Diabetes Dataset")
abline(v = best_k_reg, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
legend("topright", legend = sprintf("Best K=%d", best_k_reg), col = "red", lty = 2, bty = "n")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

best_row <- results_diab[results_diab$K == best_k_reg, ]
cat(sprintf("Best K = %d  |  RMSE = %.2f  |  R2 = %.3f\n", best_k_reg, best_row$RMSE, best_row$R2))

title: Chapter 04: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
text:
11. K-Means Clustering - Unsupervised Grouping

KNN vs K-Means — What Is the Difference?
Both algorithms have a K and both use distances, but they solve completely different problems:








Feature
KNN (K-Nearest Neighbors)
K-Means Clustering




Learning type
Supervised (needs labels)
Unsupervised (no labels needed)


Goal
Classify new points / predict values
Discover hidden groups in data


K refers to
Number of neighbours to consult
Number of clusters to form


Training
Lazy — just stores all data
Iterative centroid update


Output
Class label or numeric value
Cluster assignment (0, 1, 2, …)


Distance used for
Finding the K closest training points
Assigning each point to its nearest centroid




Simple rule: if you have labels → use KNN (supervised). If you have no labels → use K-Means (unsupervised).




11.1 The Real-World Analogy
Imagine a teacher receives 200 student essays but has no marking rubric and no grades yet. She reads through them and naturally groups similar essays together: - Group A: short, poorly structured, many grammar errors - Group B: medium length, decent structure - Group C: long, well-argued, near-perfect grammar
She did K-Means clustering with K=3 — found 3 natural groups with no predefined labels!



11.2 The Algorithm Step-by-Step
INITIALISE: Randomly place K centroid points anywhere in the data space

REPEAT until centroids stop moving:
    STEP 1 — ASSIGN: For every data point, compute its distance to each centroid.
                     Assign the point to the NEAREST centroid.
    STEP 2 — UPDATE: For each cluster, move its centroid to the MEAN
                     (average) position of all points assigned to it.

STOP when centroid movement < tolerance (convergence)


11.3 Key Vocabulary







Term
Plain English




Centroid
The “center” of a cluster — the average position of all its member points


Cluster
A group of data points that are closer to each other than to other groups


Inertia
Total squared distance of every point to its nearest centroid — lower = tighter clusters


Convergence
When centroids barely move between iterations (algorithm has found a stable solution)


Elbow method
Plot inertia vs K values — look for the “knee” where adding more clusters stops helping much





11.4 When to Use K-Means
✅ Customer segmentation (group customers by purchasing behaviour) ✅ Image compression (group similar pixel colours) ✅ Document clustering (group similar articles) ✅ Anomaly detection (points far from all centroids are outliers)
❌ When clusters have very different sizes ❌ When clusters are non-spherical / ring-shaped ❌ When you don’t know a good K upfront (use elbow method to find it!)


Code
# ── K-Means Clustering — from scratch, every line explained ──────────────────
# Just like KNNClassifierScratch, this class uses ONLY base R.
# Every step is annotated so a beginner can follow along.

KMeans <- setRefClass(
  "KMeans",
  fields = list(n_clusters = "numeric", max_iter = "numeric", random_state = "ANY", tol = "numeric",
                cluster_centers_ = "matrix", labels_ = "numeric", inertia_history_ = "numeric",
                inertia_ = "numeric", n_iter_ = "numeric"),
  methods = list(
    initialize = function(n_clusters = 3, max_iter = 300, random_state = NULL, tol = 1e-4, ...) {
      n_clusters <<- n_clusters; max_iter <<- max_iter; random_state <<- random_state; tol <<- tol
      cluster_centers_ <<- matrix(numeric(0), 0, 0)
      labels_ <<- numeric(0); inertia_history_ <<- numeric(0)
      inertia_ <<- NA_real_; n_iter_ <<- 0
      callSuper(...)
    },

    assign_labels = function(X) {
      # For each data point in X, find the index of the nearest centroid (0-indexed).
      K <- nrow(cluster_centers_)
      dists <- vapply(seq_len(K), function(k) {
        sqrt(rowSums(sweep(X, 2, cluster_centers_[k, ], "-")^2))
      }, numeric(nrow(X)))   # shape: (n_samples, K), always a matrix even if K==1
      apply(dists, 1, which.min) - 1L
    },

    compute_inertia = function(X, labels, centers) {
      # Inertia = sum of squared distances from each point to its cluster centroid.
      total <- 0.0
      for (k in 0:(n_clusters - 1)) {
        mask <- labels == k
        if (any(mask)) {
          diff <- sweep(X[mask, , drop = FALSE], 2, centers[k + 1, ], "-")
          total <- total + sum(diff^2)
        }
      }
      total
    },

    fit = function(X) {
      # Find K clusters in the dataset X. NO LABELS needed — this is unsupervised!
      X <- as.matrix(X)
      if (!is.null(random_state)) set.seed(random_state)

      # INITIALISATION: randomly pick K existing data points as starting centroids
      idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(X)), n_clusters, replace = FALSE)
      cluster_centers_ <<- X[idx, , drop = FALSE]

      labels_ <<- rep(0L, nrow(X))
      inertia_history_ <<- numeric(0)

      iteration <- 0
      for (it in seq_len(max_iter)) {
        iteration <- it

        # STEP 1: ASSIGN — find nearest centroid for every point
        new_labels <- assign_labels(X)

        # STEP 2: UPDATE — move each centroid to its cluster's mean
        new_centers <- do.call(rbind, lapply(0:(n_clusters - 1), function(k) {
          if (any(new_labels == k)) colMeans(X[new_labels == k, , drop = FALSE])
          else cluster_centers_[k + 1, ]   # keep old centroid if cluster is empty
        }))

        inertia <- compute_inertia(X, new_labels, new_centers)
        inertia_history_ <<- c(inertia_history_, inertia)

        # CONVERGENCE CHECK: did centroids move much?
        shift <- sqrt(sum((new_centers - cluster_centers_)^2))

        cluster_centers_ <<- new_centers
        labels_ <<- new_labels

        if (shift < tol) break   # centroids barely moved — stable solution!
      }

      inertia_ <<- inertia_history_[length(inertia_history_)]
      n_iter_  <<- iteration
      invisible(.self)
    },

    predict = function(X) {
      # Assign NEW (unseen) data points to the nearest existing centroid.
      assign_labels(as.matrix(X))
    },

    fit_predict = function(X) { fit(X); labels_ }
  )
)

cat("KMeans class defined!\n\n")
cat("Key attributes available AFTER calling $fit(X):\n")
cat("  $cluster_centers_  -> centroid coordinates, shape (K, n_features)\n")
cat("  $labels_           -> cluster index for each training point, shape (n_samples,)\n")
cat("  $inertia_          -> final within-cluster sum of squares (lower = better)\n")
cat("  $inertia_history_  -> vector of inertia at each iteration (shows convergence)\n")
cat("  $n_iter_           -> number of iterations until convergence\n")




Code
# ── K-Means Demo: Step-by-step on 2D blob data ───────────────────────────────
# We create 3 well-separated groups of points — but we give K-Means
# NO LABELS. It has to discover the groups entirely on its own!

set.seed(SEED)
centers_true <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(5, 0), c(2.5, 4.5))   # hidden true positions
X_km <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(i) {
  sweep(matrix(rnorm(80 * 2), ncol = 2), 2, centers_true[i, ], "+")   # 80 points per cluster
}))
X_km <- X_km[sample(nrow(X_km)), ]   # mix all points — no labels, just raw coordinates!

km <- KMeans$new(n_clusters = 3, random_state = SEED)
km$fit(X_km)

cluster_colors <- c("#E74C3C", "#2980B9", "#27AE60")

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

# Panel 1: raw data as K-Means sees it (no colours = no labels)
plot(X_km, col = "gray50", pch = 16, cex = 0.8, xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = "Feature 2",
     main = "Step 0 — Raw Data\n(No labels)")

# Panel 2: K-Means discovered clusters
plot(NULL, xlim = range(X_km[, 1]), ylim = range(X_km[, 2]), xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = "", main = "")
for (k in 0:2) {
  mask <- km$labels_ == k
  points(X_km[mask, 1], X_km[mask, 2], col = cluster_colors[k + 1], pch = 16, cex = 0.8)
}
points(km$cluster_centers_[, 1], km$cluster_centers_[, 2], col = "gold", pch = 8, cex = 3, lwd = 2)
title(main = sprintf("Step Final — K-Means Result (K=3)\nConverged in %d iterations | Inertia = %.1f",
                      km$n_iter_, km$inertia_))
legend("topright", legend = c(sprintf("Cluster %d (n=%d)", 0:2, as.numeric(table(km$labels_))), "Centroids"),
       col = c(cluster_colors, "gold"), pch = c(16, 16, 16, 8), cex = 0.6, bty = "n")

# Panel 3: discovered vs true centroids
plot(X_km, col = "lightgray", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = "", main = "")
for (k in 0:2) points(km$cluster_centers_[k + 1, 1], km$cluster_centers_[k + 1, 2],
                       col = cluster_colors[k + 1], pch = 8, cex = 2.5)
points(centers_true[, 1], centers_true[, 2], col = "black", pch = 4, cex = 2, lwd = 2)
title(main = "Discovered vs True Centroids\n(How close did K-Means get?)")
legend("topright", legend = c("Found centroid", "True (hidden) centroid"), col = "black", pch = c(8, 4),
       cex = 0.7, bty = "n")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# ── Print numerical comparison ────────────────────────────────────────────────
cat("Results Summary:\n")
cat(sprintf("  Converged in : %d iterations\n", km$n_iter_))
cat(sprintf("  Final inertia: %.2f\n", km$inertia_))
cat("\nDiscovered centroids (sorted by x):\n")
order_c <- order(km$cluster_centers_[, 1])
true_sorted <- centers_true[order(centers_true[, 1]), ]
for (i in seq_along(order_c)) {
  k <- order_c[i]
  found <- km$cluster_centers_[k, ]
  true_c <- true_sorted[i, ]
  err <- sqrt(sum((found - true_c)^2))
  cat(sprintf("  Cluster %d: found=(%.2f, %.2f), true=(%.1f, %.1f), error=%.3f\n",
              k - 1, found[1], found[2], true_c[1], true_c[2], err))
}
cat("\nK-Means found the hidden groups with NO labels — impressive!\n")




Code
# ── The Elbow Method: How to Choose K for K-Means ────────────────────────────
# Problem: K-Means requires us to set K upfront. But how do we know the right K?
# Answer: Run K-Means for K=1..10, record inertia, plot inertia vs K, and look
# for the "elbow" — the point where the curve starts to bend and flatten.

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Left panel: inertia convergence for a single K=3 run (iteration by iteration)
plot(seq_along(km$inertia_history_), km$inertia_history_, type = "o", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2.5,
     xlab = "Iteration Number", ylab = "Inertia (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares)",
     main = "K-Means Convergence (K=3)")

# Right panel: elbow plot — inertia vs number of clusters K
K_range <- 1:10
inertias <- sapply(K_range, function(k) {
  km_k <- KMeans$new(n_clusters = k, random_state = SEED)
  km_k$fit(X_km)
  km_k$inertia_
})

plot(K_range, inertias, type = "o", col = "tomato", lwd = 2.5, pch = 18,
     xlab = "K — Number of Clusters", ylab = "Inertia",
     main = "Elbow Method — Choosing K")
abline(v = 3, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
points(3, inertias[3], col = "red", pch = 16, cex = 1.5)
text(5, inertias[3] + (inertias[1] - inertias[length(inertias)]) * 0.12,
     "<- Elbow!\nBest K = 3", col = "red", cex = 0.85)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# ── Print the inertia table ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
cat("Elbow Method Table:\n")
cat(sprintf("  %3s  %10s  %14s\n", "K", "Inertia", "Drop from K-1"))
for (i in seq_along(K_range)) {
  k <- K_range[i]
  drop <- if (i > 1) inertias[i - 1] - inertias[i] else 0
  marker <- if (k == 3) " <- ELBOW (best K)" else ""
  cat(sprintf("  %3d  %10.1f  %14.1f%s\n", k, inertias[i], drop, marker))
}
cat("\nRule of thumb: choose K where the \"drop from K-1\" column stops being huge.\n")




Code
# ── KNN vs K-Means: Side-by-Side Visual Comparison ───────────────────────────
# Same dataset. Same K. Completely different algorithms and goals.

set.seed(SEED)
cmp <- make_classification(n_samples = 150, n_features = 2, n_informative = 2,
                            n_redundant = 0, n_classes = 3, random_state = SEED)
X_cmp <- cmp$X; y_cmp <- cmp$y

split_cmp <- train_test_split(X_cmp, y_cmp, test_size = 0.3, random_state = SEED)
X_cmp_tr <- split_cmp$X_train; X_cmp_te <- split_cmp$X_test
y_cmp_tr <- split_cmp$y_train; y_cmp_te <- split_cmp$y_test

# ── KNN: supervised — fits using both X and y (labels) ───────────────────────
sc_cmp <- StandardScaler$new()
X_cmp_tr_sc <- sc_cmp$fit_transform(X_cmp_tr)
X_cmp_te_sc <- sc_cmp$transform(X_cmp_te)

knn_cmp <- KNeighborsClassifier$new(n_neighbors = 5)
knn_cmp$fit(X_cmp_tr_sc, y_cmp_tr)   # needs LABELS

# ── K-Means: unsupervised — fits using ONLY X (ignores labels entirely) ──────
km_cmp <- KMeans$new(n_clusters = 3, random_state = SEED)
km_cmp$fit(X_cmp_tr_sc)              # NO labels passed — completely ignored!

colors_3 <- c("#E74C3C", "#2980B9", "#27AE60")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# ── Left panel: KNN (Supervised Classification) ──────────────────────────────
grid_cmp <- decision_boundary_grid(knn_cmp, X_cmp_tr_sc, grid_resolution = 100)
plot(NULL, xlim = range(grid_cmp$gx), ylim = range(grid_cmp$gy),
     xlab = "Feature 1 (scaled)", ylab = "Feature 2 (scaled)", main = "")
image(grid_cmp$gx, grid_cmp$gy, grid_cmp$Z, col = adjustcolor(colors_3, alpha.f = 0.25), add = TRUE)
for (cls in 0:2) {
  points(X_cmp_tr_sc[y_cmp_tr == cls, 1], X_cmp_tr_sc[y_cmp_tr == cls, 2], col = colors_3[cls + 1], pch = 16, cex = 0.9)

}
acc_cmp <- knn_cmp$score(X_cmp_te_sc, y_cmp_te)
title(main = sprintf("KNN (K=5) - SUPERVISED Classification\nNeeds labels! Test Accuracy = %.1f%%", acc_cmp * 100))

# ── Right panel: K-Means (Unsupervised Clustering) ───────────────────────────
plot(NULL, xlim = range(X_cmp_tr_sc[, 1]), ylim = range(X_cmp_tr_sc[, 2]),
     xlab = "Feature 1 (scaled)", ylab = "", main = "")
for (k in 0:2) {

  points(X_cmp_tr_sc[mask, 1], X_cmp_tr_sc[mask, 2], col = colors_3[k + 1], pch = 16, cex = 0.9)
}
points(km_cmp$cluster_centers_[, 1], km_cmp$cluster_centers_[, 2], col = "gold", pch = 8, cex = 3, lwd = 2)
title(main = sprintf("K-Means (K=3) - UNSUPERVISED Clustering\nNo labels used! Inertia = %.1f", km_cmp$inertia_))

# ── Text summary table ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cat("KEY DIFFERENCES — KNN vs K-Means\n")

title: Chapter 04: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
text:
12. The Curse of Dimensionality

The Problem
KNN relies on the idea that nearby points are similar. But in high-dimensional spaces, this idea breaks down.


Intuition
Imagine you want to cover 10% of a line segment (1D): you need a segment of length 0.1. To cover 10% of a square (2D): you need a side of length √0.1 ≈ 0.32. To cover 10% of a cube (3D): you need a side of √∛0.1 ≈ 0.46. In 10 dimensions (10D): you need a side of 0.1^(1/10) ≈ 0.79 — almost the entire space!
\[\text{Side length to cover fraction } f \text{ in } d \text{ dimensions} = f^{1/d}\]
Consequence: In high dimensions, the K nearest neighbours are no longer actually “near”. All pairwise distances become approximately equal, making KNN meaningless.


Solutions

Dimensionality reduction: PCA, t-SNE, UMAP before applying KNN
Feature selection: remove irrelevant features
Switch to a different model: tree-based models, SVMs, neural nets handle high-d better



Code
# ── Visualising the Curse of Dimensionality ───────────────────────────────────

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# ── Plot 1: Side length needed to capture 10% of the data ────────────────────
dims <- 1:50
fraction <- 0.10
side_lengths <- fraction^(1 / dims)

plot(dims, side_lengths, type = "o", col = "tomato", pch = 16, cex = 0.5,
     xlab = "Number of Dimensions", ylab = "Side Length Needed",
     main = "Side Length to Capture 10% of Data\nvs Number of Dimensions")
abline(h = 1.0, col = "gray", lty = 2)

# ── Plot 2: Distance concentration — all distances become similar ────────────
dims_test <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200)
n_samples_test <- 500
relative_contrast <- numeric(length(dims_test))

set.seed(SEED)
for (i in seq_along(dims_test)) {
  d <- dims_test[i]
  X_rand <- matrix(rnorm(n_samples_test * d), nrow = n_samples_test)
  idx <- sample(n_samples_test, 200)
  dists_sample <- c()
  for (ii in 1:(length(idx) - 1)) {
    for (jj in (ii + 1):min(ii + 4, length(idx))) {
      dists_sample <- c(dists_sample, sqrt(sum((X_rand[idx[ii], ] - X_rand[idx[jj], ])^2)))
    }
  }
  relative_contrast[i] <- (max(dists_sample) - min(dists_sample)) / (min(dists_sample) + 1e-10)
}

plot(dims_test, relative_contrast, type = "o", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2.5, pch = 15, log = "x",
     xlab = "Number of Dimensions", ylab = "Relative Distance Contrast\n(max-min)/min",
     main = "Distance Concentration in High Dimensions\n(contrast -> 0 means all distances similar)")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

cat("Key takeaway:\n")
cat("As dimensions increase:\n")
cat("  1. You need a larger and larger neighbourhood to find K neighbours\n")
cat("  2. All pairwise distances become nearly equal\n")
cat('  3. The concept of "nearest" loses meaning\n')
cat("  -> KNN performance degrades rapidly above ~20 features\n")




Code
# ── How KNN accuracy degrades as dimensionality grows ────────────────────────

n_samples_cod <- 400
dim_range <- c(2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100)
knn_accs <- numeric(length(dim_range))

for (i in seq_along(dim_range)) {
  d <- dim_range[i]
  cod <- make_classification(n_samples = n_samples_cod, n_features = d,
                              n_informative = max(2, d %/% 4), n_redundant = 0,
                              random_state = SEED)
  X_cod <- cod$X; y_cod <- cod$y
  split_cod <- train_test_split(X_cod, y_cod, test_size = 0.3, random_state = SEED)
  X_c_tr <- split_cod$X_train; X_c_te <- split_cod$X_test
  y_c_tr <- split_cod$y_train; y_c_te <- split_cod$y_test

  sc_c <- StandardScaler$new()
  X_c_tr_sc <- sc_c$fit_transform(X_c_tr)
  X_c_te_sc <- sc_c$transform(X_c_te)

  knn_c <- KNeighborsClassifier$new(n_neighbors = 5)
  knn_c$fit(X_c_tr_sc, y_c_tr)
  knn_accs[i] <- knn_c$score(X_c_te_sc, y_c_te)
}

plot(dim_range, knn_accs, type = "o", col = "tomato", lwd = 2.5, pch = 18, log = "x",
     ylim = c(0.4, 1.05), xlab = "Number of Features (Dimensions)", ylab = "Test Accuracy",
     main = "KNN Accuracy vs Dimensionality (K=5, fixed n=400 samples)")
abline(h = 0.5, col = "gray", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
text(dim_range, knn_accs + 0.03, sprintf("%.2f", knn_accs), cex = 0.8)
legend("topright", legend = "Random chance (50%)", col = "gray", lty = 2, bty = "n")

cat("As the number of features grows (with a fixed training set size),\n")
cat("KNN accuracy drops toward random chance — confirming the Curse of Dimensionality.\n")

title: Chapter 04: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
text:
Summary
In this chapter, we explored the principles and practical aspects of K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) for both classification and regression, along with the K-Means clustering algorithm for unsupervised learning. Key takeaways include the importance of feature scaling in distance-based algorithms, understanding the tradeoffs in choosing the K hyperparameter, and recognizing how high dimensionality can harm KNN performance due to the “Curse of Dimensionality.” We compared KNN and K-Means, highlighting their differences in learning type, input requirements, and outputs. The chapter also covered techniques such as cross-validation for model selection and methods for evaluating clustering, equipping you with foundational knowledge to apply and interpret these algorithms effectively.

title: Chapter 04: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
text:
Exercises

Feature scaling: Demonstrate the impact of feature scaling on KNN accuracy using any real dataset. Try min-max scaling and standardization.
Choosing K: Run KNN classification on a dataset of your choice for K values ranging from 1 to 15. Plot test accuracy versus K. What trend do you observe, and how would you choose the “best” K?
Curse of Dimensionality: Using make_classification(), simulate datasets with a fixed number of samples and gradually increase the number of features. Plot KNN accuracy as dimensionality increases (as shown above). Explain why this occurs.
Distance metrics: Compare KNN performance using Euclidean and Manhattan distance metrics. On what types of problems might one distance metric be preferable?
KNN for regression: Apply KNN regression to a synthetic dataset (e.g., make_regression). Vary K and observe bias-variance tradeoff on the test set. Plot prediction results for a few K values.
K-Means clustering demo: Use K-Means to cluster synthetic 2D data with three clusters. Visualize cluster assignments and centroids. Try different K values and discuss how inertia changes.

text:
13. Summary & Exercises

Chapter Summary — KNN







Concept
What You Learned




KNN Intuition
Ask K nearest neighbours, take majority vote (classify) or average (regress)


Distance Metrics
Euclidean (L2), Manhattan (L1), Minkowski — always scale features first!


Lazy Learner
No real training — stores all data, does all computation at prediction time


Classification
Returns the most common class label among K neighbours


Regression
Returns the mean target value among K neighbours


K hyperparameter
Small K = high variance (overfit) · Large K = high bias (underfit)


Cross-validation
Reliable, data-driven way to find the best K without touching the test set


Feature scaling
Mandatory — without scaling, large-range features dominate distances


Curse of Dimensionality
KNN degrades above ~20 features — all distances become similar, “near” loses meaning





Chapter Summary — K-Means Clustering







Concept
What You Learned




K-Means Intuition
Iteratively assign points to K centroids and re-centre until convergence


Unsupervised
Requires no labels — discovers natural groups in raw data


Centroid
The mean (average) position of all points in a cluster


Inertia
Within-cluster sum of squared distances — lower = tighter clusters


Elbow Method
Plot inertia vs K; pick the K at the “elbow” where gains flatten


Convergence
Centroids stop moving when assignments no longer change

Exercises

title: Chapter 02: Linear Regression
text: Gradient descent, cost functions, and your first trainable model

title: Chapter 02: Linear Regression
text:
2.1 Overview
Linear regression answers: “Given some input features, can we predict a continuous output?”
Example: Predict house price from size (sqft).
The idea: fit a straight line through the data so predictions are as close to reality as possible.
\[\text{Price} = w_1 \times \text{size} + w_0\]
In higher dimensions, this becomes a hyperplane instead of a line.

title: Chapter 02: Linear Regression
text:
2.2 Mathematical Formulation

The Model
Let’s break down how linear regression predicts an output from inputs:
First, imagine you have a set of input features (variables) represented as a vector: \(\mathbf{x} = [x_1, x_2, ..., x_p]\).
To make predictions, we assign a weight to each input. These weights are: \(\mathbf{w} = [w_0, w_1, ..., w_p]\), where \(w_0\) is a special weight called the bias or intercept.
The prediction (\(\hat{y}\)) for a single example is calculated as:
\[\hat{y} = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \cdots + w_p x_p\]
In other words, each input is multiplied by its corresponding weight, and the results are added together along with the bias.
We can write this calculation more compactly using vectors:
\[\hat{y} = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}\]
Here, we treat the bias as \(w_0\) and include an extra input \(x_0 = 1\) in the vector \(\mathbf{x}\). This way, the bias is just another multiplication.


The Cost Function (Mean Squared Error) — Explained
To figure out how well our model is doing, we need a way to measure how close its predictions (\(\hat{y}\)) are to the true results (\(y\)). That’s where the Mean Squared Error (MSE) comes in.
Here’s how MSE works: - For each example, take the difference between the real value and what the model predicted. - Square that difference (so that big mistakes count extra, and negatives don’t cancel positives). - Add up all those squared differences. - Divide by the number of examples to get the average.
As a formula:
\[J(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)^2\]
Why do we square the errors? Squaring makes sure all errors are positive (so they don’t cancel out), exaggerates larger mistakes (a difference of 2 counts four times as much as 1), and is mathematically convenient — it gives us a nice, smooth curve we can optimize easily.
Bottom line: The lower the MSE, the better our model is doing!

title: Chapter 02: Linear Regression
text:
2.3 Gradient Descent
Gradient descent is the “learning” part of the model below. Here is the dummy-proof version.

The Analogy: Walking Downhill in Fog
Imagine you’re standing on a hillside in thick fog and want to reach the bottom of the valley. You can’t see the valley, but you can feel the slope under your feet. So you:

Feel which direction is downhill,
Take a small step that way,
Repeat until the ground feels flat.

In our model:







Analogy
In the model




The hill
The error \(J(\mathbf{w})\) (MSE) — how wrong the predictions are for a given choice of weights


Your position
The current values of the weights \(w_0, w_1\)


The slope under your feet
The gradient — for each weight: “if I increase it slightly, does the error go up or down, and how steeply?”


The step size
The learning rate \(\alpha\) (lr in the code)


The bottom of the valley
The best-fitting line





What the Math Says
The prediction is \(\hat{y} = w_0 + w_1 x\) and the error is the MSE from Section 2.2. The gradient of the error with respect to each weight \(w_j\) is:
\[\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_j} = \frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - y_i)\, x_{ij}\]
In words: (how wrong we were on each sample) × (the input that weight was multiplying), averaged over all samples. If we’re predicting too high on big houses, the gradient for \(w_1\) is positive → we should lower \(w_1\).
The update rule is one line:
\[w_j \leftarrow w_j - \alpha \cdot \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_j}\]
The minus sign is the key: the gradient points uphill (direction of increasing error), so we step in the opposite direction.


How One Iteration of fit() Works

Start with a guess — all weights are 0, so the first prediction for every house is $0 (terrible, huge error — we’re high on the hill).
Measure the error on every sample — error = y_pred - yi. Positive means we predicted too high, negative too low.
Accumulate the gradient — gradients[j] += error * xi[j]. Each sample “votes” on which way each weight should move, weighted by its own input value. (Remember xi[0] is always 1, the bias column, so gradients[0] collects the plain errors for \(w_0\).)
Take the step — weights[j] -= lr * (2/n) * gradients[j]. Move each weight a little bit against the average gradient.
Repeat (2000 times in the demo). Each pass, the line tilts and shifts a little closer to the data. The cost_history shows the error dropping fast at first (steep hillside), then slowing as it approaches the valley floor.



Why the Learning Rate Matters

Too small (e.g., 0.0001): tiny steps — you’ll get there, but it might take millions of iterations.
Too large (e.g., 1.0): you overshoot the valley and bounce to the other side, often getting worse each step until the numbers overflow to infinity.
Just right (0.05 in the demo): fast, steady descent. (Exercise 3 at the end of the chapter asks you to experiment with this.)

This is also why the multi-feature demo (Section 2.5) normalizes features first: if “size” is in the thousands and “bedrooms” is 1–5, the hill is extremely stretched in one direction, and no single learning rate works well for both weights. Normalizing makes the valley round so the same step size works everywhere.

Jargon note: this chapter computes the gradient using all samples before each step (“batch” gradient descent). The SVM in Chapter 07 and the neural network in Chapter 11 instead update after each individual sample (“stochastic” gradient descent, SGD) — same downhill idea, just noisier, cheaper steps.

title: Chapter 02: Linear Regression
text:
2.4 Simple Linear Regression
The code below (linear_regression.R) creates a Linear Regression model from scratch in R using Gradient Descent to learn from data and make predictions.
The goal is to find the best equation:
\[
y = w_0 + w_1x
\]
Where:

(w_0) = bias/intercept (starting value)
(w_1) = weight/slope (how much output changes)


Main Parts of the Code

initialize() → Initialize the model

Sets:

lr → how big each learning step is
n_iterations → how many times to improve the model
weights → values the model learns
cost_history → stores error values


add_bias() → Add a column of 1s

Converts:

matrix(c(2, 3), ncol = 1)
into:
cbind(1, matrix(c(2, 3), ncol = 1))

This allows the model to learn the intercept ((w_0)).

predict_one() → Make one prediction

Uses current weights to calculate: \(\hat y = w^Tx\)

compute_cost() → Measure error

Calculates Mean Squared Error (MSE): \[
J=\frac1n\sum(y-\hat y)^2
\]
Lower error means better predictions.

fit() → Train the model

Adds bias
Starts weights at zero
Repeats many times:

Predict values
Calculate error
Compute gradients
Update weights using gradient descent

Stores cost every 100 iterations

predict() → Predict new values

Uses learned weights to estimate outputs for new inputs.


In short: the model repeatedly makes predictions, measures errors, updates the weights, and gradually learns the best equation for prediction.


Code
# linear_regression.R
#
# Linear Regression using Gradient Descent.
# No ML libraries — pure base R. We use a Reference Class (setRefClass) to
# mirror the Python class, with fields playing the role of `self.*` attributes.

LinearRegression <- setRefClass(
  "LinearRegression",
  fields = list(
    lr = "numeric",
    n_iterations = "numeric",
    weights = "numeric",       # c(w0 (bias), w1, w2, ..., wp)
    cost_history = "numeric"
  ),
  methods = list(
    initialize = function(learning_rate = 0.01, n_iterations = 1000, ...) {
      # Initializes the linear regression model.
      #   learning_rate: the step size for updating the weights during training
      #   n_iterations: number of times to update the weights
      lr <<- learning_rate
      n_iterations <<- n_iterations
      weights <<- numeric(0)
      cost_history <<- numeric(0)
      callSuper(...)
    },

    add_bias = function(X) {
      # Adds a bias (intercept) column to the input data.
      # X: matrix, each row is a sample.
      # Returns: matrix with a column of 1s prepended for the bias term.
      cbind(1, X)
    },

    predict_one = function(x_with_bias) {
      # Predicts the output for a single sample using current weights.
      #   y_hat = w^T x = sum(weight_i * x_i) for all i
      sum(weights * x_with_bias)
    },

    compute_cost = function(X_b, y) {
      # Computes the mean squared error (MSE) cost function.
      #   J = (1/n) * sum( (y_i - y_hat_i)^2 )
      # Lower cost means better predictions.
      n <- length(y)
      y_hat <- as.numeric(X_b %*% weights)
      sum((y - y_hat)^2) / n
    },

    fit = function(X, y) {
      # Train the linear regression model using gradient descent.
      #
      # How it works:
      # 1. Adds a bias (intercept) term to each input sample.
      # 2. Initializes the model's weights to zero.
      # 3. For each iteration:
      #    a. Computes the gradient of the cost function (MSE) with respect to each weight.
      #       For every data point, calculates the prediction error and accumulates how much
      #       each weight contributed to the error.
      #    b. Updates each weight by moving it a small step in the direction that reduces error.
      #       The amount moved depends on the learning rate (lr) and the average gradient.
      #    c. Every 100 iterations, computes the current cost and stores it in cost_history.
      # 4. Repeats these steps for the specified number of iterations.
      X_b <- add_bias(X)                # Add bias (column of ones) to X
      n <- nrow(X_b)                     # Number of samples
      p <- ncol(X_b)                     # Number of weights (features + bias)

      weights <<- rep(0.0, p)           # Initialize weights to zero

      for (iteration in 0:(n_iterations - 1)) {
        y_pred <- as.numeric(X_b %*% weights)  # Predicted values for all samples
        error <- y_pred - y                    # Prediction error (vector)
        gradients <- as.numeric(t(X_b) %*% error)  # Partial derivative wrt each weight

        # Update each weight by the gradient descent rule
        weights <<- weights - lr * (2 / n) * gradients

        # Store cost for later plotting/diagnostics every 100 iterations
        if (iteration %% 100 == 0) {
          cost_history <<- c(cost_history, compute_cost(X_b, y))
        }
      }

      invisible(.self)
    },

    predict = function(X) {
      # Predict output for a matrix of samples.
      X_b <- add_bias(X)
      as.numeric(X_b %*% weights)
    }
  )
)

# ── Metrics ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

mse <- function(y_true, y_pred) {
  sum((y_true - y_pred)^2) / length(y_true)
}

rmse <- function(y_true, y_pred) {
  sqrt(mse(y_true, y_pred))
}

r_squared <- function(y_true, y_pred) {
  # Coefficient of determination R^2.
  y_mean <- sum(y_true) / length(y_true)
  ss_tot <- sum((y_true - y_mean)^2)
  ss_res <- sum((y_true - y_pred)^2)
  1 - (ss_res / ss_tot)
}

# ── Demo ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# Dataset: House size (sqft / 1000) -> Price ($1000s)
X_train <- matrix(c(0.8, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 1.0, 1.8), ncol = 1)
y_train <- c(150, 200, 250, 320, 400, 175, 290)

X_test <- matrix(c(1.1, 2.2, 0.9), ncol = 1)
y_test <- c(190, 350, 160)

# Train
model <- LinearRegression$new(learning_rate = 0.05, n_iterations = 2000)
model$fit(X_train, y_train)

cat("Learned weights (w0=bias, w1=size coefficient):\n")
cat(sprintf("  w0 = %.2f\n", model$weights[1]))
cat(sprintf("  w1 = %.2f\n", model$weights[2]))
cat(sprintf("  Equation: price = %.1f + %.1f x size\n", model$weights[1], model$weights[2]))

# Evaluate
y_pred <- model$predict(X_test)
cat("\nTest Predictions vs Actuals:\n")
for (i in seq_along(y_test)) {
  cat(sprintf("  Size=%.0fsqft -> Predicted $%.1fk, Actual $%dk\n",
              X_test[i, 1] * 1000, y_pred[i], y_test[i]))
}

cat(sprintf("\nRMSE : %.2f\n", rmse(y_test, y_pred)))
cat(sprintf("MSE : %.2f\n", mse(y_test, y_pred)))
cat(sprintf("R^2   : %.4f\n", r_squared(y_test, y_pred)))

title: Chapter 02: Linear Regression
text:
2.5 Multiple Linear Regression
Extending to multiple features (e.g., size + bedrooms + age):


Code
# Multiple features — normalize first so gradient descent is stable
# Normalize: subtract mean, divide by standard deviation
# This function normalizes each feature (column) of a matrix X so that each feature has zero
# mean and unit variance. It returns the normalized data (X_norm), the means, and the std devs.
normalize_features <- function(X) {
  # If X is empty, return empty results.
  if (nrow(X) == 0) {
    return(list(X_norm = X, means = numeric(0), stds = numeric(0)))
  }
  n_features <- ncol(X)  # Number of columns/features in X.
  # Compute the mean for each feature (column).
  means <- colMeans(X)
  # Compute the standard deviation for each feature, with a small minimum value to avoid
  # division by zero.
  stds <- sapply(seq_len(n_features), function(j) {
    max(sqrt(sum((X[, j] - means[j])^2) / nrow(X)), 1e-8)
  })
  # For each sample (row), normalize each feature by subtracting the mean and dividing by
  # the standard deviation.
  X_norm <- sweep(X, 2, means, "-")
  X_norm <- sweep(X_norm, 2, stds, "/")
  list(X_norm = X_norm, means = means, stds = stds)
}

X_train_multi <- rbind(
  c(1.2, 3, 10),   # size (k sqft), bedrooms, age (years)
  c(1.5, 3, 5),
  c(2.0, 4, 8),
  c(2.5, 4, 2),
  c(0.8, 2, 20)
)
y_train_multi <- c(200, 250, 320, 400, 140)

norm_out <- normalize_features(X_train_multi)
X_train_norm <- norm_out$X_norm
feat_means <- norm_out$means
feat_stds <- norm_out$stds

model_multi <- LinearRegression$new(learning_rate = 0.05, n_iterations = 2000)
model_multi$fit(X_train_norm, y_train_multi)

preds_multi <- model_multi$predict(X_train_norm)
cat("Multi-feature predictions vs actuals:\n")
for (i in seq_along(y_train_multi)) {
  cat(sprintf("  Predicted: %.1f  Actual: %d\n", preds_multi[i], y_train_multi[i]))
}



Important: Always normalize features when they have very different scales — without normalization the gradient descent step size becomes wildly unequal across features and the update can overflow.

title: Chapter 02: Linear Regression
text:
Summary







Concept
Formula




Linear model
\(\hat{y} = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}\)


Cost function
\(J = \frac{1}{n} \sum (y - \hat{y})^2\)


Gradient update
\(\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \alpha \cdot \frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{w}}\)


R² score
\(1 - \frac{SS_{\text{res}}}{SS_{\text{tot}}}\)

title: Chapter 00: Prerequisites & Setup
text:
0.2 Math Refresher

Vectors and Matrices
A vector is an ordered list of numbers: \(\mathbf{x} = [x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n]\) A matrix is a 2D array of numbers with rows and columns.
Dot product (used constantly in ML):
\[\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{w} = x_1 w_1 + x_2 w_2 + \cdots + x_n w_n\]


Summation Notation
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \text{ means } x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n\]


Derivatives (Calculus basics)
The derivative \(\frac{df}{dx}\) measures how much \(f\) changes when \(x\) changes slightly. Key rule: if \(f(x) = x^2\), then \(\frac{df}{dx} = 2x\)


Logarithms
\(\log(x)\) is the inverse of exponentiation. Used in probability and loss functions. Key property: \(\log(a \times b) = \log(a) + \log(b)\)

title: Chapter 00: Prerequisites & Setup
text:
0.6 Train/Test Split (From Scratch)


Code
train_test_split <- function(X, y, test_ratio = 0.2, seed = 42) {
  # For beginners:
  # This function breaks your data into two parts:
  # - A training set (to learn from)
  # - A test set (to check if learning is good)
  #
  # How it works, step-by-step:
  # 1. "set.seed(seed)": This makes sure you always get the same split every time you run it.
  # 2. "n <- nrow(X)": Count how many data points you have.
  # 3. "indices <- sample(seq_len(n))": Shuffle the positions of the data randomly.
  # 4. "split_at <- floor(n * (1 - test_ratio))": Figure out where to cut the shuffled list.
  # 5. "train_idx <- indices[1:split_at]": First part goes to training.
  # 6. "test_idx <- indices[(split_at+1):n]": The rest goes to testing.
  # 7. Slice X/y by those positions and return the new split data!
  #
  # Example:
  #   split <- train_test_split(X, y)
  #   X_train <- split$X_train; X_test <- split$X_test
  #   y_train <- split$y_train; y_test <- split$y_test

  set.seed(seed)              # So "shuffling" is the same every time
  n <- nrow(X)                 # Total number of data points
  indices <- sample(seq_len(n))  # Shuffled data positions

  split_at <- floor(n * (1 - test_ratio))  # Where to cut for train/test
  train_idx <- indices[seq_len(split_at)]
  test_idx  <- indices[(split_at + 1):n]

  list(
    X_train = X[train_idx, , drop = FALSE],
    X_test  = X[test_idx, , drop = FALSE],
    y_train = y[train_idx],
    y_test  = y[test_idx]
  )
}

title: Chapter 00: Prerequisites & Setup
text:
0.7 Feature Normalization
Most ML algorithms work better when features are on the same scale.
Min-Max Scaling maps values to \([0, 1]\):
\[x_{\text{scaled}} = \frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}\]
Z-score Standardization maps to mean=0, std=1:
\[x_{\text{std}} = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\]


Code
min_max_scale <- function(X) {
  # Scale each feature column in X to the [0, 1] range using min-max normalization.
  #
  # Parameters:
  #   X: matrix (rows are samples, columns are features)
  #
  # Returns:
  #   scaled: matrix, same shape as X, but each feature column is scaled to [0, 1]
  #   mins: vector of minimum values for each feature column (used for scaling/inverse-transform)
  #   maxs: vector of maximum values for each feature column (used for scaling/inverse-transform)
  #
  # How it works:
  #   1. For each feature column, compute the minimum and maximum values.
  #   2. Subtract the min and divide by the range (max - min) for that feature,
  #      so every feature value maps to [0, 1].
  #   3. The small value (1e-8) in the denominator prevents division by zero if all values are constant.
  #
  # Example:
  #   X <- matrix(c(2, 4, 6, 10, 20, 15), nrow = 3)
  #   out <- min_max_scale(X)
  #   out$scaled

  mins <- apply(X, 2, min)
  maxs <- apply(X, 2, max)
  ranges <- maxs - mins + 1e-8
  scaled <- sweep(X, 2, mins, "-")
  scaled <- sweep(scaled, 2, ranges, "/")
  list(scaled = scaled, mins = mins, maxs = maxs)
}

title: Machine Learning in R
text:
Machine learning has a reputation for being intimidating — a wall of Greek symbols, black-box libraries, and jargon that makes it feel like something only a specialist could ever understand. This tutorial is built on the opposite belief: that machine learning is a collection of simple, sensible ideas, and that the fastest way to truly understand any of them is to build it yourself.
At its heart, machine learning is just this: instead of writing rules by hand, you show a program examples and let it discover the rules on its own. A spam filter isn’t told what spam looks like — it learns from thousands of labeled emails. That single shift, from programming instructions to learning from data, is the whole revolution. Everything else is detail.
And the details are more approachable than they look. Behind every impressive model — a neural network that recognizes faces, a language model that writes text, a system that recommends your next film — sits arithmetic you already know: multiply some numbers, add them up, nudge them in the right direction, repeat. There is no magic step. When you write these models from scratch, in plain base R, the mystery dissolves and what remains is something you can reason about, debug, and trust.
That is the promise of this tutorial. We won’t hide the machinery behind a library call. We’ll derive the ideas, write the code line by line, and run it until it works — so that by the end you won’t just use machine learning, you’ll understand exactly what it’s doing and why. No hand-waving, and no tears.
Machine Learning in R is a free, open-source tutorial that teaches every major ML algorithm by building it from scratch using only base R — no caret, no tidymodels, no keras, no torch, no black boxes.

title: Machine Learning in R
text:
Who Is It For?
This tutorial is designed for:

R users who want to understand ML from first principles
Students taking an introductory ML course and looking for a practical companion
Engineers who use ML packages and want to demystify what’s happening under the hood
Anyone curious about the mathematics behind modern AI systems

You need: basic R (variables, loops, functions, vectors, data frames) and high-school algebra. No prior ML experience required. For a more comprehensive introduction to R, see R for Data Science.

title: Machine Learning in R
text:
Philosophy

“I hear and I forget. I see and I remember. I do and I understand.” — Confucius


“The best way to understand an algorithm is to implement it from scratch.”

Every algorithm in this tutorial is implemented without ML packages. This means:

No hidden behaviour — you can read every line
Genuine understanding — you can modify and experiment
Portable knowledge — the math translates to any language or framework

This tutorial uses only base R for all core algorithm implementations.
No caret, no tidymodels, no keras, no torch — just vectors, matrices, and explicit loops.
This forces you to truly understand what each algorithm is doing, not just call train().

title: Machine Learning in R
section: Why Tutorials Still Matter in the AI Era
text:
Why Tutorials Still Matter in the AI Era
We now live in a world where a working model can appear in seconds. Ask a coding assistant for logistic regression, a CNN, or a transformer, and it will usually produce something that runs. Packages, boilerplates, and large language models have made it easy to ship machine learning code without ever writing a loss function, a gradient update, or a split that actually prevents leakage.
That convenience is real. It is also a trap if it becomes a substitute for understanding.
When you depend on AI to write the code without the theory behind the model, several things go wrong at once:

You cannot tell good output from confident nonsense. An assistant may use the wrong loss, shuffle time-series data, apply the wrong activation, or treat a leakage-filled accuracy as success. If you do not know what the model is supposed to do, you cannot catch it.
You cannot debug. When training diverges, accuracy plateaus, or a production model silently fails, the stack trace is not enough. You need to know whether the problem is the data, the objective, the optimizer, the capacity of the model, or the evaluation.
You cannot choose. “Just use a neural net” is not a decision. Linear models, trees, kernels, and deep networks make different assumptions. Without those assumptions, every problem looks like a prompt.
You cannot adapt. Copy-pasted pipelines work on the demo. They break on missing values, class imbalance, non-stationary data, small samples, and domain shift — the cases that actually matter.
You become dependent on the tool. The assistant can generate model <- train(...). It cannot give you judgment. Judgment comes from having derived the math and implemented the algorithm yourself at least once.

AI is a powerful multiplier for people who already know what they are asking for. It is a liability for people who only know how to ask. The difference is theory: loss functions, inductive bias, overfitting, regularization, evaluation, and the geometry of the model class.
That is what this tutorial is for.
It does not compete with Copilot, ChatGPT, or tidymodels. Those tools are how most production work gets done. The point is to make you the person who can direct them: who can read the generated code, reject a wrong architecture, rewrite a broken training loop, and explain why a model succeeded or failed.






Important



The rule of this era: use AI to write faster, not to think less. If you cannot implement the algorithm without a package, you do not yet understand it well enough to trust AI-generated code that claims to.


A from-scratch tutorial is slower than prompting. That slowness is the feature. Typing a gradient by hand, watching a decision tree split, or deriving backpropagation on a napkin is how the black box becomes a box you can open. After that, using a package — or asking an assistant to use one — is a choice, not a dependency.
If you skip the theory, you will always be waiting for the next model to tell you what to do. If you learn it once, AI becomes what it should be: an accelerator for someone who already knows the map.

🧮 Mathematical Prerequisites
Relevant to: Chapter 00 — Prerequisites & Setup

Linear Algebra

3Blue1Brown — Essence of Linear Algebra (YouTube series, 2016)
Visual, intuitive introduction to vectors, matrices, and transformations. Best 3 hours you’ll spend on linear algebra.
→ youtube.com/playlist?list=PLZHQObOWTQDPD3MizzM2xVFitgF8hE_ab
Gilbert Strang — Linear Algebra (MIT 18.06) (Lecture series)
The gold standard university course. Covers everything from dot products to SVD.
→ ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-06sc-linear-algebra-fall-2011
Deisenroth, M.P., Faisal, A.A., & Ong, C.S. (2020). Mathematics for Machine Learning, Ch. 2–4. Cambridge University Press.



Calculus & Optimization

3Blue1Brown — Essence of Calculus (YouTube series, 2017)
Builds intuition for derivatives, chain rule, and gradients — exactly what you need for backpropagation.
→ youtube.com/playlist?list=PLZHQObOWTQDMsr9K-rj53DwVRMYO3t5Yr
Nocedal, J. & Wright, S. (2006). Numerical Optimization (2nd ed.). Springer.
Comprehensive reference on gradient descent, quasi-Newton methods, constrained optimization.



Probability & Statistics

Khan Academy — Statistics and Probability (Free course)
Covers all the basics: distributions, Bayes’ theorem, expectation, variance.
→ khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability
DeGroot, M.H. & Schervish, M.J. (2012). Probability and Statistics (4th ed.). Pearson.

title: References & Further Reading
text:
🟢 Beginner Chapters

Chapter 01 — Introduction to Machine Learning

Mitchell, T. (1997). Machine Learning. McGraw-Hill.
Classic textbook; Chapter 1 gives the cleanest definition of ML you’ll find.
Domingos, P. (2012). A few useful things to know about machine learning. Communications of the ACM, 55(10), 78–87.
Readable 9-page overview; covers the bias-variance tradeoff, overfitting, feature engineering.
Andrew Ng — Machine Learning Specialization (Coursera, 2022)
Best entry-point structured course. Covers supervised, unsupervised, and RL across three courses.
→ coursera.org/specializations/machine-learning-introduction



Chapter 02 — Linear Regression

James et al. (2021). ISLR, Ch. 3: Linear Regression. (Free PDF available)
Excellent chapter covering simple and multiple regression, subset selection, and regularization.
Hastie et al. (2009). ESL, Ch. 3: Linear Methods for Regression.
More rigorous treatment including geometric interpretation and the hat matrix.
Ng, A. (2022). CS229 Lecture Notes: Linear Regression and Gradient Descent.
→ cs229.stanford.edu/notes2022fall/main_notes.pdf
Gauss, C.F. (1809). Theoria Motus Corporum Coelestium. (Historical)
The original least-squares derivation — over 200 years old and still the foundation.



Chapter 03 — Logistic Regression

Cox, D.R. (1958). The regression analysis of binary sequences. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 20(2), 215–232.
The original logistic regression paper.
James et al. (2021). ISLR, Ch. 4: Classification. (Free PDF)
Clear coverage of logistic regression, LDA, and decision boundaries.
Ng, A. (2022). CS229 Lecture Notes: Classification and Logistic Regression.
Derives the log-likelihood and gradient update from first principles.
StatQuest: Logistic Regression (YouTube, Josh Starmer)
Clear visual explanation of odds, log-odds, and the sigmoid function.
→ youtu.be/yIYKR4sgzI8



Chapter 04 — K-Nearest Neighbors

Cover, T. & Hart, P. (1967). Nearest neighbor pattern classification. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 13(1), 21–27.
The foundational KNN paper. Proves that KNN error rate is at most twice the Bayes error.
Fix, E. & Hodges, J.L. (1951). Discriminatory Analysis, Nonparametric Discrimination: Consistency Properties. USAF School of Aviation Medicine Technical Report.
The original unpublished report that introduced the KNN concept.
Bellman, R. (1961). Adaptive Control Processes: A Guided Tour. Princeton University Press.
Where the term “curse of dimensionality” was coined.
James et al. (2021). ISLR, Ch. 2.2.3: K-Nearest Neighbors.



Chapter 05 — Naive Bayes

Bayes, T. (1763). An essay towards solving a problem in the doctrine of chances. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 53, 370–418. (Historical)
The original Bayes’ theorem paper, published posthumously.
McCallum, A. & Nigam, K. (1998). A comparison of event models for Naive Bayes text classification. AAAI Workshop on Learning for Text Categorization.
Compares Bernoulli NB vs Multinomial NB for document classification — highly cited.
Zhang, H. (2004). The optimality of Naive Bayes. FLAIRS Conference.
Explains why the “naive” independence assumption works surprisingly well in practice.
Manning, C.D., Raghavan, P., & Schütze, H. (2008). Introduction to Information Retrieval, Ch. 13. Cambridge University Press.
Excellent treatment of NB for text; freely available online.
