title: Chapter 04: Generalized Linear Models (GLMs)
text:
4.7 Regularization — Preventing Overfitting
Imagine your model is like a student trying to memorize every detail for a test. If it memorizes too much, it remembers the noise and does badly on new exams! Regularization is like telling the student: “Don’t focus only on memorizing all the weird little details—keep things simple!”
Regularization methods (like Ridge and Lasso) add a “penalty” if your model’s coefficients (the numbers it learns) get too big. This helps the model focus on the important patterns and ignore random noise, making it perform better on new, unseen data.

4.7.1 The Overfitting Problem
Imagine you’re trying to learn for a test, but instead of understanding the big concepts, you just memorize every little detail from your notes—even the random mistakes! If the questions on the real test are a bit different, this “memorizing everything” strategy doesn’t work well. You ace your practice (training) but do badly on the real (test) exam. This is called overfitting.
In machine learning, overfitting happens when a model pays too much attention to the training data, even its random quirks and errors, instead of learning the actual patterns. This means it won’t generalize well to new, unseen data.
Regularization is a trick that helps the model not memorize so much. It adds a penalty when the model’s learned numbers (coefficients) get too big or wild. You can think of it as telling the model: “Hey, don’t get too fancy! Keep it simple.”
Mathematically, if \(J(\boldsymbol{\beta})\) is the original measure of model ‘badness’ (called the loss), we add a penalty to get:
\[J_{\text{reg}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = J(\boldsymbol{\beta}) + \text{penalty}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\]
This means the model will prefer smaller, simpler coefficient values, making it less likely to overfit. It trades a little bit of accuracy (bias) for a much bigger gain in reliability (less wild predictions) on new data.



4.7.2 Ridge Regression (L2 Penalty)
Imagine you have a model that is trying to predict scores from some features, but it “cheats” by making its coefficients (the numbers that multiply each feature) really big so it fits the training data exactly, even memorizing the noise.
Ridge regression prevents this by penalizing the model when its coefficients become too large. It says: “Don’t go wild with those numbers! If you make your coefficients too big, you’ll get a penalty.”
Here’s what’s happening mathematically: - The ordinary least squares (OLS) loss function that a model tries to minimize is:
\[
  J(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \frac{1}{n}\|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2
  \] where: - \(\mathbf{y}\): the vector of true outputs - \(\mathbf{X}\): the matrix of feature values - \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\): the vector of coefficients - \(n\): the number of data points

Ridge regression adds a penalty for large coefficients, controlled by a parameter \(\lambda\):
\[
J_{\text{ridge}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \frac{1}{n}\|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2 \; + \; \lambda\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2^2
\] where \(\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2^2 = \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2\) is the sum of squared coefficients, and \(\lambda \geq 0\) determines how strongly we care about shrinking the coefficients.
The total cost is now: (ordinary error from bad predictions) + (penalty for big coefficients) = total loss the model tries to minimize.

What does Ridge Regression actually do? - All the feature coefficients are “shrunk” closer to zero, making the model less wild, but usually not exactly zero (they rarely get set to exactly zero). - This is useful when you think most features are relevant. - Typically, the intercept (starting value or bias) is not penalized, only the other coefficients.
Short version: Ridge acts like a teacher who stops your model from relying too heavily on individual features, encouraging it to find simpler, more general solutions that work better on new data. It says: “Don’t memorize—generalize!”



4.7.3 Lasso Regression (L1 Penalty)
Think of Lasso regression as a way to make your model simpler by actually setting some of the feature weights to exactly zero, telling the model to ignore some features completely!
Imagine you have a model that uses a bunch of features to predict something. Sometimes, not all those features really matter. Lasso regression helps the model “choose” which features are most important by shrinking the less important ones all the way to zero, basically doing feature selection for you, automatically.
The loss (cost) function for Lasso looks like this:
\[
J_{\text{lasso}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \frac{1}{n}\|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2 + \lambda \|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_1
\]

The first part: how badly your model predictions miss the real results.
The second part: a penalty that grows with the total size of the coefficients (using their absolute values, thanks to the \(L_1\) penalty).
\(\lambda\) decides how much you punish the model for using big coefficients.

What’s unique about Lasso?

When you increase \(\lambda\), some feature coefficients get pushed all the way to exactly zero—meaning those features are dropped from the model.
This leads to sparse (simpler) solutions—great when only a few features are actually useful.

How does the model figure out which ones to set to zero? - There isn’t a simple “solve it all at once” formula (because the \(L_1\) penalty is not smooth at zero). - Instead, it uses a trick called coordinate descent: it tweaks one coefficient at a time using something called a “soft-thresholding operator,” which nudges small values to zero and shrinks bigger ones.
Why use Lasso? - It helps with feature selection: only the important features stay; the rest get set to zero! - Very handy when you have lots of possibilities but only a few truly matter.



4.7.4 Elastic Net (L1 + L2)- Explained for Dummies
Imagine you want a model that gets the best of both worlds: - Lasso: Makes your model simpler by setting some coefficients exactly to zero (so it ignores some features entirely) - Ridge: Shrinks all the coefficients, but keeps all features (good when you think most features matter, especially if some are similar to each other)
Elastic Net combines both!
Think of Elastic Net as a referee that says: > “Hey model, keep things simple by ignoring useless features AND don’t let any one feature take over, especially when a bunch of them are alike!”
The formula (don’t worry, you only need the idea!):
\[
J_{en}(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \text{prediction error} + \lambda_1 \times \text{(Lasso penalty)} + \lambda_2 \times \text{(Ridge penalty)}
\]
Or, spelled out: \[
J_{\text{en}}(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \frac{1}{n}\|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2\
\quad+\quad \lambda_1 \sum |\beta_j| \quad+\quad \lambda_2 \sum \beta_j^2
\]
What does Elastic Net do that’s special? - If a few features are important, but you have lots, it will set some coefficients to exactly zero (like Lasso). - If several features are similar/correlated (like “height in cm” and “height in inches”), it tends to keep or drop them together (like Ridge). - You get a built-in feature selector and an insurance policy against weird effects when features are similar.
Tuning: - \(\lambda_1\) controls how much you force coefficients to zero (Lasso part). - \(\lambda_2\) controls how much you shrink all coefficients together (Ridge part). - Set \(\lambda_1 = 0\) and you get Ridge. - Set \(\lambda_2 = 0\) and you get Lasso!
In short: Elastic Net = Lasso + Ridge. It makes your model both sparse and stable—a great default if you’re not sure which regularization to pick.



4.7.5 How do you pick \(\lambda\)? (For Dummies)
Think of \(\lambda\) as a “penalty strength” knob: - Turn it up, and your model cares more about keeping things simple (shrinking coefficients, dropping unhelpful features). - Turn it down, and your model cares less (risk overfitting, but could fit noise!).
But how do you know where to set the knob? You don’t guess—you let the data decide!
The trick: 1. Try lots of lambda values (try turning the knob to many settings) 2. For each one, check how well your model does on new data (not the same data you trained on) 3. Pick the lambda that works best on “unseen” data
The common way to do this: - K-fold cross-validation: Split your data into “K” groups, train on some, test on others, shuffle, and repeat. This helps you see if your chosen lambda will actually work on new data. - (Some fancier methods use “AIC”, “BIC” scores, but the main idea is the same—pick the penalty that works best without peeking at the answers.)
Quick tip: Always standardise (scale) your features first - regularisation works better!


Ridge Regression from scratch


Code
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
#  Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net Regression explained for dummies
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# These are three different types of linear regression models that help prevent overfitting.
# They do this by adding a penalty to large coefficients (the "weights") in the model.

# 1. Ridge Regression (L2 regularization):
#    - Adds a penalty based on the SQUARE of the size of the coefficients (but not the bias).
#    - Keeps all coefficients, but makes them smaller.
#    - Useful if you think ALL features are relevant, but maybe not equally.

RidgeRegression <- setRefClass(
  "RidgeRegression",
  fields = list(lam = "numeric", coef_ = "numeric", loss_history_ = "numeric"),
  methods = list(
    initialize = function(lam = 1.0, ...) {
      lam <<- lam
      coef_ <<- numeric(0); loss_history_ <<- numeric(0)
      callSuper(...)
    },

    add_bias = function(X) cbind(1, X),

    fit = function(X, y) fit_ols(X, y),   # Alias for fit_ols

    fit_ols = function(X, y) {
      # Closed-form Ridge: One-step solution. Don't penalize the intercept.
      X_b <- add_bias(X)
      n <- nrow(X_b); p <- ncol(X_b)
      I_pen <- diag(p)
      I_pen[1, 1] <- 0.0                          # No penalty for the bias term
      A <- t(X_b) %*% X_b + n * lam * I_pen
      coef_ <<- as.numeric(solve(A, t(X_b) %*% y))
      invisible(.self)
    },

    fit_gd = function(X, y, lr = 0.01, n_iter = 2000) {
      X_b <- add_bias(X)
      n <- nrow(X_b); p <- ncol(X_b)
      coef_ <<- rep(0, p)
      loss_history_ <<- numeric(0)
      pen_mask <- rep(1, p); pen_mask[1] <- 0.0   # Don't penalize bias
      for (i in seq_len(n_iter)) {
        residuals <- as.numeric(X_b %*% coef_) - y
        mse_grad  <- 2 * as.numeric(t(X_b) %*% residuals) / n
        l2_grad   <- 2 * lam * coef_ * pen_mask
        coef_ <<- coef_ - lr * (mse_grad + l2_grad)
        loss <- mean(residuals^2) + lam * sum((coef_ * pen_mask)^2)
        loss_history_ <<- c(loss_history_, loss)
      }
      invisible(.self)
    },

    predict = function(X) as.numeric(add_bias(X) %*% coef_),

    score_r2 = function(X, y) {
      y_hat <- predict(X)
      1 - sum((y - y_hat)^2) / sum((y - mean(y))^2)
    }
  )
)

# 2. Lasso Regression (L1 regularization):
#    - Adds a penalty based on the ABSOLUTE VALUE of coefficients (again, not the bias).
#    - Can make some coefficients exactly ZERO (automatic feature selection!).
#    - Useful if you think ONLY SOME features matter.

LassoRegression <- setRefClass(
  "LassoRegression",
  fields = list(lam = "numeric", n_iter = "numeric", tol = "numeric",
                coef_ = "numeric", loss_history_ = "numeric"),
  methods = list(
    initialize = function(lam = 1.0, n_iter = 2000, tol = 1e-6, ...) {
      lam <<- lam; n_iter <<- n_iter; tol <<- tol
      coef_ <<- numeric(0); loss_history_ <<- numeric(0)
      callSuper(...)
    },

    soft_threshold = function(rho, delta) {
      # Returns 0 if rho is smaller than delta, else shrinks toward zero.
      sign(rho) * pmax(abs(rho) - delta, 0.0)
    },

    add_bias = function(X) cbind(1, X),

    fit = function(X, y) {
      # Coordinate descent: updates one coefficient at a time.
      X_b <- add_bias(X)
      n <- nrow(X_b); p <- ncol(X_b)
      coef_ <<- rep(0, p)
      loss_history_ <<- numeric(0)
      z <- colSums(X_b^2) / n   # Precompute: each column's squared sum

      for (iteration in seq_len(n_iter)) {
        coef_old <- coef_
        for (j in seq_len(p)) {
          # For each coefficient: temporarily hold it out and calculate its update.
          r_j <- y - as.numeric(X_b %*% coef_) + coef_[j] * X_b[, j]
          rho_j <- sum(X_b[, j] * r_j) / n

          if (j == 1) {
            coef_[j] <<- rho_j / z[j]                       # Don't penalize bias
          } else {
            coef_[j] <<- soft_threshold(rho_j, lam) / z[j]  # Shrink toward zero
          }
        }

        residuals <- y - as.numeric(X_b %*% coef_)
        loss <- mean(residuals^2) + lam * sum(abs(coef_[-1]))
        loss_history_ <<- c(loss_history_, loss)

        if (max(abs(coef_ - coef_old)) < tol) break
      }
      invisible(.self)
    },

    predict = function(X) as.numeric(add_bias(X) %*% coef_),

    score_r2 = function(X, y) {
      y_hat <- predict(X)
      1 - sum((y - y_hat)^2) / sum((y - mean(y))^2)
    }
  )
)

# 3. Elastic Net:
#    - A mix of Ridge and Lasso.
#    - Adds BOTH L1 and L2 penalties.
#    - Useful when features are correlated (it groups them) AND you want feature selection.

ElasticNet <- setRefClass(
  "ElasticNet",
  fields = list(lam1 = "numeric", lam2 = "numeric", n_iter = "numeric", tol = "numeric",
                coef_ = "numeric", loss_history_ = "numeric"),
  methods = list(
    initialize = function(lam1 = 1.0, lam2 = 1.0, n_iter = 2000, tol = 1e-6, ...) {
      lam1 <<- lam1; lam2 <<- lam2; n_iter <<- n_iter; tol <<- tol
      coef_ <<- numeric(0); loss_history_ <<- numeric(0)
      callSuper(...)
    },

    soft_threshold = function(rho, delta) sign(rho) * pmax(abs(rho) - delta, 0.0),

    add_bias = function(X) cbind(1, X),

    fit = function(X, y) {
      X_b <- add_bias(X)
      n <- nrow(X_b); p <- ncol(X_b)
      coef_ <<- rep(0, p)
      loss_history_ <<- numeric(0)
      z <- colSums(X_b^2) / n

      for (iteration in seq_len(n_iter)) {
        coef_old <- coef_
        for (j in seq_len(p)) {
          r_j   <- y - as.numeric(X_b %*% coef_) + coef_[j] * X_b[, j]
          rho_j <- sum(X_b[, j] * r_j) / n

          if (j == 1) {
            coef_[j] <<- rho_j / z[j]                         # Don't penalize bias
          } else {
            denom <- z[j] + 2 * lam2
            coef_[j] <<- soft_threshold(rho_j, lam1) / denom  # Shrink by L1, then L2
          }
        }

        residuals <- y - as.numeric(X_b %*% coef_)
        loss <- (mean(residuals^2)
                 + lam1 * sum(abs(coef_[-1]))
                 + lam2 * sum(coef_[-1]^2))
        loss_history_ <<- c(loss_history_, loss)

        if (max(abs(coef_ - coef_old)) < tol) break
      }
      invisible(.self)
    },

    predict = function(X) as.numeric(add_bias(X) %*% coef_),

    score_r2 = function(X, y) {
      y_hat <- predict(X)
      1 - sum((y - y_hat)^2) / sum((y - mean(y))^2)
    }
  )
)

cat("Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet defined (and explained for dummies).\n")




Code
# ── Demo: Regularization Comparison ─────────────────────────────────────────

# --- Simulate high-dimensional data with sparse signal ---
set.seed(5)
n <- 150; p_total <- 30           # 150 samples, 30 features
n_true <- 5                       # only 5 features are truly relevant

# True coefficients: 5 non-zero, 25 zero
beta_true <- rep(0, p_total)
beta_true[1:n_true] <- c(3.0, -2.5, 2.0, -1.5, 1.0)
beta_true <- sample(beta_true)     # shuffle

X_reg <- matrix(rnorm(n * p_total), nrow = n)
y_reg <- as.numeric(X_reg %*% beta_true) + rnorm(n) * 1.5

# Add correlated features (pairs) — Elastic Net handles these well
X_reg[, 11] <- X_reg[, 1] + 0.1 * rnorm(n)
X_reg[, 12] <- X_reg[, 2] + 0.1 * rnorm(n)

# Standardise
mu_r <- colMeans(X_reg)
sd_r <- apply(X_reg, 2, function(col) sqrt(mean((col - mean(col))^2)))
X_reg_std <- sweep(sweep(X_reg, 2, mu_r, "-"), 2, sd_r, "/")

idx <- sample(n)
split_r <- floor(0.8 * n)
X_tr_r <- X_reg_std[idx[1:split_r], ];       y_tr_r <- y_reg[idx[1:split_r]]
X_te_r <- X_reg_std[idx[(split_r + 1):n], ]; y_te_r <- y_reg[idx[(split_r + 1):n]]

# ── Fit models ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ols_model   <- LinearRegressionGLM$new()$fit_ols(X_tr_r, y_tr_r)
ridge_model <- RidgeRegression$new(lam = 0.1)$fit_ols(X_tr_r, y_tr_r)
lasso_model <- LassoRegression$new(lam = 0.05, n_iter = 3000)$fit(X_tr_r, y_tr_r)
en_model    <- ElasticNet$new(lam1 = 0.03, lam2 = 0.05, n_iter = 3000)$fit(X_tr_r, y_tr_r)

models <- list(OLS = ols_model, Ridge = ridge_model, Lasso = lasso_model, ElasticNet = en_model)

cat(sprintf("%-12s %10s %10s %12s\n", "Model", "Train R2", "Test R2", "Non-zero B"))
cat(strrep("-", 46), "\n")
for (name in names(models)) {
  m <- models[[name]]
  tr2 <- m$score_r2(X_tr_r, y_tr_r)
  te2 <- m$score_r2(X_te_r, y_te_r)
  nnz <- sum(abs(m$coef_[-1]) > 1e-4)   # exclude bias
  cat(sprintf("%-12s %10.4f %10.4f %12d\n", name, tr2, te2, nnz))
}

# ── Plots ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))

plot_data <- list(
  list(name = "OLS",        coefs = ols_model$coef_[-1],   col = COLORS[1]),
  list(name = "Ridge",      coefs = ridge_model$coef_[-1], col = COLORS[2]),
  list(name = "Lasso",      coefs = lasso_model$coef_[-1], col = COLORS[3]),
  list(name = "ElasticNet", coefs = en_model$coef_[-1],    col = COLORS[4])
)

for (pd in plot_data) {
  bp <- barplot(pd$coefs, col = pd$col, main = paste(pd$name, "Coefficients"),
                xlab = "Feature index", ylab = "Coefficient")
  points(bp, beta_true, pch = 15, col = adjustcolor("black", alpha.f = 0.4))
  abline(h = 0, lwd = 0.5)
  legend("topright", legend = "True B", pch = 15, col = adjustcolor("black", alpha.f = 0.4), bty = "n")
}

# 5. Coefficient path vs lambda for Lasso
lambdas <- 10^seq(-3, 1, length.out = 40)
paths <- matrix(0, nrow = length(lambdas), ncol = p_total)
for (i in seq_along(lambdas)) {
  m <- LassoRegression$new(lam = lambdas[i], n_iter = 2000)$fit(X_tr_r, y_tr_r)
  paths[i, ] <- m$coef_[-1]
}
path_colors <- ifelse(apply(abs(paths), 2, max) > 0.1,
                       adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.7), adjustcolor("grey", 0.15))
matplot(lambdas, paths, type = "l", log = "x", lty = 1, col = path_colors,
        xlab = "lambda (log scale)", ylab = "Coefficient", main = "Lasso Coefficient Path")
abline(h = 0, lwd = 0.5)

# 6. Test R2 vs lambda for Ridge / Lasso
r2_ridge <- sapply(lambdas, function(lv) RidgeRegression$new(lam = lv)$fit_ols(X_tr_r, y_tr_r)$score_r2(X_te_r, y_te_r))
r2_lasso <- sapply(lambdas, function(lv) LassoRegression$new(lam = lv, n_iter = 2000)$fit(X_tr_r, y_tr_r)$score_r2(X_te_r, y_te_r))
plot(lambdas, r2_ridge, type = "l", log = "x", col = COLORS[2], lwd = 2,
     xlab = "lambda (log scale)", ylab = "Test R2", main = "Test R2 vs Regularisation Strength",
     ylim = range(c(r2_ridge, r2_lasso)))
lines(lambdas, r2_lasso, col = COLORS[3], lwd = 2)
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Ridge", "Lasso"), col = COLORS[2:3], lwd = 2, bty = "n")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

title: Chapter 04: Generalized Linear Models (GLMs)
section: 4.8 Picking the Best \(\lambda\) with K-Fold Cross-Validation (Simple Explanation)
text:
4.8 Picking the Best \(\lambda\) with K-Fold Cross-Validation (Simple Explanation)
Instead of picking the regularisation strength (λ) randomly or by trial and error, we use a strategy called K-Fold Cross-Validation. This just means: 1. Try lots of possible λ values. 2. For each value, test how well it works by splitting the data into pieces (“folds”), training on some pieces and checking performance on the piece left out. 3. Average the errors across all the pieces for each lambda. 4. Choose the λ that gives the lowest average error.
In short: let the computer choose the best λ for us in a fair way!

Algorithm
for each candidate λ:
    for each fold k = 1 … K:
        fit model on all folds except k
        evaluate on fold k
    cv_error(λ) = mean(fold errors)
choose λ* = argmin cv_error(λ)


Code
# ── K-Fold CV for Ridge and Lasso ────────────────────────────────────────────

# Runs K-Fold cross-validation for a given model factory and hyperparameter grid.
#   X, y: data
#   make_model: function(lam) -> a fresh, unfitted model object
#   param_grid: values of the hyperparameter to try
#   k_folds: number of folds (default 5)
# Returns: vector of mean validation MSEs (one per hyperparameter value)
kfold_cv <- function(X, y, make_model, param_grid, k_folds = 5) {
  n <- length(y)
  fold_size <- n %/% k_folds
  idx <- sample(n)               # Shuffle indices
  cv_scores <- numeric(length(param_grid))

  for (li in seq_along(param_grid)) {
    lam_val <- param_grid[li]
    fold_mses <- numeric(k_folds)
    for (k in 0:(k_folds - 1)) {
      val_idx   <- idx[(k * fold_size + 1):((k + 1) * fold_size)]   # validation fold
      train_idx <- setdiff(idx, val_idx)                            # everything else

      X_cv_tr <- X[train_idx, ]; y_cv_tr <- y[train_idx]
      X_cv_va <- X[val_idx, ];   y_cv_va <- y[val_idx]

      m <- make_model(lam_val)
      m$fit(X_cv_tr, y_cv_tr)
      fold_mses[k + 1] <- mse(y_cv_va, m$predict(X_cv_va))
    }
    cv_scores[li] <- mean(fold_mses)
  }
  cv_scores
}

set.seed(6)
lam_grid <- 10^seq(-3, 1, length.out = 50)

cv_ridge <- kfold_cv(X_reg_std, y_reg, function(lam) RidgeRegression$new(lam = lam), lam_grid)
cv_lasso <- kfold_cv(X_reg_std, y_reg, function(lam) LassoRegression$new(lam = lam, n_iter = 2000), lam_grid)

best_ridge_lam <- lam_grid[which.min(cv_ridge)]
best_lasso_lam <- lam_grid[which.min(cv_lasso)]

cat(sprintf("Best Ridge lambda: %.4f   CV-MSE: %.4f\n", best_ridge_lam, min(cv_ridge)))
cat(sprintf("Best Lasso lambda: %.4f   CV-MSE: %.4f\n", best_lasso_lam, min(cv_lasso)))

# ── Plot ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
plot(lam_grid, cv_ridge, type = "l", log = "x", col = COLORS[2], lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Regularisation Strength lambda (log scale)", ylab = "Cross-Validated MSE",
     main = "5-Fold CV: Selecting lambda", ylim = range(c(cv_ridge, cv_lasso)))
lines(lam_grid, cv_lasso, col = COLORS[3], lwd = 2)
abline(v = best_ridge_lam, col = COLORS[2], lty = 2)
abline(v = best_lasso_lam, col = COLORS[3], lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c(sprintf("Ridge (best=%.3f)", best_ridge_lam),
                              sprintf("Lasso (best=%.3f)", best_lasso_lam)),
       col = COLORS[2:3], lwd = 2, bty = "n")

title: Chapter 05: Naive Bayes
text: Bayes’ Theorem, Gaussian & Multinomial Naive Bayes, and Laplace smoothing — from scratch

title: Chapter 05: Naive Bayes
text:
5.1 Overview
Naive Bayes is a probabilistic classifier based on Bayes’ Theorem. It asks: “Given these features, which class is most probable?”
The “naive” part: it assumes all features are conditionally independent given the class, an unrealistic but surprisingly effective assumption.

title: Chapter 05: Naive Bayes
text:
5.2 Bayes’ Theorem
Imagine you’re trying to guess which team someone supports based on the shirt they’re wearing. Bayes’ Theorem is like a rule that helps you figure out: “Given what I see, what’s the most likely team?”
The big formula looks like this:
\[P(y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{P(\mathbf{x} \mid y) \cdot P(y)}{P(\mathbf{x})}\]
But what does that mean in plain English? - \(P(y \mid \mathbf{x})\): How likely is it that it’s team \(y\) if I see features \(\mathbf{x}\)? (This is what we really want to know) - \(P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)\): If I already know it’s team \(y\), how likely am I to see these features? (Like: If they’re a fan, how likely are they to wear a red shirt?) - \(P(y)\): How common is team \(y\) in general? (Do a lot of people support this team?) - \(P(\mathbf{x})\): How common is it to see these features at all? (How common is it to wear a red shirt, no matter the team?)
The last term (\(P(\mathbf{x})\)) is just a normalizing thing — for comparing which team is most likely, we can ignore it.
How does the classifier pick a class?
It just asks: for each team, what’s the total score (probability) if I combine all the clues/features? The team with the highest score wins.
In symbols:
\[\hat{y} = \arg\max_y \left[ P(y) \cdot \prod_j P(x_j \mid y) \right]\]
(Translation: For every class \(y\), multiply how common \(y\) is by how likely all the features \(x_j\) are if you were in \(y\). Pick the biggest!)
To make the math easier (because multiplying a lot of small numbers can make computers confused), we often use logs:
\[\hat{y} = \arg\max_y \left[ \log P(y) + \sum_j \log P(x_j \mid y) \right]\]
(Now you’re just adding numbers instead of multiplying.)

title: Chapter 05: Naive Bayes
text:
5.3 Variants of Naive Bayes
There are several “flavors” of Naive Bayes, each designed for different types of data. They all use the same basic Bayes’ rule, but make different assumptions about how the features behave.

Gaussian Naive Bayes:

Assumption: Each feature \(x_j\) is normally distributed (follows a bell curve) within each class.
When to use: When your features are continuous (e.g., age, height, pixel intensity).

Bernoulli Naive Bayes:

Assumption: Each feature \(x_j\) is binary (can only be 0 or 1) within each class.
When to use: When your data consists of binary features, such as whether a word appears in a document or not.

Multinomial Naive Bayes:

Assumption: Features represent counts (non-negative integers), such as the number of times each word appears.
When to use: Especially good for document classification where features are word counts or frequencies.


In summary: - Use Gaussian NB for real-valued features, - Bernoulli NB for binary features, - or Multinomial NB for count data. They all work under the “naive” assumption of feature independence, but their probability calculations are tailored to the nature of your input data.

title: Chapter 05: Naive Bayes
text:
5.4 Gaussian Naive Bayes
Imagine you have numbers (like ages, heights, or exam scores) as features. Gaussian Naive Bayes pretends that, for each class, these numbers form a classic “bell curve” (like how most people are close to average height, and only a few are really tall or really short).
For each class and each feature, it figures out: - What is the average value for this feature in this class? (That’s called the “mean” \(\mu\).) - How much do the values tend to vary around that average? (That’s called the “variance” \(\sigma^2\).)
The formula below just says, “Given a value, how likely is it to appear if we’re in class \(c\)?” (You don’t have to worry too much about the math! It just turns the feature value, mean, and variance into a probability, using the standard bell curve formula.)
\[P(x_j \mid y=c) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x_j - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]
Explanation: This equation gives the probability of seeing a certain feature value \(x_j\), assuming we know the class is \(c\). - \(\mu\) is the average (mean) value of feature \(j\) in class \(c\). - \(\sigma^2\) is how much that feature varies (its variance) in class \(c\). - The formula is just the “bell curve” (Gaussian/Normal distribution) probability formula. - It assigns higher probability when \(x_j\) is close to the average, and lower probability when it’s far from the average. This lets Naive Bayes decide, for a given class, how “typical” a feature value is.
In short: - For every class, and for each number-feature, remember the average and how spread out it is. - When classifying something new, ask: “For each class, if I plugged this new value into the bell curve for this class, how likely would it be?” Combine all the results, and pick the class with the best total “score.”

title: Chapter 05: Naive Bayes
Chapter 05: Naive Bayes
text:
5.6 Laplace Smoothing (Dummies Explanation)
Let’s say our spam filter never saw the word “banana” in any spam email it learned from. If a new email contains “banana,” the math would say there’s a 0% chance it’s spam, just because “banana” never showed up in training. That’s not good! One missing word can ruin our whole prediction.
Laplace Smoothing is a simple trick to fix this: We just pretend every possible word showed up at least once in each class! In other words, we add a tiny “fake” count (\(\alpha\)) to every word, even if we never actually saw it.
The formula looks like this:
\[
P(x_j \mid y=c) = \frac{\text{count}(x_j, c) + \alpha}{\text{total words in } c + \alpha \times (\text{number of words})}
\]
If we set \(\alpha=1\), it’s called “add-one smoothing:” Every word gets one bonus point in all categories, making sure nothing ever gets a probability of zero.



Code
# Example: Laplace Smoothing by hand

# Suppose we have the following word counts for two classes:
spam_counts <- c(free = 3, win = 2, money = 1)
ham_counts  <- c(meeting = 2, report = 2, money = 1)
vocab <- sort(union(names(spam_counts), names(ham_counts)))   # All words seen

# Without Laplace smoothing:
word_prob_no_smoothing <- function(word, counts, total) {
  c_val <- if (word %in% names(counts)) counts[[word]] else 0
  c_val / total
}

total_spam <- sum(spam_counts)
total_ham  <- sum(ham_counts)
cat("Without smoothing:\n")
for (w in vocab) {
  cat(sprintf("P(%s|spam) = %.2f\n", w, word_prob_no_smoothing(w, spam_counts, total_spam)))
  cat(sprintf("P(%s|ham)  = %.2f\n", w, word_prob_no_smoothing(w, ham_counts, total_ham)))
}

# With Laplace (add-1) smoothing:
word_prob_laplace <- function(word, counts, total, V, alpha = 1) {
  c_val <- if (word %in% names(counts)) counts[[word]] else 0
  (c_val + alpha) / (total + alpha * V)
}

V <- length(vocab)
cat("\nWith Laplace (add-1) smoothing:\n")
for (w in vocab) {
  cat(sprintf("P(%s|spam) = %.2f\n", w, word_prob_laplace(w, spam_counts, total_spam, V)))
  cat(sprintf("P(%s|ham)  = %.2f\n", w, word_prob_laplace(w, ham_counts, total_ham, V)))
}

title: Chapter 07: Support Vector Machines (SVM)
text: Margins, soft margins, hinge loss, kernels, and a from-scratch SGD implementation

title: Chapter 07: Support Vector Machines (SVM)
text:
7.1 Overview
Imagine you want to separate two groups with a straight line (or a flat surface in more dimensions). SVM tries to draw this line so that it is as far away as possible from any point in both groups.
Instead of just finding any line that splits the groups, SVM looks for the line that gives the biggest “buffer zone” (margin) between them. This helps the model make better predictions on new, unseen data.
“Support vectors” are the specific data points that are closest to this separating line. They are important because they determine exactly where this line is placed.

title: Chapter 07: Support Vector Machines (SVM)
text:
7.2 Mathematical Formulation

Linear SVM (Hard Margin)
We want to split two groups using a straight line (or flat surface in higher dimensions).
SVM wants to find the line that has the biggest gap (margin) between the two groups — not just any line that separates them.
Imagine you lined up two groups of people and put the widest possible rope between them. The people closest to the rope decide where it goes — these are the “support vectors.”
Mathematically, SVM tries to: - Place a line (hyperplane) as far away from both groups as possible - Make sure all points are on the correct side, and not too close to the line
The rule for classifying each dot is: - If it’s on the right side of the line for its own group and at least 1 “unit” away, we’re happy.
The wider the margin (gap), the better. To get the widest gap, the mathy way is: - Make the numbers (\(\mathbf{w}\)) that define the line as small as possible, but still keep all points on the correct side.
Formal-ish: \[y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}_i + b) \geq 1\] for all points \(i\). (This just means: each point is on the correct side and not too close to the line.)
The training goal is: \[ \text{Make } \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 \text{ as small as possible, so the gap is as big as possible!} \]
All while making sure every point is separated by at least a margin of 1 from the line.


Code
# We use e1071::svm() here (an R interface to libsvm, the same engine behind
# sklearn.svm.SVC) purely to draw an illustrative margin/boundary plot — the
# from-scratch SVM implementation comes later in Section 7.4.

set.seed(7)
X1 <- sweep(matrix(rnorm(9 * 2), ncol = 2), 2, c(-2, -2), "+")
X2 <- sweep(matrix(rnorm(9 * 2), ncol = 2), 2, c(2, 2), "+")
X <- rbind(X1, X2)
y <- factor(c(rep(-1, 9), rep(1, 9)), levels = c(-1, 1))

# Fit linear SVM (for demo purpose only)
clf <- e1071::svm(X, y, kernel = "linear", cost = 1000, scale = FALSE)

# Plot the data
plot(X1[, 1], X1[, 2], col = "red", pch = 16,
     xlim = range(X[, 1]) + c(-1, 1), ylim = range(X[, 2]) + c(-1, 1),
     xlab = expression(x[1]), ylab = expression(x[2]),
     main = "Linear SVM: Decision Boundary and Margins")
points(X2[, 1], X2[, 2], col = "blue", pch = 16)

# Plot separator: build a grid and evaluate the decision function on it
xlim <- range(X[, 1]) + c(-1, 1); ylim <- range(X[, 2]) + c(-1, 1)
xx <- seq(xlim[1], xlim[2], length.out = 60)
yy <- seq(ylim[1], ylim[2], length.out = 60)
grid <- as.matrix(expand.grid(xx, yy))
colnames(grid) <- colnames(X)
Z <- matrix(attr(predict(clf, grid, decision.values = TRUE), "decision.values"), nrow = length(xx))

# Decision boundary and margins
contour(xx, yy, Z, levels = c(-1, 1), lty = 2, add = TRUE, drawlabels = FALSE)
contour(xx, yy, Z, levels = 0, lty = 1, lwd = 2, add = TRUE, drawlabels = FALSE)

# Highlight Support Vectors
sv <- clf$SV
points(sv[, 1], sv[, 2], pch = 1, cex = 2.2, lwd = 1.5)

legend("topleft", legend = c("Class -1", "Class +1", "Support Vectors", "Boundary (solid)", "Margin (dashed)"),
       col = c("red", "blue", "black", "black", "black"), pch = c(16, 16, 1, NA, NA),
       lty = c(NA, NA, NA, 1, 2), bty = "n")




Soft Margin SVM (for beginners)
Sometimes, in real life, there’s no way to perfectly separate two types of things (classes) with a straight line. A Soft Margin SVM lets us make some mistakes (“misclassifications”) to get a better overall result.
To do this, we introduce something called slack variables \(\xi_i\), which are just numbers that measure how much each point is breaking the rule. Bigger \(\xi_i\) means the point is either inside the margin or on the wrong side of the boundary.
The SVM now tries to: - Make the margin as wide as possible (keep \(\|\mathbf{w}\|^2\) small) - But it also allows mistakes, and adds up how “bad” they are (the sum of the \(\xi_i\)) - The trade-off is controlled by a parameter called C
In simple terms, the SVM solves this: \[
\text{Minimize: } \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + C \sum_i \xi_i \\
\text{Subject to: } y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}_i + b) \geq 1 - \xi_i\ \text{and}\ \xi_i \geq 0
\]
What does C do? - Small C (low value): The SVM will allow more mistakes (wider margin, but sloppier), which can help prevent overfitting (“high bias”). - Large C (high value): The SVM will be strict with mistakes (narrower margin, fits the data better), but might overfit (“high variance”).
In summary: - Soft Margin SVM lets some points be on the wrong side, but tries to keep the margin wide. - C lets you decide what’s more important: fewer mistakes or a bigger safety margin.


Code
# Generate some data that is not perfectly separable
set.seed(1)
X <- rbind(sweep(matrix(rnorm(15 * 2), ncol = 2), 2, c(2, 2), "-"),
           sweep(matrix(rnorm(15 * 2), ncol = 2), 2, c(2, 2), "+"))
Y <- c(rep(1, 15), rep(-1, 15))
# Add some noise - flip the label of 3 points to force misclassification
Y[1]  <- -1   # (Python index 0)
Y[17] <- 1    # (Python index 16)
Y[26] <- 1    # (Python index 25)
Y <- factor(Y, levels = c(-1, 1))

# Fit SVM model with soft margin (small C allows some errors)
clf <- e1071::svm(X, Y, kernel = "linear", cost = 0.7, scale = FALSE)

# Plot data points, coloring by label
plot(X[Y == 1, 1], X[Y == 1, 2], col = "blue", pch = 16,
     xlim = range(X[, 1]) + c(-0.5, 0.5), ylim = range(X[, 2]) + c(-0.5, 0.5),
     xlab = expression(x[1]), ylab = expression(x[2]),
     main = "Soft Margin SVM: Imperfectly Separable Data")
points(X[Y == -1, 1], X[Y == -1, 2], col = "red", pch = 16)

# Show support vectors
sv <- clf$SV
points(sv[, 1], sv[, 2], pch = 1, cex = 2.2, lwd = 2)

# Create grid to plot decision boundary and margins
xlim <- range(X[, 1]) + c(-0.5, 0.5); ylim <- range(X[, 2]) + c(-0.5, 0.5)
xx <- seq(xlim[1], xlim[2], length.out = 150)
yy <- seq(ylim[1], ylim[2], length.out = 150)
grid <- as.matrix(expand.grid(xx, yy))
colnames(grid) <- colnames(X)
Z <- matrix(attr(predict(clf, grid, decision.values = TRUE), "decision.values"), nrow = length(xx))

# Plot decision boundary and soft margins
contour(xx, yy, Z, levels = c(-1, 1), lty = 2, add = TRUE, drawlabels = FALSE)
contour(xx, yy, Z, levels = 0, lty = 1, lwd = 2, add = TRUE, drawlabels = FALSE)

legend("topright", legend = c("Class +1", "Class -1", "Support Vectors"),
       col = c("blue", "red", "black"), pch = c(16, 16, 1), bty = "n")




Hinge Loss
The hinge loss is a way for SVMs to figure out how “bad” a guess was. Imagine you want your SVM to not just get the answer right, but to be really sure—so sure that every point is not just on the right side, but far from the border.
For each point, hinge loss does this: - If the point is on the correct side and a safe distance away: loss = 0 (no penalty). - If the point is either wrong or too close to the border: the farther it is from a comfortable margin, the bigger the penalty.
The formula looks like this (don’t worry if it seems scary):
\[
L_{\text{hinge}}(y, \hat{y}) = \max(0, 1 - y \cdot \hat{y})
\]

\(y\) is the real answer (+1 or -1).
\(\hat{y}\) is your SVM’s guess for the point (it’s a score, not just a class).
If \(y \cdot \hat{y}\) is 1 or more, life is good (loss is 0).
If not, the “badness” grows the further you get from perfect.

Why do we care? Because SVM doesn’t just want correct answers, it wants answers that are confident.
In practice, SVMs balance two things: 1. Hinge loss (make as few and as small mistakes as possible), 2. Keeping the weights small (so the separation isn’t wild—called regularization).
That total objective looks like:
\[
J(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i \max(0, 1 - y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}_i + b)) + \lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^2
\]
This just means: “Let’s minimize mistakes (hinge loss) + don’t get too crazy with the separator (regularization).” That’s what makes SVMs powerful and reliable.

title: Chapter 07: Support Vector Machines (SVM)
text:
7.3 The Kernel Trick (For Dummies)
Imagine your data is mixed up in a way that drawing any straight line (or plane) can’t separate the categories—no matter how hard you try! SVMs have a superpower called the kernel trick for this.
Here’s the idea: - What if instead of working in the world you see (like drawing a line on paper), you could “lift” the points up into a magical, invisible world with more dimensions? - In this new space, the points might spread out so nicely that a straight line can separate them. (It’s like taking a tangled-up string and spreading it out so it’s straight.)
But wait: doing all that math sounds super hard, right? Here’s where the magic happens. - The kernel trick lets you “pretend” you’re doing this crazy mapping—without actually doing it! - Instead, it gives you a formula (the kernel function) that does all the hard work in the background.
In math-jargon: - Instead of transforming both points (\(\mathbf{x}_i\) and \(\mathbf{x}_j\)) to a high dimension and then taking their dot product, - You just use the kernel function: \(K(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)\), and it acts like you did all that work.
So: Kernel = the shortcut that lets SVMs draw wiggly, complicated lines to separate messy data, without doing mind-bending math.

Types of Kernels in SVM
SVMs get their “superpower” from kernels. Each kernel is like a recipe for how to compare two data points. Here are the common ones, explained simply:
1. Linear Kernel: - What it does: Compares two points just by seeing how much they point in the “same direction” — like classic SVM. - Equation: \(\mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{x}_j\) (just multiply and add up the features) - For dummies: “Is A like B? Add up their matching parts.” - When to use: When a straight line (or plane) can separate your classes.
2. Polynomial Kernel: - What it does: Lets you draw “curvy” separator lines by comparing not just the features, but their combinations as well. - Equation: \((\mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{x}_j + c)^d\) (\(c\) shifts things; \(d\) is how wiggly the line is) - For dummies: “Take the regular A·B, add a number, and make it bigger by multiplying it by itself a few times!” - When to use: When you think a curve (not a line) can separate the data.
3. RBF (Radial Basis Function) / Gaussian Kernel: - What it does: Looks at how close or far apart two points are. Close = very similar, far = not similar. - Equation: \(\exp\left(-\gamma \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j\|^2\right)\) - (If \(x_i = x_j\), then output is biggest: \(e^0 = 1\); if they’re far, output shrinks.) - For dummies: “If points are close, they’re friends; if far, they’re strangers.” - When to use: The default for messy, tangled data.
4. Sigmoid Kernel: - What it does: Acts kind of like a mini neural network layer—squishes values between -1 and 1. - Equation: \(\tanh(\kappa \mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{x}_j + c)\) - For dummies: “Do the usual compare, scale/stretch it, add a number, squish the answer so it’s never too big or small.” - When to use: Rare - typically if you want to mimic neural-network-style decisions.
Summary: - Kernel = shortcut formula for ‘are these points similar?’ - Each kind gives SVM a new way to separate data, from boring lines to wild scribbles, all without actually changing the data’s coordinates!

title: Chapter 09: K-Means Clustering
text:
9.1 Overview
K-Means is the most widely used unsupervised clustering algorithm.
Goal: partition \(n\) data points into \(K\) clusters such that each point belongs to the cluster with the nearest mean (centroid).
No labels needed — the algorithm discovers structure on its own.

title: Chapter 09: K-Means Clustering
text:
9.2 The Algorithm
Imagine you have a bunch of points and you want to group them so that similar points end up together. That’s what K-Means does! Here’s how it works in simple terms:

Pick a number, K. This is how many groups (clusters) you want to find.
Randomly put down K points—think of them as “group centers” (centroids).
Do these steps over and over until things stop changing:

For each point, figure out which group center (centroid) it’s closest to. Assign the point to that group.
For each group, move its center to the average location of all the points now in that group. (This is like saying, “Where is the middle of my group now?”)


You stop when the groups don’t really change anymore (either the points stop jumping from group to group, or the group centers barely move).

title: Chapter 09: K-Means Clustering
text:
9.3 Mathematical Objective
What does K-Means try to do — for dummies, with math:
The goal of K-Means is to group your data points so that points in the same group (cluster) are as close as possible to each other, using their mean as the “center.”
Here’s what it’s trying to minimize:
\[J = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in C_k} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2\]
Let’s break this down:

You choose \(K\) — how many clusters you want.
For each cluster \(k\), you have a center (called a centroid) \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\). It’s just the average (mean) of all the points in that cluster.
For every data point \(\mathbf{x}_i\), you look at which cluster it’s assigned to (let’s call that group \(C_k\)).
You measure the squared distance (\(\|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2\)) from that point to its cluster center.
The algorithm adds up all these squared distances, for all the points and all clusters.

In plain English: K-Means keeps trying to group the points and move the cluster centers to make this total “sum of squared distances to centers” as small as possible. (Picture it as people huddling as close to their group leader as they can!)
Fun fact: This is called the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS).
Math can be tricky: Since this problem isn’t “nice” (non-convex), where you start (initial cluster centers) can change the result you get.

title: Chapter 11: Neural Networks (MLP)
text: Perceptrons, forward/backprop from scratch, and hyperparameter tuning on real data

title: Chapter 11: Neural Networks (MLP)
text:
11.1 Overview
A neural network is a layered architecture of interconnected “neurons”. Each layer transforms its input and passes it forward — like an assembly line of feature detectors.
Inspired by (but not a literal model of) biological neurons.

title: Chapter 11: Neural Networks (MLP)
text:
11.2 What is a Neural Network?
A neural network is a computer system designed to recognize patterns. You can think of it like a simplified version of how the human brain works. It is made up of layers of tiny units called “neurons” that are connected together.

11.3 How Does It Work? Steps for Beginners:

Input Layer:

The neural network takes in data (for example, pictures or numbers) through the first layer, called the input layer.
Each neuron in this layer represents an input feature (like a pixel in an image or a measurement in a table).

Hidden Layers:

The information from the input layer moves through one or more hidden layers.
Inside each neuron, the data is multiplied by some numbers called ‘weights’, then added up and passed through a special math function (called an “activation function”) that decides what to keep or ignore.
This lets the network learn complex patterns or rules about your data.

Output Layer:

Finally, the processed information reaches the output layer.
The output layer gives the answer, prediction, or classification (for example, “cat” or “dog”, or a number between 0 and 1).

Learning (Training):

At the start, the neural network guesses with random weights.
We show it lots of examples with known answers and compare its prediction to the correct answer.
It then makes small changes to its weights to do better next time.
This learning process is called “training”, and it happens many times until the network gets good at predicting.


In summary: A neural network is like a big system of “if this, then that” rules—but instead of writing the rules by hand, the network figures them out automatically by learning from examples!

title: Chapter 11: Neural Networks (MLP)
text:
11.3 Key Neural Network Concepts
Neural networks are made up of simple parts called neurons, which are arranged in layers. The main building block is the neuron (or perceptron), which takes inputs, applies weights and biases, and then passes the result through a special function called an activation function. This activation function helps the network learn complex, non-linear patterns.
When data moves through the network from the input to the output layer, it’s called the forward pass. The network then learns by comparing its output to the correct answer and adjusting its internal parameters using a method known as backpropagation. This process helps the network get better over time at recognizing patterns and making predictions.

11.3.1 The Perceptron (Building Block)
Imagine a “neuron” as a tiny calculator. It takes in some numbers (inputs), multiplies each by its own special setting (called a weight), adds them up, and then does one last tweak (adding a bias, which is just another number).
Here’s the equation:
\[\text{output} = \text{activation}(w_1 \cdot x_1 + w_2 \cdot x_2 + \cdots + w_p \cdot x_p + b)\]

\(x_1, x_2, ..., x_p\) = your input values (like pixels or measurements)
\(w_1, w_2, ..., w_p\) = “weights” (numbers the model learns)
\(b\) = bias (an extra number the model learns)
activation = a special function that decides what gets passed on (see below)

So, for each input: 1. Multiply input value by its weight 2. Add them all up 3. Add the bias 4. Pass the result through an activation function (the “activation” turns raw numbers into something useful, like “yes/no” or a score)


11.3.2 Activation Function
An activation function is like a decision-making step inside each tiny “neuron” of a neural network. It takes the result calculated by a neuron (a number, often called \(z\) or “signal in”) and turns it into something useful for the next layer, often squashing or shaping the number in some way.
Think of it as a light switch or a filter that decides: “Should I let this signal pass, and if so, how much?”
Why do we need it? Without activation functions, a neural network is just a fancy version of a straight line—no matter how many layers, it can’t learn complex patterns. Activation functions add non-linearity, letting your network learn curves, twists, and everything in between.



Types of Activation Functions
Here are some of the most popular types, written with their math, what they mean, and where they’re often used:









Name
Formula
What does it do?
Typical Usage




Sigmoid
\(\displaystyle\text{Sigmoid}(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\)
Squashes any number to 0–1.
Final layer for probabilities, e.g., “Is it a cat?”


ReLU
\(\displaystyle\text{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)\)
Sets negative numbers to 0, keeps positives.
Most hidden layers (makes learning faster!)


Tanh
\(\displaystyle\text{tanh}(z) = \frac{e^z-e^{-z}}{e^z+e^{-z}}\)
Squashes to -1 to +1
For data that swings both ways, sometimes in hidden layers


Softmax
\(\displaystyle\text{Softmax}(z_j) = \frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_i e^{z_i}}\)
Turns a list of numbers into a set of probabilities that add up to 1
Output layer for picking one category out of many (cat, dog, hamster)




In plain language: - Sigmoid: Like a dimmer switch, smoothly goes from “off” to “on” (0 to 1). Used when you want a probability. - ReLU: Like a broken light—only turns on for positive signals, ignores anything negative. Makes training quicker! - Tanh: Like a seesaw—goes from strongly negative (-1), through zero, to strongly positive (+1). Good for balancing data that swings both ways. - Softmax: Like a voting machine—turns the outputs into percentages that all add up to 100%, so you can “pick a winner” in classification tasks.
In summary: The activation function is the magic ingredient that lets neural networks learn things that are more complicated than simple lines. It helps shape the answers your network can discover!


Code
# Visualize the activation functions in a panel

sigmoid_viz <- function(z) 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
relu_viz <- function(z) pmax(0, z)
tanh_viz <- function(z) tanh(z)
softmax_viz <- function(z_mat) {
  # z_mat: matrix with one row per class, columns = points
  exp_z <- exp(sweep(z_mat, 2, apply(z_mat, 2, max), "-"))
  sweep(exp_z, 2, colSums(exp_z), "/")
}

z <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 300)
z_softmax <- rbind(z - 2, z, z + 2)   # simulate 3-class input

par(mfrow = c(1, 4))

plot(z, sigmoid_viz(z), type = "l", col = "purple", xlab = "z", ylab = "output",
     main = "Sigmoid", ylim = c(-0.1, 1.1)); grid()

plot(z, relu_viz(z), type = "l", col = "blue", xlab = "z", ylab = "output",
     main = "ReLU", ylim = c(-1, 5.25)); grid()

plot(z, tanh_viz(z), type = "l", col = "orange", xlab = "z", ylab = "output",
     main = "Tanh", ylim = c(-1.1, 1.1)); grid()

softmax_vals <- softmax_viz(z_softmax)
plot(z, softmax_vals[1, ], type = "l", col = "red", xlab = "z", ylab = "probability",
     main = "Softmax (3 classes)", ylim = c(-0.05, 1.05))
lines(z, softmax_vals[2, ], col = "green")
lines(z, softmax_vals[3, ], col = "grey40")
legend("topright", legend = c("Class 1", "Class 2", "Class 3"),
       col = c("red", "green", "grey40"), lwd = 1, cex = 0.7, bty = "n")
grid()

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))




Common activation functions: Dummies Edition
Think of the “activation function” as the final decision-making step for a neuron—the math shortcut that tells it how to react to its input.









Name
What it looks like (formula)
What does it do?
Where is it used?




Sigmoid
\(\displaystyle\text{Sigmoid}(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\)
Squashes to 0–1
Yes/no probs (outputs)


ReLU
\(\displaystyle\text{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)\)
0 if negative, else z
Hidden layers, speed boost!


Tanh
\(\displaystyle \text{tanh}(z) = \frac{e^z-e^{-z}}{e^z+e^{-z}}\)
Squashes to -1..1
Ups & downs, balance


Softmax
\(\displaystyle\text{Softmax}(z_j) = \frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_i e^{z_i}}\)
Converts to probability sum = 1
Pick a category (cats/dogs)



Silly analogy: - Sigmoid: Like a dimmer switch—smoothly turns up from “no” (0) to “yes” (1). - ReLU: Like a door—shuts (0) for negative, wide open for positive! - Tanh: Like a balance scale—tips between “negative” (-1) and “positive” (+1). - Softmax: Like an election—each category gets its fair share of probability votes, sum always 1.
Bottom line: The neuron combines your inputs, adds a bias, then pulls out one of these calculators to turn the jumble into a clear, useful output!

title: Chapter 11: Neural Networks (MLP)
text:
11.3.4 Forward Pass
Let’s break down how a neural network passes your input through all its layers, step by step:

Start with your input: \[\mathbf{a}^{(0)} = \mathbf{x}\] (This just means: the first “activation” is your input data.)
At each layer: \[\mathbf{z}^{(l)} = \mathbf{W}^{(l)} \cdot \mathbf{a}^{(l-1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(l)}\] (Take last layer’s output, multiply by that layer’s weights, add bias — like making a fancy sandwich out of the last layer’s ingredients!)
\[\mathbf{a}^{(l)} = f(\mathbf{z}^{(l)})\] (Now, squish that result through an “activation function” — so it’s not just a plain number, but something useful! This is how neurons decide to “fire” or not.)
Output: \[\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{a}^{(L)}\] (Final layer pops out your prediction. Ta-da!)

Bottom line: At each step, you’re just taking the last answer, doing a little math (weights and bias), squishing it through a function, and marching on to the next “layer-brain cell” until you get your output!

title: Chapter 11: Neural Networks (MLP)
text:
11.3.5 Backpropagation
What is Backprop? It’s just a step-by-step way to figure out how much each weight and bias in your network should change, so your neural network gets better at its job!
The “backward” part: You start at the end (the output), see how wrong you were (the loss), and work backwards to find out who to blame in each layer.

“Dumbed Down” Equations with Explanations:

1. How does the loss change if I nudge a weight or bias?

Imagine a super simple neuron:
\(z = w \cdot a_\text{prev} + b\) \(a = f(z)\) (like sigmoid of \(z\)) \(L\) = loss (e.g., how far our guess is from truth)

For a single weight \(w\): \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} \cdot \frac{\partial a}{\partial z} \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial w}\]
Fill in each “link in the chain”: - \(\frac{\partial z}{\partial w} = a_\text{prev}\) (the input that fed this weight) - \(\frac{\partial a}{\partial z} = f'(z)\) (derivative of activation function) - \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial a}\) (depends on loss function & output)
So, it’s like: > “How much did my guess hurt?”, times > “How much does the squishing function pass that on?”, times > “How much did this particular weight actually contribute?”
Vectorized for whole layer \(l\): \[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(l)}} =
\left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(l)}} \right)
\cdot
\left( \mathbf{a}^{(l-1)} \right)^\top
\]
For the biases: \[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{b}^{(l)}} =
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(l)}}
\] (Just the error signal, since bias only adds a constant.)


2. Passing the blame backward:

The “blame” (error, called \(\delta\) or “delta”) for a layer is: \[
\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{z}^{(l)}}
\]
To find the error for a hidden layer, you “pass back” from the next layer: \[
\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l)} =
(\mathbf{W}^{(l+1)})^\top \cdot \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(l+1)} \odot f'\left(\mathbf{z}^{(l)}\right)
\] where \(\odot\) means element-wise (Hadamard) multiplication, and \(f'\) is “how much can this neuron still change the output?” (the slope of activation).


Silly analogy: Think of each layer like workers on an assembly line: “How much did my work have to do with the final mistake?” Then, pass the blame to the previous worker, with adjustments for how much their work mattered!

title: Chapter 11: Neural Networks (MLP)
text:
11.4 Deep Learning, Step by Step
A walk through how a neural network learns, and what each one actually means.

title: Chapter 11: Neural Networks (MLP)
section: The big idea in one breath
text:
The big idea in one breath
A neural network learns the way a person does: it makes a guess, checks how wrong it was, then goes back and adjusts — and repeats this thousands of times until the guesses get good.
That loop has four named parts, and everything below is just those four parts in slow motion:

Forward propagation → Loss → Backpropagation → Gradient descent → (repeat)





Neural Network Training Steps



The building block: one neuron
A neuron is a tiny calculator. It takes some numbers in, multiplies each by an importance knob called a weight, adds them up, adds a small offset called a bias, and then passes the result through a squashing function.
The squashing function (also called the activation function) compresses the neuron’s output into a fixed range—usually between 0 and 1, or -1 and 1—no matter how large or small the input. This helps the network deal with extreme values and lets it learn and represent non-linear patterns. Common squashing functions are the sigmoid, tanh, and ReLU.
Stack a few neurons side‑by‑side and you get a layer. Stack several layers front‑to‑back — like Lego bricks — and you get a deep neural network (the “deep” just means “many layers”).
Notation cheat‑sheet (don’t memorize, just glance back here):



Symbol
Plain meaning




\(\mathbf{x}\)
the input data (what you feed in)


\(\mathbf{W}\)
weights — the “importance knobs” the network learns


\(\mathbf{b}\)
bias — a small nudge/offset


\(\mathbf{z}\)
the weighted sum (before squashing)


\(\sigma\)
activation function (the squasher)


\(\mathbf{a}\)
activation — the neuron’s output


\(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\)
the prediction


\(\mathbf{y}\)
the true answer


\(\mathcal{L}\)
loss — a single “how wrong were we?” score


\(\eta\)
learning rate — how big a step we take when adjusting


\((l)\)
which layer we’re talking about






Step 1: Input: hand the network the data
\[\mathbf{a}^{(0)} = \mathbf{x}\]
In English: we call the raw input the “activation of layer 0.” Nothing fancy is happening yet — this is just saying “the starting point is whatever data you fed in.” If you’re classifying a photo, \(\mathbf{x}\) is the pixels.



Step 2: Weighted sum: mix the inputs
\[\mathbf{z}^{(l)} = \mathbf{W}^{(l)}\,\mathbf{a}^{(l-1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(l)}\]
In English: every neuron takes the outputs of the previous layer, multiplies each by its weight (how much it cares about that input), adds them all up, and adds its bias.
Dummy analogy: it’s a weighted recipe. If you’re guessing whether a photo is a cat, “pointy ears” might get a big weight and “background color” a tiny one. The bias is like a chef’s baseline seasoning added no matter what.



Step 3: Activation: decide how strongly to fire
\[\mathbf{a}^{(l)} = \sigma\!\left(\mathbf{z}^{(l)}\right)\]
In English: the weighted sum is pushed through an activation function \(\sigma\). This does two jobs: it keeps numbers in a sensible range, and — crucially — it adds non‑linearity so the network can learn curvy, complicated patterns instead of just straight lines.
Common squashers: - ReLU: \(\sigma(z) = \max(0, z)\) — “if negative, output 0; otherwise pass it through.” Simple and the most popular. - Sigmoid: \(\sigma(z) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\) — squashes anything into a 0–1 range, like a probability.
Dummy analogy: a neuron deciding whether to “fire,” like a dimmer switch that stays off until the signal is strong enough.
Steps 2 and 3 repeat for every layer, feeding forward. That’s why it’s called forward propagation.



Step 4: Prediction: the network’s final guess
\[\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{a}^{(L)} = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\mathbf{z}^{(L)}\right)\]
In English: the last layer (\(L\)) produces the answer. For classification we usually pass it through softmax, which turns raw scores into probabilities that add up to 1.
\[\mathrm{softmax}(z_i) = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}\]
Dummy analogy: the network says “I’m 80% sure this is a cat, 15% a dog, 5% a fox.” This is the “future” — we’ve traveled forward and seen the outcome.

title: Chapter 11: Neural Networks (MLP)
section: Step 5: Loss: measure how wrong we were
text:
Step 5: Loss: measure how wrong we were
\[\mathcal{L} = -\sum_i y_i \,\log \hat{y}_i \quad \text{(cross‑entropy, for classification)}\]
In English: the loss is a single number scoring how far the prediction \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\) is from the truth \(\mathbf{y}\). Big loss = very wrong. Small loss = doing great.
For predicting numbers (regression) instead of categories, a common choice is Mean Squared Error:
\[\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \left(y_i - \hat{y}_i\right)^2\]
Dummy analogy: this is the network looking at its guess and its report card and going “ouch, I was way off.” This mistake is exactly what it’s about to learn from.


Step 6: Backpropagation starts: blame the output
\[\delta^{(L)} = \hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y}\]
In English: now we travel back in time. We start at the output and compute the error signal \(\delta\) — literally “prediction minus truth.” It says how much, and in which direction, each output neuron was off.
Dummy analogy: you got the wrong answer on a test, so you first figure out by how much your final answer missed.



Step 7: Backpropagation continues: share the blame backward
\[\delta^{(l)} = \left(\mathbf{W}^{(l+1)\top}\,\delta^{(l+1)}\right) \odot \sigma'\!\left(\mathbf{z}^{(l)}\right)\]
In English: the error is passed backward layer by layer. Each hidden neuron gets a share of the blame based on (a) how much it fed into the neurons ahead of it (the \(\mathbf{W}^\top\) part) and (b) how sensitive it was at that moment (the \(\sigma'\) part, the slope of the activation). The \(\odot\) just means “multiply element‑by‑element.”
Dummy analogy: it’s a chain of accountability. The final mistake gets traced back through the network — “you contributed this much to the error, and you this much” — so everyone knows their part.
This is the “backpropagation” (backward propagation of errors) that beginners find scary. It’s really just the chain rule from calculus, applied politely, layer by layer.



Step 8: Gradients: how much did each weight matter?
\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)}\,\mathbf{a}^{(l-1)\top}\]
In English: the gradient answers “if I wiggle this weight a tiny bit, does the loss go up or down, and how fast?” A big gradient means that weight has a big effect on the error.
Dummy analogy: for every knob in the machine, we now know which way to turn it and how much it matters for reducing the mistake.



Step 9: Gradient descent: nudge the weights to be less wrong
\[\mathbf{W}^{(l)} \leftarrow \mathbf{W}^{(l)} - \eta\,\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(l)}}\]
In English: finally we update every weight: move it a small step in the direction that lowers the loss. The step size is the learning rate \(\eta\) — small enough to be safe, big enough to make progress. (Biases update the same way.)
Dummy analogy — walking downhill in fog: the loss is a valley. The gradient tells you which way is up, so you step the opposite way, down. Take too big a step (\(\eta\) too large) and you overshoot the valley; too small and you crawl forever.



Step 10: Repeat: learn from mistakes, again and again
Now jump back to Step 1 with the freshly nudged weights and do it all over. One full pass over the training data is called an epoch, and networks train for many epochs.
Each loop, the prediction gets a little better and the loss curve slopes downward — the visual proof that, just like people, the network is learning from its mistakes.
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │                                              │
        ▼                                              │
   Forward pass ──► Loss ──► Backprop ──► Update weights┘
   (predict the       (how    (assign      (nudge to be
    future)          wrong?)   blame)       less wrong)



The whole thing on one page









#
Step
Equation
What it really means




1
Input
\(\mathbf{a}^{(0)}=\mathbf{x}\)
feed in the data


2
Weighted sum
\(\mathbf{z}^{(l)}=\mathbf{W}^{(l)}\mathbf{a}^{(l-1)}+\mathbf{b}^{(l)}\)
mix inputs by importance


3
Activation
\(\mathbf{a}^{(l)}=\sigma(\mathbf{z}^{(l)})\)
decide how strongly to fire


4
Prediction
\(\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{z}^{(L)})\)
make the final guess


5
Loss
\(\mathcal{L}=-\sum_i y_i\log\hat{y}_i\)
score how wrong we were


6
Output error
\(\delta^{(L)}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\mathbf{y}\)
measure the miss at the end


7
Hidden error
\(\delta^{(l)}=(\mathbf{W}^{(l+1)\top}\delta^{(l+1)})\odot\sigma'(\mathbf{z}^{(l)})\)
share blame backward


8
Gradients
\(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{W}^{(l)}}=\delta^{(l)}\mathbf{a}^{(l-1)\top}\)
how much each weight matters


9
Update
\(\mathbf{W}^{(l)}\leftarrow\mathbf{W}^{(l)}-\eta\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{W}^{(l)}}\)
nudge weights downhill


10
Repeat
—
do it again until loss is small






Five words that will make you sound like an expert

Weights & biases — the numbers the network learns; everything else is fixed math.
Forward propagation — pushing data through to get a prediction.
Loss function — the single score of “how wrong.”
Backpropagation — the chain rule sending the error backward to assign blame.
Gradient descent — walking the weights downhill to shrink the loss.

That’s the entire game. Everything fancier — CNNs for images, RNNs/Transformers for sequences, dropout, batch‑norm — is a variation on this same four‑part loop.

title: Chapter 11: Neural Networks (MLP)
text:
11.5 From-Scratch R Implementation


Code
# neural_network.R

sigmoid <- function(z) 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-pmin(pmax(z, -500), 500)))
sigmoid_deriv <- function(a) a * (1 - a)
relu_act <- function(z) pmax(0.0, z)
relu_deriv <- function(z) as.numeric(z > 0)
tanh_fn <- function(z) tanh(z)
tanh_deriv <- function(a) 1.0 - a^2   # given a = tanh(z)

# A fully connected layer, represented as a plain list (not a class) for speed —
# `layer$W`, `layer$b`, plus caches for backprop. Functions below operate on/return
# an updated copy of the layer, mirroring the Python `DenseLayer` object's fields.

make_dense_layer <- function(n_in, n_out, activation = "relu") {
  scale <- sqrt(2.0 / n_in)   # He initialization
  list(
    W = matrix(rnorm(n_out * n_in, 0, scale), nrow = n_out, ncol = n_in),
    b = rep(0.0, n_out),
    activation = activation,
    z = NULL, a = NULL, a_prev = NULL
  )
}

layer_activate <- function(layer, z) {
  switch(layer$activation,
    sigmoid = sigmoid(z),
    relu = relu_act(z),
    tanh = tanh_fn(z),
    z   # linear
  )
}

layer_activate_deriv <- function(layer, val, z) {
  switch(layer$activation,
    sigmoid = sigmoid_deriv(val),
    relu = relu_deriv(z),
    tanh = tanh_deriv(val),
    rep(1.0, length(z))
  )
}

layer_forward <- function(layer, a_prev) {
  layer$a_prev <- a_prev
  layer$z <- as.numeric(layer$W %*% a_prev) + layer$b
  layer$a <- layer_activate(layer, layer$z)
  layer
}

layer_backward <- function(layer, delta_next) {
  # delta_next: gradient w.r.t. this layer's output (a)
  delta <- delta_next * layer_activate_deriv(layer, layer$a, layer$z)   # gradient through activation
  dW <- outer(delta, layer$a_prev)               # gradient for W
  db <- delta                                     # gradient for b
  delta_prev <- as.numeric(t(layer$W) %*% delta)  # gradient to pass back to previous layer
  list(delta_prev = delta_prev, dW = dW, db = db)
}

# Multilayer Perceptron.
# Supports arbitrary architectures, binary and multiclass classification.
# Also can do regression if last activation is linear.
# Pure base R — no ML libraries.

MLP <- setRefClass(
  "MLP",
  fields = list(layers = "list", lr = "numeric", n_epochs = "numeric",
                loss_history = "numeric", val_loss_history = "numeric", task = "character"),
  methods = list(
    initialize = function(layer_sizes, activations = NULL, lr = 0.01, n_epochs = 100,
                          task = "classification", ...) {
      # layer_sizes: e.g. c(2, 4, 4, 1) -> 2 inputs, two hidden layers, 1 output
      # activations: vector of activations per layer (excluding input)
      # task: 'classification' or 'regression'
      n_layers <- length(layer_sizes) - 1
      if (is.null(activations)) {
        if (task == "classification") {
          activations <- c(rep("relu", n_layers - 1), "sigmoid")
        } else {
          activations <- c(rep("relu", n_layers - 1), "linear")
        }
      }
      layers <<- lapply(seq_len(n_layers), function(i) {
        make_dense_layer(layer_sizes[i], layer_sizes[i + 1], activations[i])
      })
      lr <<- lr; n_epochs <<- n_epochs
      loss_history <<- numeric(0); val_loss_history <<- numeric(0)
      task <<- task
      callSuper(...)
    },

    forward_one = function(x) {
      a <- x
      for (i in seq_along(layers)) {
        layers[[i]] <<- layer_forward(layers[[i]], a)
        a <- layers[[i]]$a
      }
      a
    },

    bce_loss = function(y_hat, y_true) {
      # Binary cross-entropy loss.
      yh <- pmin(pmax(y_hat, 1e-15), 1 - 1e-15)
      mean(-(y_true * log(yh) + (1 - y_true) * log(1 - yh)))
    },

    mse_loss = function(y_hat, y_true) mean((y_hat - y_true)^2),

    fit = function(X, y, X_val = NULL, y_val = NULL) {
      n <- nrow(X)
      for (epoch in seq_len(n_epochs)) {
        indices <- sample(n)    # shuffle
        total_loss <- 0.0

        for (i in indices) {
          xi <- X[i, ]; yi <- y[i]

          # Forward pass
          output <- forward_one(xi)
          yh <- output[1]

          if (task == "classification") {
            yh_c <- min(max(yh, 1e-15), 1 - 1e-15)
            total_loss <- total_loss - (yi * log(yh_c) + (1 - yi) * log(1 - yh_c))
            # Output gradient: d(BCE)/d(yh) for sigmoid output = yh - yi
            delta <- yh - yi
          } else {   # regression (MSE loss)
            total_loss <- total_loss + (yh - yi)^2
            delta <- 2 * (yh - yi)     # d(MSE) / d(yh)
          }

          # Backward pass through layers (reversed)
          grads <- vector("list", length(layers))
          for (li in rev(seq_along(layers))) {
            res <- layer_backward(layers[[li]], delta)
            delta <- res$delta_prev
            grads[[li]] <- list(dW = res$dW, db = res$db)
          }

          # Update weights
          for (li in seq_along(layers)) {
            layers[[li]]$W <<- layers[[li]]$W - lr * grads[[li]]$dW
            layers[[li]]$b <<- layers[[li]]$b - lr * grads[[li]]$db
          }
        }

        # Save training loss
        train_loss <- total_loss / n
        loss_history <<- c(loss_history, train_loss)

        # Optionally, evaluate validation loss
        if (!is.null(X_val) && !is.null(y_val)) {
          val_loss <- evaluate(X_val, y_val)
          val_loss_history <<- c(val_loss_history, val_loss)
        }
      }

      invisible(.self)
    },

    predict_proba = function(X) {
      # Only meaningful for classification
      vapply(seq_len(nrow(X)), function(i) forward_one(X[i, ])[1], numeric(1))
    },

    predict = function(X, threshold = 0.5) {
      if (task == "classification") {
        as.integer(predict_proba(X) >= threshold)
      } else {
        vapply(seq_len(nrow(X)), function(i) forward_one(X[i, ])[1], numeric(1))
      }
    },

    evaluate = function(X, y) {
      # Compute loss on provided data
      y_hat <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(X)), function(i) forward_one(X[i, ])[1], numeric(1))
      if (task == "classification") bce_loss(y_hat, y) else mse_loss(y_hat, y)
    },

    accuracy = function(X, y) {
      # Only for classification
      preds <- predict(X)
      mean(preds == y)
    },

    r2_score = function(X, y) {
      # Only for regression
      preds <- predict(X)
      mean_y <- mean(y)
      ss_tot <- sum((y - mean_y)^2)
      ss_res <- sum((y - preds)^2)
      if (ss_tot != 0) 1 - ss_res / ss_tot else 0.0
    }
  )
)




Code
# ── Demos: Classification and Regression on Splits ─────────────────────────────

train_val_test_split <- function(X, y, train_frac = 0.6, val_frac = 0.2, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)
  n <- nrow(X)
  idx <- sample(n)
  n_train <- floor(train_frac * n)
  n_val <- floor(val_frac * n)
  train_idx <- idx[1:n_train]
  val_idx <- idx[(n_train + 1):(n_train + n_val)]
  test_idx <- idx[(n_train + n_val + 1):n]
  list(X_train = X[train_idx, , drop = FALSE], y_train = y[train_idx],
       X_val   = X[val_idx, , drop = FALSE],   y_val   = y[val_idx],
       X_test  = X[test_idx, , drop = FALSE],  y_test  = y[test_idx])
}

cat("==== Binary Classification: XOR Problem ====\n")
# Demo data: XOR (repeat for more samples)
X_cls <- matrix(rep(c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1), 20), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
y_cls <- rep(c(0, 1, 1, 0), 20)

split1 <- train_val_test_split(X_cls, y_cls, train_frac = 0.5, val_frac = 0.25, seed = 10)
X_train <- split1$X_train; y_train <- split1$y_train
X_val   <- split1$X_val;   y_val   <- split1$y_val
X_test  <- split1$X_test;  y_test  <- split1$y_test

mlp_cls <- MLP$new(layer_sizes = c(2, 4, 1), activations = c("relu", "sigmoid"),
                    lr = 0.1, n_epochs = 300)
mlp_cls$fit(X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val)

cat(sprintf("Train Accuracy:     %.3f\n", mlp_cls$accuracy(X_train, y_train)))
cat(sprintf("Validation Accuracy: %.3f\n", mlp_cls$accuracy(X_val, y_val)))
cat(sprintf("Test Accuracy:      %.3f\n", mlp_cls$accuracy(X_test, y_test)))
cat(sprintf("Final Train Loss: %.4f\n", tail(mlp_cls$loss_history, 1)))
if (length(mlp_cls$val_loss_history) > 0) {
  cat(sprintf("Final Val Loss:   %.4f\n", tail(mlp_cls$val_loss_history, 1)))
}

cat("\nPredictions on Test:\n")
for (i in 1:min(8, nrow(X_test))) {
  prob <- mlp_cls$predict_proba(matrix(X_test[i, ], nrow = 1))
  pred <- ifelse(prob >= 0.5, 1, 0)
  mark <- if (pred == y_test[i]) "OK" else "X"
  cat(sprintf("  [%d %d] -> prob=%.3f  pred=%d  true=%d  %s\n",
              X_test[i, 1], X_test[i, 2], prob, pred, y_test[i], mark))
}

cat("\n==== Regression: Noisy Sine Curve ====\n")
# Demo data: simple regression problem (sine curve with noise)
X_reg <- matrix((0:39) / 40.0, ncol = 1)
set.seed(1)
y_reg <- sin(2 * pi * X_reg[, 1]) + rnorm(40, 0, 0.1)

split2 <- train_val_test_split(X_reg, y_reg, train_frac = 0.6, val_frac = 0.2, seed = 22)
Xr_train <- split2$X_train; yr_train <- split2$y_train
Xr_val   <- split2$X_val;   yr_val   <- split2$y_val
Xr_test  <- split2$X_test;  yr_test  <- split2$y_test

mlp_reg <- MLP$new(layer_sizes = c(1, 8, 1), activations = c("tanh", "linear"),
                    lr = 0.05, n_epochs = 300, task = "regression")
mlp_reg$fit(Xr_train, yr_train, Xr_val, yr_val)

cat(sprintf("Train RMSE:     %.3f\n", sqrt(mlp_reg$evaluate(Xr_train, yr_train))))
cat(sprintf("Val RMSE:       %.3f\n", sqrt(mlp_reg$evaluate(Xr_val, yr_val))))
cat(sprintf("Test RMSE:      %.3f\n", sqrt(mlp_reg$evaluate(Xr_test, yr_test))))
cat(sprintf("Train R2:       %.3f\n", mlp_reg$r2_score(Xr_train, yr_train)))
cat(sprintf("Val R2:         %.3f\n", mlp_reg$r2_score(Xr_val, yr_val)))
cat(sprintf("Test R2:        %.3f\n", mlp_reg$r2_score(Xr_test, yr_test)))

cat("\nRegression test predictions:\n")
for (i in 1:min(6, nrow(Xr_test))) {
  pred <- mlp_reg$predict(matrix(Xr_test[i, ], nrow = 1))
  cat(sprintf("  [%.3f] -> pred=%.3f  true=%.3f\n", Xr_test[i, 1], pred, yr_test[i]))
}
