13.8.9 The six architectures in code
Each builder returns a model assembled purely from the engine above. Sequential chains layers; Residual adds the skip; ConcatSkip implements DenseNet’s concatenation; UNet is a small custom module that manages its long skips.


Code
# "cba" stands for Conv-BatchNorm-Activation: a common combo in neural nets.
cba <- function(cin, cout, k = 3, s = 1, p = 1, act_fn = function() ReLU$new(), seed = 0) {
  Sequential$new(Conv2D$new(cin, cout, k, s, p, seed = seed), BatchNorm2D$new(cout), act_fn())
}

# DenseNet primitive: output = concat(x, block(x)) along channels.
ConcatSkip <- setRefClass("ConcatSkip", fields = list(block = "ANY", cx = "numeric"),
  methods = list(
    initialize = function(block_, ...) block <<- block_,
    forward = function(x, train = TRUE) {
      cx <<- dim(x)[2]
      h <- block$forward(x, train)
      abind_channels(x, h)
    },
    backward = function(gy) {
      d <- dim(gy)
      gskip <- gy[, 1:cx, , , drop = FALSE]
      gh <- gy[, (cx + 1):d[2], , , drop = FALSE]
      gskip + block$backward(gh)
    },
    params = function() block$params()
  ))

# 1) AlexNet: one of the first famous convolutional neural nets.
build_alexnet <- function() {
  Sequential$new(
    Conv2D$new(1, 16, 3, 1, 1, seed = 1), ReLU$new(), MaxPool2D$new(2, 2),
    Conv2D$new(16, 32, 3, 1, 1, seed = 2), ReLU$new(), MaxPool2D$new(2, 2),
    Flatten$new(),
    Dense$new(32 * 7 * 7, 64, seed = 3), ReLU$new(), Dropout$new(0.25),
    Dense$new(64, 10, seed = 4)
  )
}

# 2) ResNet: uses "residual" connections, allowing the network to "skip" layers
build_resnet <- function() {
  resblock <- function(ch, seed) {
    Sequential$new(
      Residual$new(Sequential$new(
        Conv2D$new(ch, ch, 3, 1, 1, seed = seed), BatchNorm2D$new(ch), ReLU$new(),
        Conv2D$new(ch, ch, 3, 1, 1, seed = seed + 1), BatchNorm2D$new(ch)
      )),
      ReLU$new()
    )
  }
  Sequential$new(
    Conv2D$new(1, 16, 3, 1, 1, seed = 1), BatchNorm2D$new(16), ReLU$new(),
    resblock(16, 10),
    MaxPool2D$new(2, 2),
    resblock(16, 20),
    MaxPool2D$new(2, 2),
    GlobalAvgPool$new(),
    Dense$new(16, 10, seed = 5)
  )
}

# 3) DenseNet: each layer gets inputs from all previous layers (via ConcatSkip)
build_densenet <- function() {
  dlayer <- function(cin, seed) Sequential$new(BatchNorm2D$new(cin), ReLU$new(), Conv2D$new(cin, 8, 3, 1, 1, seed = seed))
  Sequential$new(
    Conv2D$new(1, 16, 3, 1, 1, seed = 1), BatchNorm2D$new(16), ReLU$new(),
    ConcatSkip$new(dlayer(16, 10)),   # 16+8 = 24
    ConcatSkip$new(dlayer(24, 11)),   # 24+8 = 32
    ConcatSkip$new(dlayer(32, 12)),   # 32+8 = 40
    Conv2D$new(40, 20, 1, 1, 0, seed = 13), AvgPool2D$new(2, 2),
    GlobalAvgPool$new(), Dense$new(20, 10, seed = 14)
  )
}

# 4) EfficientNet: MBConv blocks with squeeze-and-excite
build_efficientnet <- function() {
  mbconv <- Sequential$new(
    Conv2D$new(16, 32, 1, 1, 0, seed = 10), BatchNorm2D$new(32), SiLU$new(),        # expand
    DepthwiseConv2D$new(32, 3, 1, 1, seed = 11), BatchNorm2D$new(32), SiLU$new(),   # depthwise
    SEBlock$new(32, r = 4, seed = 12),                                              # squeeze-excite
    Conv2D$new(32, 16, 1, 1, 0, seed = 13), BatchNorm2D$new(16)                     # project back
  )
  Sequential$new(
    Conv2D$new(1, 16, 3, 1, 1, seed = 1), BatchNorm2D$new(16), SiLU$new(),
    Residual$new(mbconv),
    MaxPool2D$new(2, 2),
    GlobalAvgPool$new(), Dense$new(16, 10, seed = 5)
  )
}

# 5) ConvNeXt: depthwise convolutions + layer normalization
build_convnext <- function() {
  block <- Sequential$new(
    DepthwiseConv2D$new(24, 7, 1, 3, seed = 2),
    LayerNorm2D$new(24),
    Conv2D$new(24, 96, 1, 1, 0, seed = 3), GELU$new(),
    Conv2D$new(96, 24, 1, 1, 0, seed = 4)
  )
  Sequential$new(
    Conv2D$new(1, 24, 4, 4, 0, seed = 1), LayerNorm2D$new(24),   # patchify
    Residual$new(block),
    GlobalAvgPool$new(), Dense$new(24, 10, seed = 5)
  )
}

# 6) UNet: encoder-decoder with long skip connections, adapted for classification.
UNet <- setRefClass(
  "UNet",
  fields = list(enc1 = "ANY", pool1 = "ANY", enc2 = "ANY", pool2 = "ANY", bott = "ANY",
                up2 = "ANY", dec2 = "ANY", up1 = "ANY", dec1 = "ANY", gap = "ANY", fc = "ANY",
                e1 = "ANY", e2 = "ANY"),
  methods = list(
    initialize = function(...) {
      enc1 <<- cba(1, 16, seed = 1)
      pool1 <<- MaxPool2D$new(2, 2)
      enc2 <<- cba(16, 32, seed = 2)
      pool2 <<- MaxPool2D$new(2, 2)
      bott <<- cba(32, 32, seed = 3)
      up2 <<- Upsample2x$new()
      dec2 <<- cba(32 + 32, 32, seed = 4)
      up1 <<- Upsample2x$new()
      dec1 <<- cba(32 + 16, 16, seed = 5)
      gap <<- GlobalAvgPool$new()
      fc <<- Dense$new(16, 10, seed = 6)
    },
    forward = function(x, train = TRUE) {
      e1 <<- enc1$forward(x, train)              # 16x28x28
      p1 <- pool1$forward(e1, train)              # 16x14x14
      e2 <<- enc2$forward(p1, train)              # 32x14x14
      p2 <- pool2$forward(e2, train)              # 32x7x7
      b <- bott$forward(p2, train)                # 32x7x7
      u2 <- up2$forward(b, train)                 # 32x14x14
      c2 <- abind_channels(u2, e2)                # 64x14x14
      d2 <- dec2$forward(c2, train)               # 32x14x14
      u1 <- up1$forward(d2, train)                # 32x28x28
      c1 <- abind_channels(u1, e1)                # 48x28x28
      d1 <- dec1$forward(c1, train)               # 16x28x28
      g <- gap$forward(d1, train)
      fc$forward(g, train)
    },
    backward = function(gy) {
      gg <- fc$backward(gy)
      gd1 <- gap$backward(gg)
      gc1 <- dec1$backward(gd1)
      gu1 <- gc1[, 1:32, , , drop = FALSE]; ge1_skip <- gc1[, 33:48, , , drop = FALSE]
      gd2 <- up1$backward(gu1)
      gc2 <- dec2$backward(gd2)
      gu2 <- gc2[, 1:32, , , drop = FALSE]; ge2_skip <- gc2[, 33:64, , , drop = FALSE]
      gb <- up2$backward(gu2)
      gp2 <- bott$backward(gb)
      ge2 <- pool2$backward(gp2) + ge2_skip
      gp1 <- enc2$backward(ge2)
      ge1 <- pool1$backward(gp1) + ge1_skip
      enc1$backward(ge1)
    },
    params = function() {
      ps <- list()
      for (m in list(enc1, enc2, bott, dec2, dec1, fc)) ps <- c(ps, m$params())
      ps
    }
  ))

BUILDERS <- list(
  "AlexNet" = build_alexnet,
  "ResNet" = build_resnet,
  "DenseNet" = build_densenet,
  "EfficientNet" = build_efficientnet,
  "ConvNeXt" = build_convnext,
  "U-Net" = function() UNet$new()
)

load_idx_images_at3 <- function(path, indices) {
  con <- gzfile(path, "rb"); on.exit(close(con))
  magic <- readBin(con, integer(), n = 1, size = 4, endian = "big")
  n <- readBin(con, integer(), n = 1, size = 4, endian = "big")
  rows <- readBin(con, integer(), n = 1, size = 4, endian = "big")
  cols_ <- readBin(con, integer(), n = 1, size = 4, endian = "big")
  buf <- readBin(con, raw(), n = n * rows * cols_)
  size <- rows * cols_
  lapply(indices, function(i) {
    base <- i * size
    px <- as.integer(buf[(base + 1):(base + size)]) / 255.0
    matrix(px, nrow = rows, ncol = cols_, byrow = TRUE)
  })
}

The TinyCNN (single conv layer + max-pool + dense head) and its training loop are reproduced from Chapter 12 so the comparison is honest and self-contained.


Code
# Simple explanations of a tiny convolutional neural network (CNN), for beginners.
# (Reproduced from Chapter 12, unchanged.)

conv2d <- function(image, kernel, stride = 1, padding = 0) {
  H <- nrow(image); W <- ncol(image); f <- nrow(kernel)
  if (padding > 0) {
    padded <- matrix(0.0, H + 2 * padding, W + 2 * padding)
    padded[(padding + 1):(padding + H), (padding + 1):(padding + W)] <- image
  } else padded <- image
  pH <- nrow(padded); pW <- ncol(padded)
  out_H <- (pH - f) %/% stride + 1; out_W <- (pW - f) %/% stride + 1
  output <- matrix(0.0, out_H, out_W)
  for (i in seq_len(out_H)) {
    ri <- (i - 1) * stride + 1
    for (j in seq_len(out_W)) {
      rj <- (j - 1) * stride + 1
      output[i, j] <- sum(padded[ri:(ri + f - 1), rj:(rj + f - 1)] * kernel)
    }
  }
  output
}

relu_2d <- function(fm) pmax(fm, 0.0)   # matrix first, or pmax() drops dim!

flatten <- function(fms) unlist(lapply(fms, function(fm) as.numeric(t(fm))))

softmax_v <- function(logits) { m <- max(logits); e <- exp(logits - m); e / sum(e) }

cross_entropy_v <- function(probs, y_onehot) -sum(y_onehot * log(pmax(probs, 1e-12)))

one_hot_v <- function(label, n_classes = 10) { v <- rep(0.0, n_classes); v[label + 1] <- 1.0; v }

accuracy_v <- function(y_true, y_pred) mean(y_true == y_pred)

fc_forward_v <- function(x, W, b) as.numeric(W %*% x) + b

fc_backward_v <- function(dout, x, W) {
  list(dx = as.numeric(t(W) %*% dout), dW = outer(dout, x), db = dout)
}

conv2d_backward_v <- function(d_out, image, kernel, stride = 1, padding = 0) {
  H <- nrow(image); W <- ncol(image); f <- nrow(kernel)
  if (padding > 0) {
    padded <- matrix(0.0, H + 2 * padding, W + 2 * padding)
    padded[(padding + 1):(padding + H), (padding + 1):(padding + W)] <- image
  } else padded <- image
  d_kernel <- matrix(0.0, f, f)
  d_padded <- matrix(0.0, nrow(padded), ncol(padded))
  out_H <- nrow(d_out); out_W <- ncol(d_out)
  for (i in seq_len(out_H)) {
    ri <- (i - 1) * stride + 1
    for (j in seq_len(out_W)) {
      rj <- (j - 1) * stride + 1
      g <- d_out[i, j]
      patch <- padded[ri:(ri + f - 1), rj:(rj + f - 1)]
      d_kernel <- d_kernel + patch * g
      d_padded[ri:(ri + f - 1), rj:(rj + f - 1)] <- d_padded[ri:(ri + f - 1), rj:(rj + f - 1)] + kernel * g
    }
  }
  d_image <- if (padding > 0) d_padded[(padding + 1):(padding + H), (padding + 1):(padding + W)] else d_padded
  list(d_kernel = d_kernel, d_image = d_image)
}

relu_2d_backward_v <- function(d_out, pre_relu) d_out * (pre_relu > 0)

max_pool2d_forward_cache_v <- function(feature_map, pool_size = 2, stride = 2) {
  H <- nrow(feature_map); W <- ncol(feature_map)
  out_H <- (H - pool_size) %/% stride + 1; out_W <- (W - pool_size) %/% stride + 1
  output <- matrix(0.0, out_H, out_W)
  switch_r <- matrix(0L, out_H, out_W); switch_c <- matrix(0L, out_H, out_W)
  for (i in seq_len(out_H)) {
    ri <- (i - 1) * stride + 1
    for (j in seq_len(out_W)) {
      rj <- (j - 1) * stride + 1
      block <- feature_map[ri:(ri + pool_size - 1), rj:(rj + pool_size - 1)]
      mi <- which(block == max(block), arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
      output[i, j] <- block[mi[1], mi[2]]
      switch_r[i, j] <- ri + mi[1] - 1; switch_c[i, j] <- rj + mi[2] - 1
    }
  }
  list(output = output, switch_r = switch_r, switch_c = switch_c)
}

max_pool2d_backward_v <- function(d_out, switch_r, switch_c, in_H, in_W) {
  d_in <- matrix(0.0, in_H, in_W)
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(d_out))) for (j in seq_len(ncol(d_out))) {
    r <- switch_r[i, j]; c <- switch_c[i, j]
    d_in[r, c] <- d_in[r, c] + d_out[i, j]
  }
  d_in
}

flatten_backward_v <- function(d_flat, shapes) {
  grads <- list(); idx <- 1
  for (s in shapes) {
    Hh <- s[1]; Ww <- s[2]; n <- Hh * Ww
    grads[[length(grads) + 1]] <- matrix(d_flat[idx:(idx + n - 1)], nrow = Hh, ncol = Ww, byrow = TRUE)
    idx <- idx + n
  }
  grads
}

TinyCNN <- setRefClass(
  "TinyCNN",
  fields = list(n_filters = "numeric", n_classes = "numeric", lr = "numeric", n_flat = "numeric",
                kernels = "list", biases_c = "numeric", W = "matrix", b = "numeric", cache_ = "ANY"),
  methods = list(
    initialize = function(n_filters = 4, n_classes = 10, lr = 0.05, seed = 42, ...) {
      set.seed(seed)
      n_filters <<- n_filters; n_classes <<- n_classes; lr <<- lr
      scale_k <- sqrt(2.0 / 9.0)
      kernels <<- lapply(seq_len(n_filters), function(k) matrix(rnorm(9, 0, scale_k), 3, 3))
      biases_c <<- rep(0.0, n_filters)
      n_flat <<- 14 * 14 * n_filters
      scale_w <- sqrt(2.0 / n_flat)
      W <<- matrix(rnorm(n_classes * n_flat, 0, scale_w), nrow = n_classes, ncol = n_flat)
      b <<- rep(0.0, n_classes)
      cache_ <<- NULL
      callSuper(...)
    },
    forward = function(image) {
      pre_relus <- list(); post_relus <- list(); pools <- list(); switch_rs <- list(); switch_cs <- list()
      for (k in seq_len(n_filters)) {
        conv <- conv2d(image, kernels[[k]], stride = 1, padding = 1) + biases_c[k]
        pre_relus[[k]] <- conv
        act <- relu_2d(conv)
        post_relus[[k]] <- act
        pc <- max_pool2d_forward_cache_v(act, pool_size = 2, stride = 2)
        pools[[k]] <- pc$output; switch_rs[[k]] <- pc$switch_r; switch_cs[[k]] <- pc$switch_c
      }
      flat <- flatten(pools)
      logits <- fc_forward_v(flat, W, b)
      probs <- softmax_v(logits)
      cache_ <<- list(image = image, pre_relus = pre_relus, post_relus = post_relus, pools = pools,
                       switch_rs = switch_rs, switch_cs = switch_cs, flat = flat, probs = probs)
      probs
    },
    backward = function(y_onehot) {
      c_ <- cache_
      d_logits <- c_$probs - y_onehot
      fcb <- fc_backward_v(d_logits, c_$flat, W)
      pool_h <- nrow(c_$pools[[1]]); pool_w <- ncol(c_$pools[[1]])
      shapes <- rep(list(c(pool_h, pool_w)), n_filters)
      d_pools <- flatten_backward_v(fcb$dx, shapes)
      for (k in seq_len(n_filters)) {
        d_act <- max_pool2d_backward_v(d_pools[[k]], c_$switch_rs[[k]], c_$switch_cs[[k]],
                                        in_H = nrow(c_$post_relus[[k]]), in_W = ncol(c_$post_relus[[k]]))
        d_conv <- relu_2d_backward_v(d_act, c_$pre_relus[[k]])
        d_bias <- sum(d_conv)
        cb <- conv2d_backward_v(d_conv, c_$image, kernels[[k]], stride = 1, padding = 1)
        kernels[[k]] <<- kernels[[k]] - lr * cb$d_kernel
        biases_c[k] <<- biases_c[k] - lr * d_bias
      }
      W <<- W - lr * fcb$dW
      b <<- b - lr * fcb$db
    },
    predict_one = function(image) { probs <- forward(image); which.max(probs) - 1L },
    predict_batch = function(images) sapply(images, function(img) predict_one(img))
  )
)

train_cnn <- function(model, X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, epochs = 5, batch_size = 20) {
  history <- list(train_loss = numeric(0), val_loss = numeric(0), val_acc = numeric(0))
  n <- length(X_train)
  for (epoch in seq_len(epochs)) {
    order_ <- sample(n)
    running_loss <- 0.0
    for (start in seq(1, n, by = batch_size)) {
      end_ <- min(start + batch_size - 1, n)
      for (i in order_[start:end_]) {
        probs <- model$forward(X_train[[i]])
        y_oh <- one_hot_v(y_train[i])
        running_loss <- running_loss + cross_entropy_v(probs, y_oh)
        model$backward(y_oh)
      }
    }
    train_loss <- running_loss / n
    val_preds <- model$predict_batch(X_val)
    val_loss <- mean(sapply(seq_along(X_val), function(i) cross_entropy_v(model$forward(X_val[[i]]), one_hot_v(y_val[i]))))
    val_acc <- accuracy_v(y_val, val_preds)
    history$train_loss <- c(history$train_loss, train_loss)
    history$val_loss <- c(history$val_loss, val_loss)
    history$val_acc <- c(history$val_acc, val_acc)
    cat(sprintf("    epoch %d/%d  loss=%.3f  val_acc=%.1f%%\n", epoch, epochs, train_loss, val_acc * 100))
  }
  history
}

cat("Chapter-12 baseline TinyCNN ready.\n")




13.8.12 Train, validate & test every model
We train each network on the identical split. The Chapter-12 CNN uses its own per-sample loop; the six advanced models share one mini-batch training loop with the Adam optimiser. We record parameter count, wall-clock training time, and test accuracy.

This cell does the heavy lifting — expect a few minutes. DenseNet and EfficientNet are BatchNorm-heavy and converge more slowly, so they benefit most from raising EPOCHS.



Code
count_params <- function(model) sum(sapply(model$params(), function(p) length(p$get())))

train_numpy <- function(model, epochs, bs, lr) {
  opt <- Adam$new(lr = lr)
  n <- dim(Xtr)[1]
  hist <- list(train_loss = numeric(0), val_acc = numeric(0))
  for (ep in seq_len(epochs)) {
    set.seed(ep)
    idx <- sample(n)
    tot <- 0.0
    for (s in seq(1, n, by = bs)) {
      e <- min(s + bs - 1, n)
      b <- idx[s:e]
      logits <- model$forward(Xtr[b, , , , drop = FALSE], train = TRUE)
      res <- softmax_cross_entropy(logits, ytr[b])
      model$backward(res$dlogits)
      opt$step(model$params())
      tot <- tot + res$loss * length(b)
    }
    val_logits <- model$forward(Xva, train = FALSE)
    va <- mean(apply(val_logits, 1, which.max) - 1 == yva)
    hist$train_loss <- c(hist$train_loss, tot / n)
    hist$val_acc <- c(hist$val_acc, va)
    cat(sprintf("    epoch %d/%d  loss=%.3f  val_acc=%.1f%%\n", ep, epochs, tot / n, va * 100))
  }
  hist
}

test_np <- function(model) {
  logits <- model$forward(Xte, train = FALSE)
  mean(apply(logits, 1, which.max) - 1 == yte)
}

results <- list(); histories <- list()

# --- 1. Train and test the simple Chapter-12 CNN baseline ---
cat("CNN (Chapter 12) ...\n")
set.seed(42)
cnn <- TinyCNN$new(n_filters = 8, n_classes = 10, lr = 0.05, seed = 42)
t0 <- Sys.time()
h <- train_cnn(cnn, X_train_l, y_train, X_val_l, y_val, epochs = EPOCHS, batch_size = BATCH)
dt <- as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs")
p12 <- 8 * 9 + 8 + (14 * 14 * 8) * 10 + 10
results[["CNN (Ch.12)"]] <- list(params = p12, test = accuracy_v(y_test, cnn$predict_batch(X_test_l)), time = dt)
histories[["CNN (Ch.12)"]] <- h$val_acc
cat(sprintf("    test_acc=%.1f%%  (%.1fs)\n\n", results[["CNN (Ch.12)"]]$test * 100, dt))

# --- 2. Train and evaluate each of the 6 advanced models ---
for (name in names(BUILDERS)) {
  cat(sprintf("%s ...\n", name))
  set.seed(0)
  model <- BUILDERS[[name]]()
  t0 <- Sys.time()
  hist <- train_numpy(model, EPOCHS, BATCH, LR)
  dt <- as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs")
  results[[name]] <- list(params = count_params(model), test = test_np(model), time = dt)
  histories[[name]] <- hist$val_acc
  cat(sprintf("    test_acc=%.1f%%  (%.1fs)\n\n", results[[name]]$test * 100, dt))
}

cat("Done.\n")




13.8.13 Results & comparison
Test accuracy, parameter count, and training time side by side, plus the validation-accuracy curves. (Absolute numbers depend on the subset size and EPOCHS; the relative behaviour is the interesting part.)


Code
order_ <- c("CNN (Ch.12)", "AlexNet", "ResNet", "DenseNet", "EfficientNet", "ConvNeXt", "U-Net")
order_ <- order_[order_ %in% names(results)]

cat(sprintf("%-14s%10s%10s%10s\n", "Model", "Params", "Test acc", "Time (s)"))
cat(strrep("-", 44), "\n")
for (m in order_) {
  r <- results[[m]]
  cat(sprintf("%-14s%10d%9.1f%%%10.1f\n", m, r$params, r$test * 100, r$time))
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(7, 4, 3, 1))

accs <- sapply(order_, function(m) results[[m]]$test * 100)
barcols <- c("#888888", rep("#2c7fb8", length(order_) - 1))
bp <- barplot(accs, names.arg = order_, col = barcols, ylim = c(0, 100), las = 2,
              ylab = "Test accuracy (%)", main = "Test accuracy on MNIST subset")
text(bp, accs + 3, sprintf("%.0f", accs), cex = 0.8)

plot(NULL, xlim = c(1, EPOCHS), ylim = c(0, 100), xlab = "Epoch", ylab = "Validation accuracy (%)",
     main = "Validation accuracy vs epoch")
palette_cols <- rainbow(length(order_))
for (i in seq_along(order_)) {
  m <- order_[i]
  lines(seq_along(histories[[m]]), histories[[m]] * 100, type = "o", col = palette_cols[i], pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
}
legend("bottomright", legend = order_, col = palette_cols, lwd = 1, cex = 0.6, ncol = 2, bty = "n")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))




13.8.14 What to take away

The plumbing is universal. Six very different networks were built from one small set of hand-written layers. Convolution + a few composition patterns (sequential, residual-add, dense-concat, encoder–decoder) is genuinely all modern vision architectures are made of.
Skip connections dominate. ResNet (add), DenseNet (concat) and U-Net (long concat) all revolve around routing information — and gradients — around blocks rather than only through them.
Efficiency ≠ accuracy on toy data. EfficientNet and ConvNeXt are designed to shine at ImageNet scale with heavy training; on a tiny MNIST subset with a handful of epochs their sophistication (SE gates, LayerNorm, large kernels) doesn’t get to pay off, and BatchNorm-heavy models need more epochs for their running statistics to settle. Raise TRAIN_PER_CLASS and EPOCHS to watch the gap change.
Parameters vs. accuracy. Note how few parameters DenseNet/EfficientNet use relative to AlexNet’s dense head — the whole point of the post-2015 architectures.

Try it yourself. (1) Push TRAIN_PER_CLASS=200, EPOCHS=15 and re-rank the models. (2) Give DenseNet a second dense block. (3) Turn the U-Net into a real segmentation demo by training it to reconstruct the digit mask instead of classifying. (4) Add a projection shortcut to ResNet so blocks can change width.

What you will learn
This chapter is built in four parts. You can read Part A on its own for the theory, or run the whole thing end‑to‑end.







Part
Content




A — Theory for dummies
Why plain RNNs forget, how the LSTM’s cell‑state highway and gates fix it, the math translated into plain English, and hand‑drawn architecture diagrams for the LSTM and every major variant (Peephole, GRU, BiLSTM, Stacked, Encoder–Decoder).


B — From scratch (R)
A real LSTM with forward pass and backpropagation‑through‑time written from nothing but base R. It genuinely trains on a signal and forecasts it.


C — Full pipeline from scratch (simulated data)
Reuse the Part B engine to train / validate / test / forecast in pure R, then compare a from‑scratch LSTM vs GRU on the same synthetic series.


D — Real data (rice prices)
The same from‑scratch LSTM on a monthly rice‑price series with oil & fertiliser covariates, using the standard series_to_supervised framing (no torch/keras) with Training / Validation / Test / Forecast RMSE.



Every code cell is explained line‑by‑line in the text around it.

title: Chapter 15: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Networks
text:
15.1 Overview
An LSTM is a smarter kind of RNN, built to fix the forgetfulness problem I mentioned. “LSTM” stands for Long Short-Term Memory, and the name is the whole idea: it can hold onto important information for a long time instead of letting it fade after a few steps.
Here’s the intuition. A plain RNN has one memory that gets completely overwritten at every step — so old information washes out fast. An LSTM adds a second, protected memory line (called the cell state) that runs straight through, like a conveyor belt. Information can ride along that belt untouched for many steps. The clever part is a set of gates — little valves that decide what gets added to the belt, what gets wiped off it, and what gets read out of it.
Think of it like keeping notes while reading a long book. The conveyor belt is your notebook. At each page you make three small decisions: cross out notes that no longer matter, jot down new important facts, and glance at the relevant notes to answer whatever you’re thinking about right now. Those three decisions are the three gates.
A Recurrent Neural Network (Chapter 14) reads a sequence one step at a time and keeps a single “memory” vector \(\mathbf{h}_t\) that it rewrites at every step:
\[\mathbf{h}_t = \tanh(\mathbf{W}\,[\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b})\]
The dummy version: imagine whispering a message down a long line of people. Each person re‑says it in their own words (\(\tanh\) squashes it a little every time). After 50 people the original message is mush. That “re‑squashing at every step” is mathematically the vanishing‑gradient problem — when the network learns, the correction signal has to travel backwards through all those \(\tanh\) squashes and gets multiplied down to almost zero. So an RNN simply cannot learn long‑range dependencies.

title: Chapter 15: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Networks
section: 15.2 The LSTM fix: add a memory highway
text:
15.2 The LSTM fix: add a memory highway
The LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) keeps the ordinary hidden state \(\mathbf{h}_t\) and adds a second line, the cell state \(\mathbf{C}_t\). Think of \(\mathbf{C}_t\) as a conveyor belt running straight across the top of the network. Information can ride the belt for hundreds of steps almost untouched — the only things allowed to change it are simple, learnable valves called gates.
There are three gates, each a little neural layer that outputs numbers between 0 and 1 (a \(\sigma\) / sigmoid), acting like a dimmer switch:










Gate
Symbol
Dummy meaning
“0 means…”
“1 means…”




Forget
\(\mathbf{f}_t\)
how much old memory to keep
erase it
keep all of it


Input
\(\mathbf{i}_t\)
how much new info to write
write nothing
write it all


Output
\(\mathbf{o}_t\)
how much memory to reveal now
stay silent
speak fully



Because the belt is updated by addition (not repeated multiplication/squashing), the learning signal can flow back across many steps without vanishing. That single design choice is the whole magic.
Let’s set up our tools and draw the difference.


Code
# --- Setup: set random seed, and define a consistent plotting style ---
SEED <- 42
set.seed(SEED)

par(mgp = c(2.2, 0.7, 0), las = 1)
cat("R", R.version.string, "\n")



Drawing Toolkits
Below three helpers are the only drawing primitives we need: - draw_box() draws a rectangle with a centred label (used for cells and gates). - draw_op() draws a circle for a pointwise operation — × (element‑wise multiply) or + (add). - draw_arrow() draws a directed arrow between two points.
Colours are fixed in the Cpal list so the green cell‑state highway, yellow gates, and red operations stay consistent across every figure.


Code
# ── Simple drawing kit: these are small helper functions for making our neural network diagrams.
#    You can think of these as LEGO pieces that draw _boxes_ (with text), _circles_ (for math ops),
#    and _arrows_ (to show connections). We also set standard colors so things always look the same.

# This list just stores colors for things in our diagrams:
# - cell: blue boxes for cells/memory
# - gate: yellow boxes for gates
# - op: red circles for math operations like add and multiply
# - state: green lines for memory highways
# - line: grayish lines for arrows/edges
# - act: purple for activation boxes (rarely used)
# - txt: text color (dark blue)
Cpal <- list(
  cell = "#E8F0FE", gate = "#FDE68A", op = "#FCA5A5", state = "#A7F3D0",
  line = "#334155", act = "#C4B5FD", txt = "#1E293B"
)

draw_box <- function(x, y, w, h, label, fc, cex = 0.9, bold = FALSE) {
  # Draws a rectangle ("box") with bottom-left corner at (x, y), width w, height h.
  rect(x, y, x + w, y + h, col = fc, border = Cpal$line, lwd = 1.5)
  text(x + w / 2, y + h / 2, label, cex = cex, font = if (bold) 2 else 1, col = Cpal$txt)
}

draw_op <- function(x, y, sym, r = 0.16, fc = NULL) {
  # Draws a small circle (used for things like "x" or "+" operations).
  symbols(x, y, circles = r, inches = FALSE, add = TRUE,
          bg = if (is.null(fc)) Cpal$op else fc, fg = Cpal$line, lwd = 1.5)
  text(x, y, sym, cex = 1.0, font = 2)
}

draw_arrow <- function(x0, y0, x1, y1, color = NULL, lw = 1.8) {
  # Draws an arrow from (x0,y0) to (x1,y1).
  arrows(x0, y0, x1, y1, length = 0.09, angle = 22,
         col = if (is.null(color)) Cpal$line else color, lwd = lw)
}

cat("drawing toolkit ready\n")




Diagram 1: Vanilla RNN


Code
# ── Diagram 1: Vanilla RNN (one fading memory) vs LSTM (extra C highway) ──

# The purpose of this code is to make two simple diagrams showing the difference between a normal
# (vanilla) RNN and an LSTM. Both diagrams show a sequence of "cells" passing information forward;
# the diagrams help explain why LSTMs remember things better.

par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))

# === First Diagram: Vanilla RNN (top plot) ===
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 11), ylim = c(0, 3), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     main = "Vanilla RNN — one memory line, re-squashed at every step", font.main = 2)
for (k in 0:3) {
  x <- 1 + k * 2.6
  draw_box(x, 1, 1.3, 1, "RNN\ncell", Cpal$cell, bold = TRUE)
  draw_arrow(x - 0.7, 1.5, x, 1.5)
  if (k < 3) draw_arrow(x + 1.3, 1.5, x + 1.9, 1.5, color = "#DC2626")  # memory fades
  text(x + 0.65, 0.5, bquote(x[.(k + 1)]))
  draw_arrow(x + 0.65, 0.75, x + 0.65, 1.0)
}
text(10.3, 1.95, "gradient\nfades", col = "#DC2626", cex = 0.8)

# === Second Diagram: LSTM (bottom plot) ===
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 11), ylim = c(0, 3), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     main = expression(bold("LSTM — a cell-state 'highway' " * C[t] * " carries memory almost untouched")))
for (k in 0:3) {
  x <- 1 + k * 2.6
  draw_box(x, 0.9, 1.3, 1.1, "LSTM\ncell", Cpal$cell, bold = TRUE)
  draw_arrow(x - 0.7, 1.15, x, 1.15)
  if (k < 3) draw_arrow(x + 1.3, 1.15, x + 1.9, 1.15)
  draw_arrow(x - 0.7, 2.4, x, 2.4, color = "#059669", lw = 3)
  if (k < 3) draw_arrow(x + 1.3, 2.4, x + 1.9, 2.4, color = "#059669", lw = 3)
  text(x + 0.65, 0.35, bquote(x[.(k + 1)]))
  draw_arrow(x + 0.65, 0.55, x + 0.65, 0.9)
}
text(0.15, 2.4, "C", col = "#059669", font = 2)
text(0.15, 1.15, "h", font = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


Reading the picture. In the RNN (top) there is a single red memory link; the learning signal has to squeeze through every cell and fades. In the LSTM (bottom) the thick green line \(C\) is the highway: it runs across the top and is only lightly edited at each cell, so memory — and gradients — survive.

title: Chapter 15: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Networks
section: 15.3 The math, one gate at a time
text:
15.3 The math, one gate at a time
At each step \(t\) the cell receives the new input \(\mathbf{x}_t\), the previous hidden state \(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}\), and the previous belt value \(\mathbf{C}_{t-1}\). It glues \(\mathbf{x}_t\) and \(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}\) together (written \([\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t]\)) and computes:
\[\mathbf{f}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_f\,[\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_f) \qquad \textbf{Forget gate}\] > “Looking at the new input and my last thought, what fraction of each memory slot should I keep?” Output is between 0 (drop) and 1 (keep).
\[\mathbf{i}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_i\,[\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_i) \qquad \textbf{Input gate}\] > “How much am I allowed to write into each memory slot right now?”
\[\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_t = \tanh(\mathbf{W}_g\,[\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_g) \qquad \textbf{Candidate}\] > “Here is the actual new content I’m proposing to write” (range \(-1\) to \(1\)).
\[\mathbf{C}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{C}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{g}}_t \qquad \textbf{Update the belt}\] > The key line. Keep a fraction \(\mathbf{f}_t\) of the old belt, then add a fraction \(\mathbf{i}_t\) of the new content. Notice it is an addition — that is why gradients don’t vanish.
\[\mathbf{o}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_o\,[\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_o) \qquad \textbf{Output gate}\] > “How much of the belt should I reveal as my answer this step?”
\[\mathbf{h}_t = \mathbf{o}_t \odot \tanh(\mathbf{C}_t) \qquad \textbf{Hidden state}\] > Squash the belt to \([-1,1]\) and let the output gate decide how much of it leaves the cell.
Symbols: \(\sigma\) = sigmoid (0→1 dimmer), \(\tanh\) = squash to \([-1,1]\), \(\odot\) = element‑wise multiply, \([\cdot,\cdot]\) = concatenate.

Diagram: Inside one LSTM Cell


Code
# ── Diagram 2: what happens INSIDE one LSTM cell ──
par(mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 11), ylim = c(0, 7), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
rect(1.3, 1.0, 1.3 + 8.4, 1.0 + 4.6, border = Cpal$line, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "#F8FAFC")
text(5.5, 5.9, "Inside one LSTM cell at time step t", cex = 1.1, font = 2)

# top green highway C: multiply by forget, then add new content
draw_arrow(0.2, 4.9, 3.5, 4.9, color = "#059669", lw = 3); draw_op(3.9, 4.9, "×")
draw_arrow(4.06, 4.9, 6.0, 4.9, color = "#059669", lw = 3); draw_op(6.4, 4.9, "+", fc = Cpal$state)
draw_arrow(6.56, 4.9, 10.6, 4.9, color = "#059669", lw = 3)
text(0.2, 5.25, expression(C[t-1]), col = "#059669"); text(9.9, 5.25, expression(C[t]), col = "#059669")

# bottom inputs h_{t-1}, x_t
draw_arrow(0.2, 1.7, 2.0, 1.7); text(0.2, 2.0, expression(h[t-1]))
text(0.2, 0.55, expression(x[t])); draw_arrow(0.45, 0.7, 2.0, 1.5)

# gate boxes
draw_box(2.1, 2.3, 1.0, 0.7, "σ\nforget f", Cpal$gate, cex = 0.7)
draw_box(3.4, 2.3, 1.0, 0.7, "σ\ninput i", Cpal$gate, cex = 0.7)
draw_box(4.7, 2.3, 1.0, 0.7, "tanh\ncand g~", Cpal$act, cex = 0.7)
draw_box(7.6, 2.3, 1.0, 0.7, "σ\nout o", Cpal$gate, cex = 0.7)

draw_arrow(2.6, 3.0, 3.9, 4.74)                       # forget -> x on highway
draw_op(5.05, 3.7, "×")                           # i * g
draw_arrow(3.9, 3.0, 5.05, 3.54); draw_arrow(5.2, 3.0, 5.05, 3.54)
draw_arrow(5.05, 3.86, 6.4, 4.74)                      # -> + on highway

draw_op(8.1, 3.7, "×")                            # o * tanh(C)
rect(8.9, 4.55, 8.9 + 0.9, 4.55 + 0.7, col = Cpal$act, border = Cpal$line, lwd = 1.3)
text(9.35, 4.9, "tanh", cex = 0.8)
draw_arrow(8.9, 4.9, 8.25, 3.86); draw_arrow(8.1, 3.0, 8.1, 3.54)
draw_arrow(8.1, 3.86, 8.1, 1.7); draw_arrow(8.1, 1.7, 10.6, 1.7)
text(9.9, 2.0, expression(h[t]))

lines(c(2.0, 2.0), c(1.5, 3.4), col = Cpal$line, lwd = 1.2, lty = 3)   # input bus
for (gx in c(2.6, 3.9, 5.2, 8.1)) lines(c(2.0, gx), c(3.4, 3.0), col = Cpal$line, lwd = 0.8, lty = 3)


Trace the flow. The green belt \(C_{t-1}\) enters top‑left, gets multiplied by the forget gate (×), then has the new content added (+) to become \(C_t\). New content is the input gate times the candidate (\(i \odot \tilde g\)). To produce the answer \(h_t\), the belt is squashed by \(\tanh\) and multiplied by the output gate. The dotted lines show that all four gates see the same input bus \([\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t]\).

title: Chapter 15: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Networks
text:
15.4 How many parameters?
For hidden size \(H\) and input size \(D\) each gate has a weight matrix of shape \((H,\,H+D)\) plus a bias of size \(H\). There are 4 gates, so:
\[\#\text{params} = 4\,\big[H(H+D) + H\big] = 4H(H+D+1)\]
A GRU has 3 such blocks instead of 4, and a Stacked/Bidirectional model multiplies this by the number of layers/directions. We will print exact counts from our own parameter arrays later.

title: Chapter 15: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Networks
text:
15.5 The variants

(a) Peephole connections
Let the gates also peek at the belt \(\mathbf{C}_{t-1}\) itself, not just \(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}\): \[\mathbf{f}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_f\,[\mathbf{C}_{t-1}, \mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_f)\] > the dimmer switches get to look at the conveyor belt directly. Helps with precise timing tasks.


(b) GRU — Gated Recurrent Unit (the lightweight cousin)
Merges the cell and hidden state and uses only two gates: update \(z\) and reset \(r\). \[\mathbf{z}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_z[\mathbf{h}_{t-1},\mathbf{x}_t]),\quad \mathbf{r}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_r[\mathbf{h}_{t-1},\mathbf{x}_t])\] \[\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t = \tanh(\mathbf{W}[\mathbf{r}_t\odot\mathbf{h}_{t-1},\mathbf{x}_t]),\quad \mathbf{h}_t = (1-\mathbf{z}_t)\odot\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{z}_t\odot\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t\] > one knob (\(z\)) blends old vs new memory; another (\(r\)) decides how much old memory to use when proposing new content. Fewer parameters, faster, often just as good.


(c) Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM)
Run one LSTM forward and another backward, then glue their hidden states together. \[\mathbf{h}_t = [\,\overrightarrow{\mathbf{h}}_t,\ \overleftarrow{\mathbf{h}}_t\,]\] > read the sentence left‑to‑right and right‑to‑left so each word is understood with full context. Great for classification/tagging where the whole sequence is known — but not for real‑time forecasting (you can’t see the future).


(d) Stacked (deep) LSTM
Feed the hidden‑state sequence of layer 1 as the input to layer 2, and so on. > layer 1 learns simple patterns, layer 2 learns patterns‑of‑patterns. More power, more compute, needs more data.


(e) Encoder–Decoder (seq2seq)
One LSTM encodes the input sequence into a context vector; a second LSTM decodes it into an output sequence. > the encoder “reads and summarises”, the decoder “writes”. This is the backbone of classic machine translation and multi‑step forecasting.


Diagram 3: the four structural variants side by side


Code
# ── Diagram 3: the four structural variants side by side ──
draw_gru <- function() {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 9), ylim = c(0, 5), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       main = "GRU cell — 2 gates, no separate cell state", font.main = 2, cex.main = 1.0)
  rect(0.8, 0.7, 0.8 + 7.4, 0.7 + 3.2, border = Cpal$line, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "#F8FAFC")
  draw_arrow(0.1, 3.3, 3.5, 3.3); text(0.1, 3.55, expression(h[t-1]), cex = 0.8)
  draw_box(2.0, 1.3, 1.0, 0.7, "σ\nreset r", Cpal$gate, cex = 0.65)
  draw_box(3.3, 1.3, 1.0, 0.7, "σ\nupd. z", Cpal$gate, cex = 0.65)
  draw_box(4.7, 1.3, 1.1, 0.7, "tanh\ncand", Cpal$act, cex = 0.65)
  draw_op(4.0, 3.3, "×"); draw_op(6.4, 3.3, "+"); draw_op(6.4, 2.2, "×")
  draw_arrow(4.16, 3.3, 6.24, 3.3); draw_arrow(6.56, 3.3, 8.3, 3.3); text(7.7, 3.55, expression(h[t]), cex = 0.8)
  draw_arrow(5.8, 1.65, 6.4, 2.04); draw_arrow(6.4, 2.36, 6.4, 3.14)
  text(0.1, 0.9, expression(x[t]), cex = 0.8); draw_arrow(0.35, 1.05, 2.0, 1.3)
}

draw_bilstm <- function() {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       main = "Bidirectional LSTM — read both ways, then concat", font.main = 2, cex.main = 1.0)
  for (k in 0:3) {
    x <- 1 + k * 2.1
    draw_box(x, 2.1, 1.1, 0.7, "LSTM →", Cpal$cell)
    draw_box(x, 1.0, 1.1, 0.7, "← LSTM", Cpal$state)
    text(x + 0.55, 0.55, bquote(x[.(k + 1)]), cex = 0.8)
    if (k < 3) {
      draw_arrow(x + 1.1, 2.45, x + 2.1, 2.45)
      draw_arrow(x + 2.1, 1.35, x + 1.1, 1.35, color = "#059669")
    }
    draw_box(x, 3.0, 1.1, 0.55, "concat", Cpal$gate, cex = 0.7)
    draw_arrow(x + 0.55, 2.8, x + 0.55, 3.0); draw_arrow(x + 0.55, 1.7, x + 0.2, 3.0)
  }
}

draw_stacked <- function() {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       main = "Stacked LSTM — layer 2 reads layer 1", font.main = 2, cex.main = 1.0)
  for (k in 0:3) {
    x <- 1 + k * 2.1
    draw_box(x, 0.9, 1.1, 0.7, "LSTM_1", Cpal$cell)
    draw_box(x, 2.1, 1.1, 0.7, "LSTM_2", Cpal$state)
    draw_arrow(x + 0.55, 1.6, x + 0.55, 2.1); text(x + 0.55, 0.45, bquote(x[.(k + 1)]), cex = 0.8)
    if (k < 3) {
      draw_arrow(x + 1.1, 1.25, x + 2.1, 1.25)
      draw_arrow(x + 1.1, 2.45, x + 2.1, 2.45)
    }
  }
}

draw_seq2seq <- function() {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 3.4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       main = "Encoder–Decoder (seq2seq)", font.main = 2, cex.main = 1.0)
  for (k in 0:2) {
    x <- 0.6 + k * 1.5
    draw_box(x, 1.2, 1.1, 0.7, "Enc", Cpal$cell)
    text(x + 0.55, 0.75, bquote(x[.(k + 1)]), cex = 0.8)
    if (k < 2) draw_arrow(x + 1.1, 1.55, x + 1.5, 1.55)
  }
  draw_arrow(5.0, 1.55, 5.7, 1.55, color = "#DC2626", lw = 2.5)
  text(5.35, 1.85, "context", col = "#DC2626", cex = 0.7)
  for (k in 0:2) {
    x <- 5.8 + k * 1.4
    draw_box(x, 1.2, 1.05, 0.7, "Dec", Cpal$state)
    text(x + 0.52, 2.4, bquote(hat(y)[.(k + 1)]), cex = 0.8); draw_arrow(x + 0.52, 1.9, x + 0.52, 2.2)
    if (k < 2) draw_arrow(x + 1.05, 1.55, x + 1.4, 1.55)
  }
}

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
draw_gru(); draw_bilstm(); draw_stacked(); draw_seq2seq()
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

title: Chapter 15: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Networks
section: 15.6.1 The standard multivariate framing: series_to_supervised + min-max scaling
text:
15.6.1 The standard multivariate framing: series_to_supervised + min-max scaling
We follow the widely-used recipe for multivariate LSTM forecasting (Brownlee’s “time series to supervised learning” pattern), but the model is our from-scratch ScratchLSTM — no torch, Keras, or TensorFlow:

Scale all 8 columns to \([0,1]\) with our own MinMax scaler.
Reframe so the 8 features at time \(t\!-\!1\) (rice price + 7 factors) are the inputs \(X\), and the rice price at time \(t\) is the target \(y\). This is a one-lag, many-to-one setup with timesteps = 1.
Split by fixed row counts into train / val / test and a final 6-month forecast hold-out.
Train ScratchLSTM(8 → 32 → 1) with the harness from Part C, then report Training / Validation / Test / Forecast RMSE separately, un-scaling with the classic “concatenate the other columns back, invert, keep column 0” trick.



Code
# -- Frame a time series as a supervised-learning table (lag features) --

# Convert a time series (or a sequence of multivariate observations) into a supervised
# learning data frame. This function creates lagged features for modeling: past observations
# as inputs (X) and future observations as outputs (y).
#
# Parameters:
#   data   : matrix of shape (n_samples, n_features). The original time series data.
#   n_in   : number of lag (input) time steps to include (e.g., n_in=1 creates features for t-1).
#   n_out  : number of future (output) time steps to predict (e.g., n_out=1 predicts t).
#   dropnan: whether to drop rows with any NA values (resulting from shifting operations).
#
# Returns: data frame where columns correspond to lagged inputs (t-n ... t-1) and forecast
# outputs (t ... t+n).
series_to_supervised <- function(data, n_in = 1, n_out = 1, dropnan = TRUE) {
  data <- as.matrix(data)
  n_vars <- ncol(data)
  n <- nrow(data)
  cols <- list()
  names_ <- c()

  # Create lagged input (X) sequences: for each lag i (from n_in to 1)
  for (i in n_in:1) {
    shifted <- rbind(matrix(NA, nrow = i, ncol = n_vars), data[1:(n - i), , drop = FALSE])
    cols[[length(cols) + 1]] <- shifted
    names_ <- c(names_, paste0("var", 1:n_vars, "(t-", i, ")"))
  }

  # Create output (y) sequences: current and future steps (from t to t+n_out-1)
  for (i in 0:(n_out - 1)) {
    shifted <- if (i == 0) data else rbind(data[(i + 1):n, , drop = FALSE], matrix(NA, nrow = i, ncol = n_vars))
    cols[[length(cols) + 1]] <- shifted
    label <- if (i == 0) paste0("var", 1:n_vars, "(t)") else paste0("var", 1:n_vars, "(t+", i, ")")
    names_ <- c(names_, label)
  }

  # Combine all columns and assign names
  agg <- do.call(cbind, cols)
  colnames(agg) <- names_
  agg <- as.data.frame(agg)

  # Optionally drop rows with any NA values (from shifting)
  if (dropnan) agg <- agg[stats::complete.cases(agg), ]
  agg
}

cat("series_to_supervised ready\n")




Code
# -- Scale to [0,1] with our MinMax, reframe, keep the columns we predict from/to --
cols_use <- c("Rice_price", "Crude_Oil", "DAP", "MP", "Rock_Phosphate", "TSP", "Urea", "VIX_Index")
values <- as.matrix(df[, cols_use])            # rice price MUST be column 1
storage.mode(values) <- "double"
n_feat <- ncol(values)                          # 8 features

scaler <- MinMax$new()                          # our from-scratch scaler (Part C)
scaled <- scaler$fit_transform(values)

reframed <- series_to_supervised(scaled, 1, 1)
# drop var2(t)..var8(t): predict ONLY rice price at time t, from all 8 factors at t-1
drop_idx <- (n_feat + 2):(2 * n_feat)
reframed <- reframed[, -drop_idx]
cat("reframed shape:", nrow(reframed), ncol(reframed), " (8 inputs + 1 target)\n")
head(reframed)



Data Splits


Code
# -- Fixed row-count splits: train / val / test + a 6-month forecast hold-out --
data_mat <- as.matrix(reframed)
n <- nrow(data_mat); N_FORECAST <- 6             # last 6 months = pure forecast test
train <- data_mat[1:260, ]                       # 260 train
val   <- data_mat[261:300, ]                     # 40  validation
test  <- data_mat[301:(n - N_FORECAST), ]        # remaining months = test
pred  <- data_mat[(n - N_FORECAST + 1):n, ]      # final 6 months = forecast

split_xy <- function(a) list(X = a[, 1:(ncol(a) - 1), drop = FALSE], y = a[, ncol(a)])
tr_s <- split_xy(train); va_s <- split_xy(val); te_s <- split_xy(test); pr_s <- split_xy(pred)

# reshape inputs to 3D [samples, timesteps=1, features] (ScratchLSTM reads (T, F) per sample)
to3d <- function(A) array(A, dim = c(nrow(A), 1, ncol(A)))
train_X <- to3d(tr_s$X); val_X <- to3d(va_s$X); test_X <- to3d(te_s$X); pred_X <- to3d(pr_s$X)
train_y <- tr_s$y; val_y <- va_s$y; test_y <- te_s$y; pred_y <- pr_s$y
cat("train", dim(train_X), "val", dim(val_X), "test", dim(test_X), "forecast", dim(pred_X), "\n")




Training


Code
# -- Train our ScratchLSTM (8 -> 32 -> 1) with the Part C harness --
model_d <- ScratchLSTM$new(input_size = n_feat, hidden_size = 32, seed = 42)
fit_d <- fit_model(model_d, train_X, train_y, val_X, val_y,
                    epochs = 120, lr = 0.01, patience = 15, seed = 0)
history_d <- fit_d$hist; ep_d <- fit_d$epochs_run
cat(sprintf("trained %d epochs | parameters: %d\n", ep_d, n_params(model_d)))




Plot Training and Validation Loss


Code
# -- Plot training vs validation loss (the classic log-loss curve) --
plot(history_d$train, type = "l", col = "steelblue", xlab = "epoch", ylab = "MSE (scaled)",
     main = "Rice-price ScratchLSTM - MSE loss per epoch",
     ylim = range(c(history_d$train, history_d$val)))
lines(history_d$val, col = "tomato")
legend("topright", legend = c("train", "val"), col = c("steelblue", "tomato"), lty = 1, bty = "n")




Evaluating each split — the inverse-scaling trick
Predictions come out on the \([0,1]\) scale. To read them in USD/tonne we glue each prediction back next to the other 7 (t-1) columns, run scaler$inverse_transform, and keep column 1 (rice price). Because min-max scaling inverts each column independently, the filler columns don’t affect the recovered price — they only make the array the right shape.


Code
# -- One helper reproduces Training / Validation / Test / Forecast RMSE --
rmse_report <- function(X3, y, name) {
  yhat <- predict_model(model_d, X3)                             # scaled prediction
  X2 <- matrix(X3, nrow = dim(X3)[1], ncol = dim(X3)[3])          # (samples, features)
  inv_yhat <- scaler$inverse_transform(cbind(yhat, X2[, -1, drop = FALSE]))[, 1]
  inv_y    <- scaler$inverse_transform(cbind(y,    X2[, -1, drop = FALSE]))[, 1]
  cat(sprintf("%s RMSE: %.3f\n", name, rmse_(inv_y, inv_yhat)))
  list(inv_y = inv_y, inv_yhat = inv_yhat)
}

invisible(rmse_report(train_X, train_y, "Training"))
invisible(rmse_report(val_X,   val_y,   "Validation"))
r_test <- rmse_report(test_X,  test_y,  "Test")
r_pred <- rmse_report(pred_X,  pred_y,  "Forecast")
inv_y_test <- r_test$inv_y; inv_yhat_test <- r_test$inv_yhat
inv_y_pred <- r_pred$inv_y; inv_yhat_pred <- r_pred$inv_yhat

# honest reference point: the naive "next = last" persistence baseline on the test slice
persist <- df$Rice_price[300:(n - N_FORECAST - 1)]
cat(sprintf("\n(persistence baseline on test RMSE: %.3f)\n", rmse_(inv_y_test, persist)))




Visualization Prediction


Code
# -- Visualise test predictions and the 6-month forecast --
test_dates <- df$Date[302:(302 + length(inv_y_test) - 1)]     # target dates for the test block
pred_dates <- df$Date[(n - N_FORECAST + 2):nrow(df)]           # last 6 target dates

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(test_dates, inv_y_test, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     main = "Test set - one-step-ahead", ylim = range(c(inv_y_test, inv_yhat_test)))
lines(test_dates, inv_yhat_test, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "tomato")
legend("topright", legend = c("actual", "ScratchLSTM"), col = c("black", "tomato"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

plot(pred_dates, inv_y_pred, type = "o", pch = 16, lwd = 2, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     main = "Final 6-month forecast", ylim = range(c(inv_y_pred, inv_yhat_pred)))
lines(pred_dates, inv_yhat_pred, type = "o", pch = 15, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "tomato")
legend("topright", legend = c("actual", "ScratchLSTM forecast"), col = c("black", "tomato"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2, pch = c(16, 15), bty = "n")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))




What Part D teaches

The professional multivariate pipeline — series_to_supervised framing, min-max scaling, fixed splits, and the concatenate-and-invert un-scaling — works with a hand-written R LSTM; no deep-learning framework is required.
We report Training, Validation, Test and Forecast RMSE separately, so over-fitting and regime shift are both visible.
Always sanity-check against persistence (“next ≈ last”): for near-random-walk prices it is a stiff baseline, and comparing to it tells you whether the LSTM is truly adding value.
To push further: increase the lag window (n_in > 1), predict log-returns instead of levels to tame the 2008-era regime shift, or forecast several months ahead with n_out > 1.

15.8 Exercises

Forget‑bias ablation. Set the forget‑gate bias to 0 in ScratchLSTM and retrain. Does the loss drop more slowly?
Stacked LSTM from scratch. Chain two ScratchLSTM cells (layer 2 reads layer 1’s hidden sequence) and back-prop through both. Does depth help on the rice data?
